#6555. Colliding Dwarf Planets Created a 'Cat's Tail' 1,000 Astronomical Units Long

Beta Pictoris (Î² Pictoris), a young main sequence star about 63 light years away, is known for having the first directly-imaged debris disk. Three planets in that disk have also been directly-imaged. One of them, Beta Pictoris c, is also the closest exoplanet to its star that has ever been directly imaged.

This is a composite image of of Beta Pictoris as seen in near infrared light. Beta Pictoris B is shown, the closest exoplanet to its star that's ever been directly imaged. Due to its proximity and other factors, it's an object of much observation and research. Image Credit: By ESO, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=5268432

Î² Pictoris is the subject of lots of research because of its youth, its proximity, its resolved debris-disk, and because its geometry makes it open to detailed observations. In particular, telescopes can get high-resolution side-views of its disk's structure, including its warped nature and its asymmetries. Astronomers have even found evidence of exocomets in the system.

In a paper published in 2024, researchers presented the JWST's first images of Î² Pictoris and its debris disk. "We report for the first time the presence of an extended secondary disk in thermal emission, with a curved extension bent away from the plane of the disk," the authors wrote. They called it a âcatâs tail,â and suggested that it was connected to other features found in the disk: a clump of carbon monoxide, a warp in the disk, and a "mid-infrared asymmetry detected on the southwest side of the disk."

Unusual features like the Cat's Tail, which extends for about 1,000 astronomical units, always pique the interest of researchers, who want to know how it was created. New research led by a University of Arizona scientist has figured out what created the unusual feature. The research is titled "Deep HST/STIS Coronagraphic Imaging of the Î² Pictoris Debris Disk: On the Scattered Light Component of the Catâs Tail," and is published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. The lead author is Arin Avsar, a PhD Candidate in planetary science in the Lunar and Planetary Laboratory at the UofA.

"The Î² Pictoris debris disk is a unique system where mid-infrared coronagraphic imaging with JWST/Mid-Infrared Imager (MIRI) revealed a new spatially resolved substructure known as the Catâs Tail," the authors write. "We present deep Hubble Space Telescope (HST)/Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) coronagraphic imaging of Î² Pic in scattered light," the authors add. Their Hubble observations were obtained in six epochs between 2012 and 2025, which they used to search for the cat's tail's scattered light.

The Î² Pictoris disk can be seen in scattered light, precisely because it's a dusty disk, and the dust scatters the light. The colour and the brightness of the scattered light reveals the properties of the dust, including the size of its grains, their porosity, and the dust's overall composition. Identifying those properties can explain where the dust came from.

"The Cat's Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies â think something like Pluto," lead author Avsar said in a press release. "Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while."

"We think the Cat's Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it's made of," Avsar explained. "It consists almost entirely of what we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they're quite black."

These panels show the cat's tail feature (white arrow) in visible light from the Hubble on the left, and in mid-infrared light from the JWST on the right. Image Credit: Arin M. Avsar et al 2026 ApJL 1010 L10

The Cat Tail's composition of organic refractory material is a clue to the objects that collided and created it. Both this research and the 2024 research show that the Cat's Tail is predominantly composed of porous organic refractory material. "In the solar system, organic refractory material best reproduces the red surface spectra of Kuiper Belt objects, most notably Pluto," the authors write. NASA's New Horizons found tholins, a type of refractory organic compound, on Pluto's surface, and on the surface of its companion, Charon. But tholins make up only a small proportion of Pluto's mass, not enough to create the Cat's Tail. "This points to organic material from the interior of the disrupted planetesimals as the likely origin of the organic refractory material seen in the Catâs Tail."

"This invites the question: do dwarf planets in exo-Kuiper Belts (like that of Î² Pic) contain enough organic material to create the Catâs Tail?" the researchers write. To answer that, they examined the amount of organics in the local ISM, which placed constraints in the amount available in the Beta Pictoris disk, where the colliding objects formed. They also examined the amount present in comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, an icy body visited by the ESA's Rosetta mission.

These measurements let the researchers calculate what the combined mass of the colliding objects must have been, in order to supply enough refractory material needed to create the tail.

"... we find that each parent body must have had a mass of â¼1â3 Ã 1021 kg to produce 2 Ã 1019 kg of organic refractory debris in the Catâs Tail," the authors write. That equates to a few percent of the mass of Earth's Moon, or about 1 to 3 times the mass of the dwarf planet Ceres. These amounts agree with the estimates in the 2024 paper that initially found the Cat's Tail.

This figure helps show how the JWST and the Hubble see things differently, and how their combined observations have a powerful symmetry. The top panel is an RGB image of the HST/STIS image presented in this work overlaid with the deconvolved F1550C image from the 2024 work. The bottom two images show a grayscale version of each dataset in the RGB image. They highlight the smooth/axisymmetric halo in the HST/STIS image in contrast to the complex substructures seen in the F1550C image. Image Credit: Arin M. Avsar et al 2026 ApJL 1010 L10

The researchers also calculated the sizes of the objects that collided. Assuming that they had bulk densities in line with the dwarf planets in our Solar System, the objects must have had radii between about 600km and 800 km. "The mass and radius range is similar to that of dwarf planets in the Kuiper Belt, like Charon and Makemake," the researchers explain.

One puzzling feature of the Cat's Tail is the size and porosity of its dust particles. They're micron-sized and very porous. "How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that's part of why we study this feature," Avsar said.

"It's possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that's how they became so porous," said co-author Kevin Wagner, an assistant research professor at the U of A Steward Observatory.

This animation shows how the Cat's Tail was created when two dwarf planets collided.

Aside from the Cat's Tail, the new Hubble observations also revealed a strange warp in Beta Pictoris' dust halo. "We also find a convex/concave morphological asymmetry in the outer halo of Î² Pic with HST/STIS," the authors write. This could be because of interactions with Beta Pictoris B, a giant gas planet that's about ten times as massive as Jupiter. "However, dedicated follow-up dynamical modeling is needed to confirm this," the authors conclude.

One of the reasons that planetary scientists are so intrigued by Beta Pictoris is because it holds clues to our own Solar System's past. It's like an analogue of our system, only much younger. While our system is about 4.6 billion years old, Beta Pictoris is only about 23 million years old. Early systems are far more chaotic than mature systems like ours, so looking at Beta Pictoris gives researchers a window into our own Solar System's past, when collisions were much more common.

Beta Pictoris, its disk, and its exoplanets are too fascinating to ignore. It will continue to the the subject of ongoing observations. When new, powerful telescopes like the ELT and the Giant Magellan Telescope come online in the next few years, it's certain that at some point they'll examine the Î² Pictoris system. Both telescopes will have the powerful capability of directly imaging exoplanets in greater detail.

These powerful telescopes may also dive deeper into the Cat's Tail, and determine why such an impact created such small, porous dust grains.

#6554. Has Substitution Culture Gone Too Far?

Guests are increasingly asking for their meals to be customized. These restaurants say it’s gone too far.

When Chanita Chayaluk decided to open her restaurant and wine bar Taan, she hoped “to showcase Thai food in Chicago in a different light,” she says. “The first [wave of] immigration of Thai people in Chicago was in the 1970s, and a lot of [Thai] food here still feels like it’s from that time.” In September, she opened with a menu including miang, a Northern Thai dish made with fermented tea leaves, and a whole, deep-fried fish in a fish-sauce caramel.

Another quirk of operating in Chicago? “We’re still pretty ‘Midwest nice,’” says Chayaluk. “We try to overaccommodate and appease the masses.” In the early days of service, guests made frequent requests for substitutions or accommodations due to preferences and dietary restrictions. “It would slow down service and speed, and that was not just affecting us, but the guest experience in many ways,” she says. With a small kitchen and staff, it was hard to keep up. “It just felt like we were Chipotle.” When a guest asked for green curry mussels “but without the mussels,” it was a turning point.

Chayaluk implemented a limited substitution policy at Taan, stating on Instagram that ingredients like fish sauce and shrimp paste are “the fabric that defines our cuisine,” and therefore, could not be removed from any dishes that include it.

A decade or so ago, substitution culture was generally frowned upon and derided. Recently, though, some restaurants report it bubbling back up—and in full force. There’s a swirl of factors that got us here: Lunch slop bowl spots primed customers to expect a detailed level of customization with their orders. Unreasonable Hospitality pushed an intensified “customer is always right” mentality. And influencers entering the food-review space have made criticism of anything—including a restaurant choosing not to honor certain dietary preferences—ripe for an immediate, viral takedown. Couple all of that with the fact that it is hard to keep a restaurant afloat these days, and you’ve got several operators giving in, whether to specific requests, or to altering their menus altogether (see also: the great de-spicification of menus.)

At the same time, restaurants like Taan and New York’s Ha’s Snack Bar—which proudly announces in its Instagram bio that everything contains fish sauce—are standing their ground.

For Lom Wong in Phoenix, Arizona, substitution and modification requests have ramped up after receiving national attention. Chef Yotaka “Sunny” Martin was recognized by the James Beard Awards last year, and the restaurant was named a Michelin Bib Gourmand in August. “[After the award,] we had more guests than we were used to picking things apart. They were asking us to modify dishes or not understanding our service style and why we weren’t coursing things in a European fashion,” says chef and co-owner Alex Martin. “[There is a] European distinction of what an award-winning restaurant looks like, so people equated that recognition with a white-tablecloth restaurant. We were just like, ‘Well, that’s not who we’ve ever been, and it’s never what our restaurant will ever be.’”

Like Taan, Lom Wong took to social media to set expectations, including that the restaurant would not “make substitutions simply to make a dish more familiar,” and that certain dishes might differ from Western expectations of them; beef might have gristle, fishes will be whole, and both choices are fully intentional. “Sunny is our guiding light of cultural context,” says Martin. “[She advises, considering if] changing something about a dish compromises the integrity of the dish.” For example, the mango salad can be ordered with the shrimp on the side, but the restaurant won’t remove beef or shrimp paste from dishes that necessitate them.

Chayaluk takes a similar approach at Taan; there is always a vegan, gluten-free option (currently a fried rice) that she describes as a “catchall” for those who can’t have other items on the menu. “We make sure that that dish is also really, really good and substantial; it’s not just an appetizer,” she says. “It’s not an afterthought.”

Staff at both restaurants are encouraged to uphold the boundaries, which both Chayaluk and Martin say are as much in place for protecting their staff’s peace as they are for ensuring quality control for guests. While there has been some backlash, the expectation-setting at the start of the meal (and before, thanks to the social media posts) has for the most part been taken well. “The way we explain [our policy] to guests is kindly saying we respect your preferences, but they’re your preferences,” says Martin, “and steering them toward dishes on the menu that might already align with those.”

#6552. No Comets Required? How the Growing Earth May Have Created Its Own Water

The origin of Earth's water is one of those foundational issues that explains our planet's habitability. The idea that water was delivered by comets and asteroids has been on the minds of planetary scientists for a long time. Both types of bodies, and especially comets, are known to have water, and both types are known to have crashed into Earth in large numbers during the planet's early ages.

But there's also a growing understanding that rocky planets form with a primordial envelope rich in hydrogen and helium that they acquire from their solar nebulae. Since water isâobviouslyâH2O, then Earth was born with substantial amounts of hydrogen, and all that's required was oxygen. Did that need to be delivered to Earth somehow?

Sort of, but not exactly, and new research shows why. It's titled "Dry pebble rain could have delivered water to Earth through hydrogen reduction of iron oxide," and it's published in Nature Geoscience. The lead authors are Susmita Garai, a graduate student in Earth and Planetary Sciences at the University of New Mexico, and Zachary Sharp, professor and director of Earth and Planetary Sciences at UNM.

"Looking out over a large body of water, it is hard to imagine that that water may have been produced 4 Â½ billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere, but it very well may have.â- Zachary Sharp, University of New Mexico.

"Water is vital to planet habitability. However, the sources of water for terrestrial planets and timing of delivery remain controversial," the authors write. There are timeline constraints for how this water could have been delivered by comets and asteriods. It has to take into account the giant impact that created the Moon, the Late Heavy Bombardment, and the abundance of certain elements in the Earth's mantle. It's difficult to fit delivery by comets and asteroids in with these constraints.

This illustration shows a young planet in its magma ocean phase. Terrestrial planets like Earth were entirely molten when they formed. It's possible that water was delivered to young planets by comets and asteroids during the magma ocean phase. Image Credit: Merikanto via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Volcanic_planet_4_r_1.png

If Earth's water didn't come from an external source and was generated locally, then it sidesteps these constraints. "Here we show experimentally how oceans of water can be produced within the high-temperature H2-rich atmosphere above a terrestrial planet growing by capture of millimetre-to-centimetre-size silicate pebbles," the authors write.

âPrevious ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites. Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism,â co-author Sharp explained in a press release. âIn order to evaluate the possibility of âpebbleâ rainâ being a source of water, we needed to construct and execute some very challenging high temperature experiments. Dr. Garaiâs efforts paid off mightily, as she found that water is produced in just minutes in the high temperature environment of the Early Earthâs atmosphere.â

When a protoplanet's mass exceeds about 0.3 Earth masses, chondrules and pebbles fall through the atmosphere slowly. For hours or even days, these pebbles are above their melting point and experience extensive FeO reduction. This removes the oxygen and releases it into the atmosphere to form water, leaving metallic iron. For this to happen, there needs to be a powerful reducing agent at high temperatures, and in this case, it's the heated hydrogen in the atmosphere.

"The gravitational potential energy released by settling pebbles directly heats the atmosphere, resulting in a steep atmospheric thermal gradient, and for large planets, very high temperatures at the surface." These temperatures can exceed 3,000 K (1650 C) and the pressure can exceed 200 bars (~197 sea-level pressure). A magma ocean also heats everything up from below.

"Together, these processes result in molten pebble rain onto the protoplanet surface, volatile loss from pebbles in the atmosphere and ingassing of hydrogen, helium and other volatiles into the magma ocean," the researchers write.

This paints a dramatic picture unlike anything a human being has ever witnessed. At the heart of it is a very young Earth in its magma ocean phase. It's a ball of molten rock, to which an atmosphere nothing like the modern atmosphere clings. Falling through that atmosphere is a rain of molten pebbles, material that's coalesced out of the solar nebula, drawn by Earth's increasing mass to accrete onto the planet's hellish surface.

This figures show how molten pebbles rained onto Earth's surface, falling through the atmosphere and off-gassing volatiles, hydrogen and helium among them. Some of the hydrogen and helium escapes, and some in-gasses into the magma ocean. Image Credit: Garai et al. 2026. NatGeo

The researchers tested this scenario by running some high-temperature laboratory experiments that came as close to the hellish conditions in Earth's Hadean eon as possible. "To quantify the amounts and the kinetics of iron reduction in pebbles settling in through a nebular atmosphere, we conducted a series of experiments in which mafic and ultramafic silicates were melted in He and H2 gas streams," the authors explain. Mafic and ultramafic are the two main categories of igneous rocks, both rich in iron and magnesium.

This image illustrates some of the lab work in the study. It shows an experimental apparatus heating silicate rock samples. Garai et al. 2026. NatGeo

The researchers heated silicate rock samples to between 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius in streams of hydrogen, and separately in streams of helium. The experiments lasted between 15 minutes and three hours. The conditions mimicked the time in Earth's growth where it was massive enough to attract a rain of pebbles and was also massive enough to have a hydrogen-rich atmosphere, super-heated and highly pressurized. The moving streams of hydrogen and helium mimicked the pebbles movement through that atmosphere.

The results showed that in the hydrogen, almost 80% of the iron oxide was converted to metallic iron, producing water vapour as a result. In the helium, the same reaction didn't occur.

The efficiency of the reduction depends on the metal fraction in the pebbles, which the researchers calculated. "Partial reduction of pebble FeO at these efficiencies yields prodigious amounts of water," they write. "At peak efficiency, several hundred ocean masses of water are produced from the A composition, and tens of ocean masses from the B composition." The A and B compositions come from previous research.

These panels show how many oceans worth of water is produced by pebbles with with different compositions and different iron concentrations. Image Credit: Garai et al. 2026. NatGeo

"We had suspected and hoped that we would produce iron metal and water in our reduction experiments, but we really had no way of knowing how fast and how much. We were quite surprised to find that extrapolation of our work suggests that hundreds of oceans worth of water were likely produced in this way. Looking out over a large body of water, it is hard to imagine that that water may have been produced 4 Â½ billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere, but it very well may have,â said Sharp.

The idea that Earth's water came from comets and asteroids was always a little shaky, though still compelling. This research shows a different way that Earth could've acquired its life-giving water. The results may also extend to other worlds around other stars, and even to our neighbour Mars.

âThe idea of pebble accretion is still relatively new. Itâs only been around for the last decade. But it seems to solve many problems that exist with the existing paradigm for planet formation,â Sharp said. âAnd now we see that it also can explain why our planet is habitable. By extension, it is reasonable to expect that other Earth-sized bodies circling other stars would also have water and possibly life.â

This work is early proof that the basic mechanism is possible. But as for how much of Earth's water actually stemmed from this, that needs more research. "The net water gain depends strongly on the amount of produced water extracted by exhaust to the nebula," the researchers write. "Although subsequent water loss by atmospheric escape is possible, water produced during pebble rain represents an early and fundamental step in the evolution of a habitable planet."

It's still possible, for instance, that other processes also played a role, and even that comets and asteroids did deliver some of our planet's water.

The source of Earth's water will remain an ongoing subject of research. Over time, the picture will become clearer.

#6551. Inside the New D.C. Restaurant That Only Sells Five Curry Steak Frites Every Night

In a Georgetown alleyway, Alfie’s serves northern Thai dishes that are built around local ingredients

The hottest new spot in Washington, D.C. focuses on the traditional heat-packed cooking methods of northern Thailand, while still using local ingredients from around the DMV. Alfie’s, from chefs Justin Ahn and Alex McCoy, started as a pop-up in Petworth in 2017 before traveling around the world, serving diners in New York and London. This year, the restaurant put down permanent roots in a Georgetown alleyway. The co-owners led us through a day in the new kitchen, preparing everything from hand-cut green papaya in som tam salad to the limited-quantity Thai steak frites with a massaman curry peppercorn sauce.In the video, the kitchen team breaks down rib-eye steaks for their take on a steak au poivre, which they only make five of each night. The steaks are carefully seared for each order, with the au poivre massaman curry sauce is finished in the pan with the leftover beef fat. Classic “bar fries” are served up with the massive 26-ounce rib-eye.

Elsewhere in the kitchen, another chef carves green papayas. The irregular slices of papaya get tossed in a funky, spicy dressing for each order. Ko calls it the “most labor intensive dish on the line;” each order is carefully mixed with fresh tomatoes, peanuts, and a palm syrup and tamarind-heavy dressing. A rich pork belly curry is simmering in the background. Gaeng hung lay (a traditional northern Thai curry) cooks down large pieces of pork belly to get that fatty layer, with pickled garlic and pineapple balancing out the rich flavors of curry paste, tamarind, and fish sauce.

Right before service, the chefs begin prepping herbs and sticky rice that has been soaking overnight and is quickly steamed for that malleable, glutinous texture. McCoy talks about how being a chef is more of a lifestyle than a job, but there’s immense payoff when you get to see diners enjoy your hard work every night. He hopes that Alfie’s will become a place where “you can just forget where you are, have a good time, and just lose yourself in the experience and the food.”

Watch the kitchen team at Aflie’s cook classic Thai dishes and fusion plates like curry steak frites in this episode of Now Open.

Members of the same people who settled Easter Island also discovered Hawaii, a new study finds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Native Hawaiians and Easter Islanders genetically descend from the same "ultravoyager" Polynesian group that crossed vast distances of ocean to reach these remote islands, a new study finds.

Easter Island (also known as Rapa Nui) and Hawaii are part of Polynesia, a group of more than 1,000 islands spread over an area of the Pacific Ocean roughly equal to the areas of North and South America combined. Hawaii and Easter Island are the farthest of these isles from each other, at about 4,500 miles (7,200 kilometers) apart — around the distance from San Francisco to Lima, Peru.

The researchers discovered the connection by analyzing the genomes of 1,050 modern individuals across Polynesia, including 317 Native Hawaiians and 12 Easter Islanders. "Each person's genome contains genetic code from both parents, and from all four grandparents, and their parents, and so on," study co-author Alexander Ioannidis, a computational geneticist at Stanford University, told Live Science. "Each genome encodes an enormous number of ancestors. So with even a few individuals, we can get information about an enormous number of people from each island."

Specifically, the scientists compared the length of chromosomal segments shared among people from different islands. The longer these shared segments are between two people, the more recently they shared a common ancestor.

Even though Hawaii and Easter Island are far-flung, the researchers discovered that the Indigenous people of Hawaii and Rapa Nui are the most genetically related to one another. The team reported its findings Oct. 8 in the journal Science.

"This was really shocking at first — these islands are so distant from one another," Ioannidis said.

The scientists found that Hawaii and Easter Island were likely both settled by members of a single "ultravoyager" culture from the Mangareva islands, about 3,440 miles (5,530 km) southeast of Hawaii and 1,600 miles (2,600 km) west of Easter Island. (In 2020, the researchers found that members of this ultravoyaging group had mixed with Indigenous people in what is now Colombia, although it's unclear if this partnering occurred on an island or on the continent.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Once you know there was this extremely capable long-distance ultravoyaging culture capable of reaching one of these islands, having it reach the other makes more sense," Ioannidis said.

The area near Mangareva, including the Austral Islands, the Society Islands, the Marquesas Islands, and the Tuamotu Archipelago, "spans an area the size of Europe," Ioannidis said. "Sailing in-between these islands would have required skilled navigation. So it makes sense that developing such long-distance navigation skills would have ultimately helped people settle far-off Easter Island and Hawaii."

All in all, these genetic findings suggest the ancestors of Native Hawaiians and Easter Islanders shared some time together as a common group after splitting away from the population of ancient Mangareva. Some members of this group then went on to settle Hawaii, and others from this Mangareva group voyaged to Easter Island.

This new genetic data linking Hawaii, Easter Island and Mangareva "agrees very well with what we see archaeologically," Patrick Kirch, an archaeologist at the University of Hawai'i at Manoa who did not take part in this research, told Live Science. "It gives scientists a lot of confidence when independent lines of evidence from different disciplines give similar results."

The researchers also investigated the effects of genetic bottlenecks that resulted when these islands were settled by small numbers of people — phenomena known as "founder effects."

"If you have a rare genetic trait that happens to occur in this small number of individuals, if this small population grows rapidly, this trait can go on to show up in a high percentage of the resulting population," Ioannidis said. "So if a rare genetic variant once only affected a few people, it can start affecting a decent number of individuals."

The scientists found that Native Polynesian populations examined in the study often experienced a compounding set of founder effects over time. This is because islands settled by a few people then went on to send out small groups to settle other islands, and so on.

Previous research has looked at the founder effects in groups of European descent, such as the Amish, Finns and Ashkenazi Jews, resulting in standard screenings for certain genetic conditions in these groups.

The new study revealed that an even stronger founder effect has been overlooked among Native Hawaiians, with founder effects more than 10 times larger than in those European groups.

"The founder effect doesn't just reflect genetic diversity, but also cultural and linguistic diversity," Kirch said. "It probably helps explain why the cultures of eastern Polynesia all share a lot in common — they all trace to one central group."

These findings not only shed light on Polynesians' past, but also their current health. The researchers found that three genetic variants that are exceedingly rare among the global population — linked with dislocated lenses in the eyes, progressive vision loss, and kidney failure — are carried by 2 to 3% of the eastern Polynesians they studied.

"There should be a lot more resources going into learning more about gene variants of potential clinical significance among this population of Native Hawaiians, which is twice as large as the U.S. Amish population," Ioannidis said. "There are really opportunities for precision health here."

Shanks, C., Huang, E. C., Thomassin, C., Emde, A., Rodière, V., Moraga, M., Sandoval, K., Merriman, T., Pascart, T., Moreno-Estrada, A., Castel, S. E., Fox, K., & Ioannidis, A. G. (2026). Message in a bottleneck: Nested founder effects from French Polynesia to Rapa Nui and Hawaiʻi. Science, 394(6820), 216–221. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aec7662

#6549. A Brief-ish History of METI. Part II: From Interplanetary to Interstellar

Welcome back to our ongoing series on the Brief-ish History of METI, where we examine the rise, development, and possible implications of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence. In our first installment, we explored some of the foundational principles and how METI emerged as a possible answer to the "SETI Paradox." In a Universe where everyone is listening, and no one is broadcasting, should we as a species take the first step?

Naturally, this subject has sparked controversy and heated debate. In a Universe so vast and filled with so many unknowns and possibilities, is it wise to announce ourselves to potential alien civilizations? If we assume only 1 in 100 are hostile, what would be the consequences of sending a message saying, "Here we are!"? On the other hand, if we choose to remain silent and only listen to the cosmos, could we be missing out? By imposing isolation on ourselves, might we be damning ourselves to extinction?

Alas, the debate over the ethics of METI is far from over and will likely continue until (dare we say it?) we make contact someday. But that's a discussion for another installment. In the meantime, we'll continue our examination of the important milestones that led to METI as a distinct field of study. And in the midst of all that, we will be looking at the luminaries who were chiefly responsible for advancing it.

By the latter half of the 20th century, SETI shifted from a relatively obscure pursuit carried out largely by independently wealthy individuals to a serious scientific endeavor. With advances in rocketry and spaceflight, and the launch of national space programs, interest in the possibility of extraterrestrial life surged again. Rather than being fueled by science fiction and scientific inaccuracies (the misinterpretation of Schiaparelli's "canali"), the fascination was fueled by questions of what humanity might find on other worlds.

Cornell Professor and SETI pioneer Frank Drake standing in front of the 25-meter Howard E. Tatel Radio Telescope at the Green Bank Observatory. Credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF

This, in turn, led to experiments designed to test the capabilities of modern technology and perhaps make contact with other intelligent beings. A prime example is The Morse Message, which scientists at the Evpatoria Planetary Radar (EPR) center in Crimea carried out between November 19th and 24th, 1962. Using the facility's RT-70 radio telescope, the science team transmitted a Morse Code signal toward Venus. The message included the letters M-I-R (Mir, the Russian word for "peace") followed by "Lenin" and "USSR."

The message's main purpose was not to contact an intelligent civilization, but to test the radar station. The signals reflected off Venus's surface and were received back on Earth about four and a half minutes after transmission. Nevertheless, this experiment occured at a time when Venus was still thought to be potentially habitable, with many scientists believing that Venus' dense cloud cover (which obscured its surface) was due to heavy precipitation.

A few months later (December 14th, 1962), the Mariner 4 probe made the first detailed measurements of the planet's surface temperature. In the years that followed, multiple Soviet probes and landers revealed the true extent of Venus' hellish conditions: a carbon dioxide atmosphere, sulfuric-acid rain, and the hottest surface temperatures in the Solar System. This forever dispelled the idea that Venus could be a watery planet covered in bogs and oceans.

More importantly, it was also during this time that a transition occured in METI, reflecting a similar transition with SETI. Rather than listening or messaging neighboring planets for signs of life (on behalf of one nation), efforts in the latter half of the 20th century would reach interstellar space. Between 1999 and 2015, the EPR center played a vital role in METI by providing the necessary communications infrastructure for multiple publicly funded experiments.

While the Cold War Era added impetus to SETI and METI efforts, with both superpowers seeing a strategic advantage in making contact first, the scientific motivation reflected a broader, more universal awareness, with messages sent on behalf of all humanity.

When it comes to the pioneering work that made the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) a legitimate scientific field, few people were more integral than Frank Drake. Born in Chicago in 1930, Drake showed an early interest in science and later pursued a degree in astronomy at Cornell University. His interest in extraterrestrial life was reinforced by a 1951 lecture by Russian-American astronomer Otto Struve. One of the most distinguished and prolific astronomers of the mid-20th century, Struve was an early SETI advocate and greatly raised its international prestige.

After receiving a B.A. in Engineering Physics, Drake served briefly in the Naval Reserve before attending graduate school at Harvard University. By 1955, he received an M.S. and Ph.D. in astronomy. From 1958 to 1963, Drake began his career as a radio astronomer with the National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO) in Green Bank, West Virginia. There, he studied radio emissions from the Solar System's planets using the GBT, as well as those coming from the center of the Milky Way.

Drake was also deeply involved in the development of the Arecibo Observatory, which began construction in 1960, and helped extend its capabilities to include radio astronomy. Originally, the observatory was designed for ionosphere studies and to help track incoming missiles in the event of nuclear war. A year before Arecibo began construction, Drake obtained the approval of Otto Struve (then director of the NRAO) to begin humanity's first true SETI experiment.

The project began observations in 1960, using the NRAO 26-meter radio telescope at the Greenbank Observatory in West Virginia to listen for possible signals from Tau Ceti and Epsilon Eridani - two Sun-like stars located 12 and 10.5 light-years from Earth (respectively). While the project did not detect any extraterrestrial signals, it garnered international attention and drew the attention of many prominent scientists. This included Carl Sagan, who met Drake a year later at the first SETI symposium, and the two began a lifelong collaboration.

It was at this symposium, held at the Greenbank Observatory, that Drake unveiled his famous equation for estimating the number of extraterrestrial civilizations (ETCs) that humanity could communicate with in our galaxy at any given time: The Drake Equation. Rather than a scientific equation or method for calculating the existence of ETI, Drake created it as a thought experiment to summarize the challenges SETI researchers face.

In essence, knowing the number of civilizations (N) meant knowing all the parameters, the most important of which was how long civilizations could broadcast before going extinct (L). At the time, scientists knew that all of these parameters, except for the first (the average rate of star formation in the Milky Way), were subject to immense uncertainties. Nevertheless, the equation remains foundational to SETI and is considered the second-best known equation in human history (the first being Einstein's equation for Special Relativity (E=mc2)

Illustration of the Drake Equation (Credit: NOIRLab/AURA/NSF/P. Marenfeld)

After completing what was arguably humanity's first true SETI experiment, Drake began work on what would become humanity's first true METI effort: The Arecibo Message. Work began in the early 1970s, as Frank Drake organized a campaign to compose a message to be broadcast via Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305-meter (1000-foot) antenna.

The message was transmitted on November 16th, 1974, at 2380 MHz with an effective bandwidth of 10 Hz and a raw carrier power of 450 kilowatts (kW). However, Arecibo's huge dish focused that energy into an incredibly narrow, directional beam that magnified its intensity exponentially, making it equivalent to a 20-gigawatt omnidirectional broadcast. This meant any radio antenna in the galaxy could detect the message, provided it was about the same size as Arecibo.

The total broadcast lasted less than three minutes and was directed at Messier 13 (M13), a globular star cluster located about 25,000 light-years from Earth. This cluster contains 300,000 to 500,000 stars and spans 145 to 165 light-years in diameter. Because of the number of stars and the cluster's age (an estimated 11.65 billion years), it was considered a likely place for an extraterrestrial civilization.

Drake composed the message with help from Carl Sagan and other prominent astronomers, who arranged it using prime numbers because they believed this would make it easier for an ETC to decode. It consisted of a 1679-binary-digit picture (210 bytes), the product of two prime numbers, arranged rectangularly into 73 lines of 23 characters per line (also prime numbers). The binary digits (ones and zeroes) were transmitted via frequency shifting at 10 bits per second.

The decoded message was a simple pictograph depicting a series of scientific, geographical, biological, and astronomical information in different colors. These included:

The legacy of the Arecibo Message is comparable only to that of Project Ozma, as both experiments are recognized as humanity's first true attempts to find ETI. The message also became the subject of a hoax in 2001, known as the "Arecibo Answer." Near the Chilbolton telescope in Hampshire, UK, an imprint was found in a crop field that was a near-replica of the original message, using the same 73 x 23 grid pattern and most of the same chemical data.

However, the section on the elements of DNA substituted silicon for carbon, implying silicon-based life, and the DNA diagram was rewritten. The image of a human body was also replaced with a figure with a bulbous head and enlarged eyes. A system of nine planets was also depicted, but with emphasis placed on the 3rd, 4th, and 5th planets. The Arecibo telescope was replaced with a replica of a crop circle found in the same field a year earlier, and the transmitter's diameter was altered.

These align with common science fiction tropes about silicon-based extraterrestrials and urban myths about "greys" or "little green men." The medium, a burnt crop circle, is also a common hoax technique, meant to resemble burn marks from a landing craft. The SETI Institute issued a statement saying that the crop formation was a hoax, undoubtedly perpetrated by the same people who had made crop circles in the same area during the previous two years.

"The crop circles are decorative, impressive, and provocative, but not informative," they wrote. "We can expect better from true extraterrestrial intelligence."

By the 1970s, SETI and METI efforts had matured considerably, with developments in one field mirroring those in the other. Beyond the Arecibo Message, this decade saw the first (and, to date, greatest) attempts to send physical messages into space, a collaborative effort led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan: the Pioneer Plaques and Voyager Golden Records. Stay tuned!

"The impact of the cosmological constant on past and future star formation," Sorini, D. et al. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, vol. 535, no. 2 (2024) -"A New Empirical Constraint on the Prevalence of Technological Species in the Universe," Frank, A. & Sullivan, W. T. Astrobiology, vol. 16, no. 5 (2015)

Arecibo (SETI 101: Core Concepts & Projects) - The SETI Institute

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon. He lives in beautiful British Columbia with his wife and family. For more information, check out his website.

#6548. The 38 Best Restaurants in Barcelona, According to a Local Food Guide

From local Catalan cuisine to a burgeoning global food scene, here are the best meals in Barcelona right now

From Barcelona’s towering churches and bustling avenues to the sun-drenched beaches and idyllic plazas, it’s obvious why this city captures visitors’ hearts. You can also eat incredibly well here, and often for not very much money — though Barcelona loves a tasting menu and the World’s 50 Best Restaurant list awarded Disfrutar the No. 1 spot last year. Despite Barcelona’s famed cuisine, it’s also easy to have a downright disappointing meal if you settle for any old paella-slinging bar along Les Rambles (known in Spanish as La Rambla) or La Barceloneta. (Tip: If a restaurant has to pay someone to stand outside and hassle pedestrians, the food isn’t worth it.)

Start with some classic tapas and paella (both great but neither entirely Catalan) and be sure to seek out local gems like bittersweet vermouth, seasonal seafood, and homestyle Catalan cuisine. But after writing and revising this list for nearly a decade, I have to insist you don’t overlook the city’s burgeoning global cuisines; save room for Calabrese paninis, Northeast Asian sharing plates with natural wines, towering fried chicken sandwiches, South Indian fish stews, and nose-to-tail yakitori.

We update this list quarterly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing Barcelona dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in euros), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in October 2026: Lluritu, a Mediterranean marisquería with three locations across the city; a parallel universe of Catalan culinary history in a former water bottling plant at Franca; and the trendy modern Catalan cuisine of Manda Huevos.

Sam Zucker is a freelance writer, photographer, filmmaker, travel Instagrammer, and gastronomic tour guide in Barcelona. He has contributed to Monocle, National Geographic’s “48 Hours” guides, Culture Trip, and Vice Travel, among others.

From Barcelona’s towering churches and bustling avenues to the sun-drenched beaches and idyllic plazas, it’s obvious why this city captures visitors’ hearts. You can also eat incredibly well here, and often for not very much money — though Barcelona loves a tasting menu and the World’s 50 Best Restaurant list awarded Disfrutar the No. 1 spot last year.
