#6539. Simple-Is-Best Stuffing

More than a decade after Victoria Granof introduced this classic Thanksgiving stuffing recipe, it remains a staff and fan favorite. As former test kitchen director Carla Lalli Music puts it, it’s “everything you want about stuffing—straight down the middle.”

The recipe earns its name: buttery bread, sautéed onions and celery, and plenty of fresh herbs, with no unnecessary extras. Irregular, torn pieces of crusty bread create craggy edges that turn golden and crisp, while the broth-and-egg mixture renders the tender, custardy middle. Fresh parsley, sage, rosemary, and thyme (sing it with us) bring familiar holiday flavor, backed by a generous amount of butter.

Homemade turkey stock is welcome, but good low-sodium chicken broth from a carton works well. (Or use vegetable broth to make this stuffing vegetarian.) Get the first bake out of the way a day ahead, saving the browning for just before dinner.

Choose a sturdy, crusty loaf, such as pane Pugliese, a French white boule, or a country-style sourdough. Skip soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy once the broth goes in. Weigh out 1 lb. before drying it—the 10-cup measurement is approximate—and don’t skip drying the torn bread in a low oven, even if your loaf is already a day old.

Why bake the stuffing covered, then uncovered?

The covered bake cooks the stuffing through while retaining moisture; the uncovered bake gives you a crisp, golden top. The interior should be tender and cohesive, not dried out. Keep an eye on the stuffing during the second bake rather than assuming it needs the full time. The finished stuffing should be golden and crisp on top and reach 165°F in the center.

Yes. Bake it covered up to three days ahead, until the center reaches 165°F, then let cool briefly and refrigerate within 2 hours. Save the uncovered browning step for serving day. Return the stuffing to a 350°F oven, uncovered, until crisp on top and 165°F in the center, about 45–60 minutes. For longer-term prep, follow our guide to making and freezing stuffing ahead.

What’s the difference between stuffing and dressing?

Stuffing usually refers to a mixture cooked inside a turkey, while dressing is baked separately—but plenty of cooks use the names interchangeably. We prefer versions cooked outside the turkey for the crisp top and edges, but feel free to call it whichever name you grew up using.

Looking for a different take? Try our Sausage-and-Herb Stuffing, Cornbread Dressing With Sausage and Corn Nuts, or any of our other favorite homemade stuffing recipes.

Preheat oven to 250°. Grease a 13x9x2" baking dish with unsalted butter and set aside. Scatter 1 lb. good-quality day-old white bread, torn into 1" pieces (about 10 cups), in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet. Bake, stirring occasionally, until dried out, about 1 hour. Let cool; transfer to a very large bowl.

Meanwhile, melt ¾ cup unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat; add 2½ cups chopped yellow onions and 1½ cups ¼" slices celery to melted butter. Stir often until just beginning to brown, about 10 minutes. Add to bowl with dried bread; stir in ½ cup chopped flat-leaf parsley, 2 Tbsp. chopped fresh sage, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh rosemary, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh thyme, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground black pepper. Drizzle in 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth and toss gently. Let cool.

Preheat oven to 350°. Whisk 2 large eggs and remaining 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth in a small bowl. Add to bread mixture; fold gently until thoroughly combined. Transfer to prepared dish, cover with foil, and bake until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center of dressing registers 160°, 35–40 minutes.

Uncover dressing; continue to bake until set and top is golden brown and crisp, 35–45 minutes longer.

Do ahead: Dressing can be baked (before browning) 1 day ahead; uncover and let cool, then cover and chill. Uncover and bake until top is golden brown and crisp, 45–60 minutes.

Leftover stuffing? Use it up in our Winter Panzanella With Stuffing Croutons →

#6538. A Nutrient Found in Red Meat Could Make Dangerous Inflammation Even Worse

A nutrient known for helping the body burn fat may also cause inflammation when the immune system is in overdrive.

Yale researchers found that L-carnitine, a nutrient abundant in red meat and widely used in exercise and weight-loss supplements, could worsen severe inflammation in mice. After a bacterial component triggered inflammation and sharply lowered blood levels of L-carnitine, restoring the nutrient made the animals sicker, suggesting the decline was protective.

The findings were published October 19 in Cell.

L-carnitine is best known for helping cells turn fat into energy. The body produces it naturally, and skeletal muscle contains particularly high concentrations.

“L-carnitine helps transport fats into mitochondria so they can be broken down for energy,” says Eric Elliott, MD, PhD, assistant professor of medicine (infectious diseases) at Yale School of Medicine (YSM) and the study’s first author. “In simpler terms, it has become synonymous with fat burning, which is why it has also gained prominence as an exercise and weight-loss supplement.”

The team was investigating metabolic changes during sepsis, a life-threatening condition in which the body’s response to infection damages its own tissues and organs. Much of that damage can come from uncontrolled inflammation rather than a failure to contain the infection.

“Sepsis is incredibly challenging,” Elliott says. “Patients with sepsis can become critically ill, and among patients with sepsis treated in intensive care units, some studies report mortality rates approaching 40%.”

To model the inflammation associated with sepsis, the researchers exposed mice to lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a bacterial component. When L-carnitine levels in the animals’ blood dropped sharply, the team tested whether restoring the nutrient would improve their outcomes.

“We predicted giving carnitine back to these animals might improve their outcomes, but they actually did much worse,” Elliott says. “That told us the reduction in carnitine was an adaptive response.”

To understand why, the researchers conducted experiments in mouse and human immune cells. They found that L-carnitine activated part of the cell’s internal alarm system called the pyrin inflammasome. This triggered an inflammatory response involving the immune signaling molecule IL-17 and increased deaths among the mice.

“What was particularly striking was how detrimental IL-17 was in this model,” Elliott says. The team now wants to investigate whether blocking IL-17 might eventually help a subset of patients with sepsis, although that possibility remains untested.

The findings offer a potential research direction in a field where treatment advances have been limited. “We have made frustratingly little progress in improving sepsis treatment beyond learning how to better deliver fluids, antibiotics, and medications that support blood pressure,” Elliott says.

Because skeletal muscle contains high levels of L-carnitine, the researchers suspected that its release from damaged muscle could help drive inflammation. Senior author Andrew Wang, MD, PhD, associate professor of medicine (rheumatology, allergy & immunology) and of immunobiology at YSM, says the pathway may have implications beyond sepsis.

“There is tantalizing genetic evidence that the pathway we uncovered could be contributing to inflammation in a variety of diseases, particularly diseases in which muscle involvement has perhaps been thought to be a casualty of the disease rather than a potential driver,” Wang says.

The team found support for this idea in rhabdomyolysis, a condition in which skeletal muscle rapidly breaks down and releases its contents into the bloodstream, potentially causing acute kidney injury. In a mouse model, L-carnitine transport and pyrin inflammasome activation contributed to inflammation, suggesting that immune cells may interpret L-carnitine released from damaged muscle as a warning signal.

The pathway could also be relevant to cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and cancer. Further research is needed to determine whether it contributes to these chronic inflammatory conditions.

People who eat meat get most of their L-carnitine from food. Vegetarians and vegans tend to make more of it within their bodies, but their overall levels remain lower. The study examined L-carnitine on its own, so the findings do not directly show how eating red meat or taking supplements affects inflammation.

“We did not study red meat as a whole, and carnitine by itself did not induce inflammation,” Elliott says. “A substantial background of inflammation was required, and we do not yet know what inflammatory context might produce this effect in people. We cannot say that carnitine supplementation or heavy red meat consumption is always harmful. It is probably safe most of the time, but there may be specific circumstances in which it becomes a problem.”

Understanding those circumstances is a priority for the team. The researchers want to learn how individual food components interact with a person’s underlying health and inflammatory state and why the same nutrient might have different effects under different conditions.

“Food science currently exists in the realm of phenomenology,” Wang says. “I think that a deep understanding of all the elements that make up food, akin to a periodic table, will be required to understand what makes a ‘good’ or ‘bad’ diet for a particular individual in a particular health state.”

Reference: “The pyrin inflammasome senses OCTN2-mediated uptake of extracellular ʟ-carnitine from muscle injury or ingestion” by Eric I. Elliott, Tomomi M. Yoshida, Susana C.B.R. Nakandakari, Scott Pope, Cuiling Zhang, Timothy Nottoli, Jae Jin Chae, Daniel L. Kastner, Richard A. Flavell, Vishwa Deep Dixit, Vijay A. Rathinam, Fayyaz S. Sutterwala and Andrew Wang, 19 October 2026, Cell. DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.015

#6537. How You Squeeze Planetary Minerals Changes Everything

Studying the interiors of planets is essential for understanding planetary formation, evolution, and their ability to potentially host life as we know it. To accomplish this, researchers use a combination of Earth as an analog, computer models, meteorites, and data collected from other planetary bodies for studying their interior compositions. As a result, scientists have determined that the elements of magnesium and silicon are the most abundant planetary building blocks. And, under extreme pressures like the interior mantle of our planet, it forms magnesium oxide (MgO) crystals. But how does this same process occur under different pressures and temperatures on other planets like gas giants and larger rocky exoplanets called super-Earths?

Now, a collaborative team of researchers from the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) and Johns Hopkins University might be one step closer to solving this conundrum. As discussed in a recent study published in Physical Review X, the researchers unveiled intriguing findings that could solve a 12-year investigation regarding the geochemical processes that occur deep inside planets, specifically related to the formation of magnesium oxide. This study is a third study in a series that builds off two previous studies, a 2015 study published in Physical Review Letters and a 2024 study published in Science Advances.

Artist's impression of the interior layers of Earth, Mars and the Moon. (Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech)

For the study, the researchers conducted a series of laboratory experiments using lasers on a cubic crystal structure of magnesium oxide to compress and simulate the extreme temperatures and pressures it experiences in planetary interiors. For example, the researchers tested as high as 572 Gigapascals (GPa) and 13,000 Kelvin (K) (12,927 degrees Celsius/23,300 degrees Fahrenheit), which are much higher than the pressures and temperatures near the center of the Earth at about 360 GPa and 6,000 K (5,727 degrees Celsius/10,340 degrees Fahrenheit), respectively.

The laser compressed the MgO cube from various directions, which challenged longstanding scientific theories that the extreme temperatures and pressures made the direction of compression irrelevant. The three directions included diagonally along the face, perpendicular to a cube face, and along the diagonal through the face.

Credit: NASA/Lunar and Planetary Institute

In the end, the researchers found that the direction of the incoming laser onto the MgO cube resulted in different responses regarding its compression. For example, while the cubeâs transformation along the diagonal through the cube, whereas the other two directions resulted in different responses, specifically disordered and irregular crystal growth behind a shock wave from the compression. While this finding refuted longstanding theories regarding the behavior of crystals based on direction, the researchers also found that the MgO cube melted at 572 GPa and 13,000 K, which set a new experimental known material record for pressure and temperature.

âMagnesium oxide is an important ingredient in our understanding of planetary interiors,â said Dr. June Wicks, who is a professor in Johns Hopkinsâ Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences and a co-author on the study. âThese experiments help us determine where it can remain solid and where it becomes liquid, which matters for how planets transport heat and evolve.â

As noted, magnesium and silicon comprise the most abundant elements in planetary interiors, with its combined form of MgO revealing the temperatures and pressures of those same planetary interiors. The three main geologic layers of a rock planetary object are the crust, mantle, and core, with the Earth having a liquid outer core and a rocky inner core, with MgO forming near the bottom of the mantle near the core-mantle boundary. However, this process is different depending on the type of planet.

For example, on super-Earth exoplanets, MgO can transform into a conductive liquid within the mantle (whereas this conductivity exists within the Earthâs outer core), resulting in magnetic fields much stronger than Earthâs. Additionally, MgO on gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn can exist either as a solid or liquid deep within their cores and depending on the temperatures.

What new insights into planetary interior processes will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

As always, keep doing science & keep looking up!

#6536. We’re in the Era of the $200 Cup of Coffee

Can coffee join the ranks of wine when it comes to high-end tastings?

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Starting this week, it’s also home to a $200 cup of coffee.

Bushwick’s Sey Coffee recently announced that it would be touring a rare Panamanian geisha from Finca Sophia, a coffee farm in Panama’s Chiriquí highlands. Sey scooped up the geisha at auction for $44,275, which comes to $6,325 per kilogram, or roughly $200 per cup. The geisha is billed as extraordinarily aromatic, floral, and juicy; Doug Cohen, Sey’s director of brand strategy, advises enjoying it with a clean palate, completely black, and taking your time with it. “As the coffee cools, different aspects of its character become apparent, and that evolution is part of the experience,” he says.

Even among fourth-wave coffee shops where prices continue to climb higher, Sey’s $200 cup is an outlier. “Coffee as a premium product is relatively new,” says Cohen. “For so long, coffee has been treated as a commodity, and its value has been constrained by that perception.” He says that both before and right after COVID, folks were becoming more curious about coffee, and educating themselves on platforms like Youtube, Discord, and online forums about how to appreciate it and “understand just how high the ceiling of quality can be.” The arrival of the $200 cup of coffee from a cafe in a neighborhood at the epicenter of conversations about both culinary innovation and gentrification feels ripe for closer examination.

So, how did this coffee end up at this price? “We have been purchasing coffee from Finca Sophia for several years,” Cohen says. “This release really grew out of that existing relationship.” When Finca’s general manager told Cohen that the farm’s yields were down by approximately 95 percent, Cohen says a bigger question was raised: “What does it mean to be a good partner when the people you have built relationships with are facing a difficult year?” Buying up the geisha beans felt like a way to both support Sey’s producer, and further develop what Cohen calls “elevated coffee experiences.”

In the 2010s, the artisanal coffeehouse wave washed over the country, and especially Brooklyn, with hipster gusto. Sey Coffee was an integral part of that boom. Initially called Lofted Coffee, it operated out of its founders’ Bushwick loft until it rebranded to Sey in 2017, and expanded operations to its present Bushwick location on Grattan Street. That space has become something of a local icon since; Sprudge called its aesthetic “shoebox crossed with an airplane hangar”; the minimal-industrial, cream-hued interiors hit a very Axel Vervoordt-with-a-cyber-sigil-tattoo note (positive). The shop’s cachet has drawn coffee lovers, artists, yuppies, and artist-yuppies; customers have snacked on the gluten-free pastries from L’imprimerie (and now, post-L’imprimerie closure, pastries from Smør), and often post up with their dogs thanks to the semi-indoor-outdoor layout.

Sey is hoping to elevate the coffee shop model to something more premium, with a stated focus on ethics and sustainability. Thus far, it’s earned acclaim for those efforts. Food & Wine named it the best coffee shop in New York and received positive media attention for opting out of tipping, choosing instead to pay its staff up to more than 80 percent above the NYC hourly minimum wage; full-time baristas can make up to $31 per hour in addition to receiving benefits and a share of the cafe’s revenue.

Increasingly, coffee is getting the same treatment as high-end dining and tasting experiences. There’s the omakase-style menu at NYC’s Driftaway Coffee, or San Francisco’s Komakase coffee tasting room, both of which steer coffee away from quick consumption and toward a world of degustation that appears to have more in common with pricier wine and spirit tastings. The expansion of “espresso house” chain Watch House stateside is also an indicator: The London-based specialty roaster expanded to a fourth location in New York City this summer, raising eyebrows for its $32 cup of coffee while also reportedly scouting for more locations in Austin, Chicago, and Miami.

The emerging demand may be just much about luxury as it is about craft. I can’t help but wonder if the $200 cup of coffee is happening in Bushwick because the Girls-era Bushwickian has grown up and wants more exclusive experiences. Is this what happens when, as culture writer Raven Smith said on his new BBC podcast last week, the indie outgrows its sleaze? “For us, this is not about pushing prices higher for the sake of it,” Cohen says. “It is about challenging how we assign value to coffee in the first place. What is an extraordinary coffee actually worth?”

As much as we may lament climbing prices for specialty coffee and espresso, why wouldn’t this happen to the category when so many other aspects of food and beverage — from cocktails to sushi to bread — are following the same trajectory? Higher consumer costs notwithstanding, the marketing of specialty beans does steer U.S. coffee culture away from its productivity-focused consumption and the work-optimized “coffee break.”

“Why do we accept that certain wines can command thousands of dollars, yet question whether coffee can have comparable value?” Cohen asks. It’s a fair question, albeit one that I’d answer with another: Once we acknowledge that coffee should command a higher price, who still gets to drink it?

#6535. Can Cats Really Go Vegan? New Research Reveals a Surprising Health Connection

More cat owners are turning to vegan diets for their pets. But is a plant-based diet actually safe for cats?

An online survey of 1,305 cats found that those eating vegan diets had 34% lower odds of being assessed as overweight than those eating conventional meat-based food.

The findings came from caregiver reports of veterinary assessments. All cats had followed their diets for at least one year, with conventional meat-based diets accounting for most (90%) and vegan diets for the remainder (10%).

Researchers calculated the difference after accounting for age, sex, neuter status, activity, and feeding practices.

The lower rates of excess weight came despite feeding habits that might have tipped the scales the other way, as Knight explained, “Interestingly, most vegan-fed cats were eating predominantly dry food and were more likely to have food available throughout the day. These are feeding patterns normally associated with increased overweight risk. Yet we still observed lower rates of overweight in this group.”

That observation came from study author Andrew Knight, an adjunct professor at Australia’s Griffith University School of Environment and Science. He emphasized that the relatively small vegan-fed group limited what researchers could conclude.

Veterinary studies estimate that around 30–60% of domestic cats are overweight or obese. Excess weight is associated with arthritis, diabetes, urinary tract disease, and reduced quality of life, giving researchers a reason to investigate dietary patterns that might help.

Caregivers of vegan-fed cats reported fewer weight-related disorders, with no cases reported for several conditions examined. However, the small number of cats in this group made those results uncertain.

“Carers feeding cats vegan diets also reported lower rates of body weight-related disorders such as osteoarthritis and other musculoskeletal and mobility problems,” Knight said. “However, the relatively small number of vegan-fed cats means these results cannot be considered conclusive.”

The survey could not establish why vegan-fed cats appeared less likely to be overweight. Researchers did not analyze the foods themselves, so explanations involving their ingredients or nutritional composition remain possibilities.

Some commercial vegan cat foods may provide more fiber and fewer calories or less fat than comparable meat-based products, potentially supporting weight control. Differences in L-carnitine, a nutrient involved in energy metabolism and maintaining lean body tissue, could also contribute.

The results do not establish that avoiding meat prevents excess weight. Determining whether the diets themselves explain the pattern would require direct measurements of food consumption, calorie intake, and body condition over time.

Knight said the findings provide a reason for further investigation, rather than a definitive answer about vegan diets and feline weight.

“We can’t conclude from this study that vegan diets definitely protect cats against becoming overweight, but we have found a consistent pattern that is worth further investigation. An ideal next step would be a larger, prospective study that directly measured what cats are eating, their energy intake, and their body condition.”

“Additionally, cat carers should always ensure their cats receive nutritionally complete diets, choosing commercial vegan foods that are appropriately supplemented to provide all essential nutrients.”

Reference: “Impacts of a vegan diet on body weight and related health disorders in 1,305 cats: an exploratory cross-sectional survey” by Andrew Knight, Alexander Bauer and Jenny L. Mace, 11 September 2026, Frontiers in Animal Science. DOI: 10.3389/fanim.2026.1939965

#6534. Sommelier-Approved Thanksgiving Wines

The challenge of picking wine for Thanksgiving is multifaceted. Your selections must be lively enough to enjoy as guests work their way through charcuterie, balanced enough to play well with turkey, and versatile enough to rub shoulders with dessert. It’s a tall order for anyone tasked with bringing the bottles to their holiday meal. To help, five beloved wine-heads from across the country weighed in on the bottles that everyone around your holiday table will adore.

Here are the crowd-pleasing offerings sure to liven up your Thanksgiving.

For Adam Robins, beverage director at State Bird Provisions and The Progress in San Francisco, there’s no better way to start a festive meal than with Champagne. Bérêche & Fils delivers classic brioche notes tempered with fruit like Bosc and Asian pears, brought together with a snap of acidity to prime the palate for the feast ahead

Les Cigales dans la Fourmilière Escarpolette Blanc 2024

Los Angeles’s Lasita is beloved for its natural wine selections and its menu of kicky Filipino favorites. Co-owners Chase and Steff Valencia adore this Languedoc orange wine, which offers notes of bold fruit—peach and apricot—and a bright acidity that can cut through even the butteriest of mashed potatoes.

Peter Lauer Riesling Schonfels Kabinett No. 111

“More people should be drinking Riesling,” says Matt Turner of Lei, one of Bon Appétit’s Best New Restaurants of 2026. He points to this German stunner with direct minerality and notes of stone fruit, which sips just as well alongside a cheesy cauliflower gratinée as a garlic-studded beef tenderloin.

At the James Beard–nominated Wild Child in Lafayette, Louisiana, natural wine rules supreme. Ian LaCour, who helps curate the bottle list, gravitates toward this muscular red. Thanks to a silky body and dusky notes of stewed red fruit, it plays well with the “heartier proteins on the Thanksgiving table.”

You’d be forgiven for being unfamiliar with macvin, a niche style of fortified wine made in France’s Jura region. But the oaky fresh apple and cider notes in this punchy bottling—akin to a less-oxidized, sweeter oloroso sherry—make for a divine digestif. “It fares well with every dessert,” says Nick Arone of Detroit’s Bar Chenin.

#6533. Earth’s “Impenetrable” Space Radiation Shield Was Just Breached From Within

Remember the big solar storm back in May 2024? The one that caused auroras as far south as Florida and Mexico? Scientists are still parsing out the impacts that storm had on the local environment, and a new paper published in Geophysical Research Letters by Yoshizumi Miyoshi of Nagoya University and his co-authors shows it might have allowed some nearby electrons to accelerate to relativistic speeds using something called a chorus wave.

To understand why thatâs important, letâs first take a look at Earthâs local radiation environment. Itâs dominated by what scientists call the Van Allen belts. These were discovered early on in the Space Age by Explorer 1, and they are Earthâs primary defense against high energy electrons and other ions spewed out by the Sun. Scientists have long split them into two categories - the âinnerâ belt is made mainly of protons, and the âouterâ belt is covered in high-energy electrons.

But in 2014, NASAâs Van Allen Probe mission discovered a noticeable boundary - the ultra-relativistic âkiller electronsâ that move near the speed of light seem to hit some sort of glass wall at around 11,500 kilometers above the Earthâs surface. To scientists, it seemed that this âshieldâ protected the inner area directly around the planet from the most dangerous form of radiation.

Fraser talks about what the Van Allen radiation belts are.

Which sounded great - until Nature decided not to do it anymore. Luckily we know when exactly that happened, because Japanâs Arase satellite (also known as the Exploration of energization and Radiation in Geospace - ERG mission), which has been flying through Earthâs magnetosphere since 2017, was watching. For its entire lifetime up to that point, it noted that high energy electrons were being held at bay. Until May 2024.

During that storm, solar wind gusts topping out at 1,200 kilometers per second compressed Earthâs magnetic field, and triggered the most intense geomagnetic disturbance since the arguably even more famous Halloween storm of 2003. As the storm peaked, Arase counted ultra-relativistic electrons at levels 5,000 times higher than the typical background. This wasn't the first time we had seen spikes in radiation during solar storms, but older spacecraft werenât able to tell what was actually happening.

Arase provided the key data to help guide the researchers, who used a mathematical method called electron phase space density. This tracks the particle distribution of those electrons by energy and motion. If, say, the electrons were coming in from outside where the protective barrier originally was, this metric should very clearly show a downward trend from outer space towards Earth. However, Arase saw a very distinct peak right where the barrier used to be. To space physics, that represents a smoking gun for âlocalâ acceleration - i.e. electrons being sped up exactly where they were detected.

NASA Goddard video about the radiation environment surrounding Earth. Credit - NASA Goddard YouTube Channel

Which then begs the question, what was accelerating them? According to the paper, it was something called a âchorus waveâ. Typically, the inner radiation belt is covered in a shroud of charged gas known as the plasmasphere. Charged gases do a great job of dampening high frequency electromagnetic waves, as they simply absorb their energy. But when the May 2024 storm hit, the plasmasphere was crushed back toward Earth, creating a void where it would normally be.

Combine that with a ânegative ionospheric stormâ, which massively depletes local plasma densities, and you create a very empty electromagnetic environment. Which is the perfect situation for chorus waves. These are low frequency electromagnetic waves, which sound like whistling when translated into audio, that are generated by lower-energy particles during magnetic storms. In a depleted plasma environment, these waves are able to transfer their energy very efficiently to the surrounding low energy electrons, boosting them from sub-million electron volt energies to multi-MeV ranges - essentially creating high energy electron radiation within what is normally an exclusion zone.

Over time this new high energy radiation spread out both towards and away from Earth - and the effect lasted for months. Its effects were visible to Arase until another solar storm hit five months later in October 2024, and changed the magnetic field situation up again.

But ultimately, this paper acts as a warning of a new type of space weather hazard - localized radiation caused not by a massive solar explosion but by a retreat of our own protective plasma sheath. As we start to expand out into the area most affected by this, itâs certainly better to be aware of that phenomenon now, but unfortunately it might require even more shielding to protect our sensitive electronic and biological cargo in the future.

Nagoya University - 2024 solar storm triggered ultra-relativistic electrons inside Earthâs âimpenetrable barrierâ

Y. Miyoshi et al - Local Acceleration of Multi-MeV Electrons Inside Earth's Impenetrable Barrier During the May 2024 Superstorm

#6532. A Hidden DNA Mechanism Could Explain How 20% of Human Cancers Develop

Mutations found in roughly 20% of human cancers may promote tumor growth by changing how DNA is organized inside cells. Researchers have identified a mechanism that allows a regulatory protein to reshape the genome’s three-dimensional structure, altering the activity of genes involved in cell division.

The study, published October 28 in Nature, links these changes to mutations affecting a protein complex called BAF. Scientists at Weill Cornell Medicine found that blocking a key protein involved in the process reversed the cancer-promoting effects in an animal model, suggesting potential new approaches to treatment.

The BAF complex helps control gene activity by regulating how accessible DNA is to other proteins. Its numerous subunits are encoded by more than two dozen genes, and mutations affecting these components occur in cancers of the breast, ovaries, liver, and lymphatic system. Until now, researchers had struggled to explain how such mutations could contribute to malignancy across so many different tissues.

The new findings challenge expectations about how BAF normally functions. “We normally think of the BAF complex as making DNA more accessible, and so we expected its loss to have the opposite effect,” Dr. Meydan said. “Instead, its loss made DNA more accessible to CTCF, with surprisingly far-reaching effects.”

CTCF helps organize DNA into distinct regions by establishing boundaries that influence which genes interact with regulatory elements. These interactions depend partly on how DNA folds and loops within the nucleus. When BAF activity is lost, CTCF gains access to sites that would normally be less accessible, potentially disrupting this intricate organization.

“The challenge for us was to find a potential cancer-promoting effect occurring across many different cell types and tissue models,” said Dr. Barisic, who is also the John P. Leonard, M.D./Gwirtzman Family Research Scholar in Lymphoma.

Using several animal and cell models with impaired BAF function, the researchers discovered that CTCF binding increased at thousands of locations throughout the genome. This widespread change reorganized DNA loops and folds, disrupting normal connections between genes and the regulatory regions that control their activity. The resulting shifts in gene expression encouraged faster cell division.

Evidence from mouse experiments and human cancer patient data further supported CTCF’s involvement. In particular, disruptions affecting CTCF were associated with better patient outcomes. The researchers also demonstrated that deleting CTCF in an animal model could reverse the effects of BAF mutations, providing experimental evidence that the protein contributes to the cancer-promoting process.

The team identified two additional protein complexes, PBAF and ISWI, that cooperate with CTCF in driving these changes. Removing either complex also blocked the effects of BAF mutations in experimental models, making all three potential targets for future therapies.

“These findings help us establish a unifying mechanism for one of the most common classes of cancer mutations, and identify CTCF and its partner proteins as candidate therapeutic targets in these cancers,” said study co-corresponding author Dr. Darko Barisic, an assistant professor of cancer biology in medicine and a member of the Sandra and Edward Meyer Cancer Center at Weill Cornell Medicine.

Although the experiments identify promising molecular targets, researchers have not yet established whether blocking these proteins can safely treat cancer in humans. The next challenge is understanding precisely how increased CTCF binding changes the genome and finding ways to interfere with that process.

“We’re currently investigating in more detail what this extensive gain of CTCF does to the genome, and we hope before long to find a drug that blocks this process,” Dr. Barisic said.

Reference: “SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin” by Sonia Debek, Cem Meydan, Christopher R. Chin, Jiali Yu, Ceyda Durmaz, Ioanna Tsialta, Benedikt Pelzer, Constance Maurer, Arnold Ou, Alejandra Laguillo-Diego, Laurianne Scourzic, Sravya Tumuluru, Matt Teater, Rui Wu, Brian Darsow, Martin A. #6531. Steal My Food Itinerary: 3 Days on Prince Edward Island

Canada’s smallest province is big on fresh produce, pristine seafood, gorgeous views, and warm conviviality.

Recently I spent a few days exploring Prince Edward Island, a place that embraces its local foodways with gusto. There’s a complex history here, with roots in Indigenous Mi’kmaq, Acadian, Irish, Scottish, and other cultures. And if one thing unites these histories, it’s the island’s abundance of seafood and produce, which have helped earn it the nickname Canada’s Food Island. How can you not want to visit Canada’s Food Island?

On a stretch of land only about 140 miles long, you can eat oysters pulled out of nearby waters, potatoes grown on local farms, dig into a juicy burger made with PEI beef, and lick ice cream made with milk from the cows you pass along those famous red-dirt roads. That’s a lot of good eating packed into a place you can drive across in an afternoon.

I had to structure my visit, therefore, around where to dine, but also include a bucket-list visit to Green Gables Heritage Place. (I am a complete freak for L.M. Montgomery’s novel Anne of Green Gables, set on PEI around the turn of the last century.) I also had to schedule time at the PEI International Shellfish Festival, which promised endless trays of freshly shucked oysters and clams, hot buttered lobster rolls, steaming bowls of mussels, and plenty of entertainment, from shucking competitions and cooking demos to live music and dancing.

My husband and I rented a car and stationed ourselves in Charlottetown, the island’s main hub. Prince Edward Island is situated in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, just a hop away from Nova Scotia. You’re never far from the ocean here, and on a sunny day, the air seems to sparkle. The island is known for its red-sand cliffs and beaches, rolling landscapes, fishing harbors, and lighthouses. If you’ve read Anne of Green Gables, you’ll know just how pretty PEI is.

We landed late Thursday afternoon, ready to hit the ground running. With just shy of three days, I had carefully mapped out the places I wanted to visit, using Charlottetown as my base.

Charlottetown isn’t big, and most things here are walkable within 20 minutes or so. First stop in PEI: Slaymaker & Nichols, a gastropub and inn with the feel of an old-fashioned supper club. It takes its name from the 19th-century circus that once performed on the site. They take cocktail making seriously here. The summery feel of the day prompted me to try the watermelon mule, with hibiscus-infused vodka and chunks of pickled watermelon. I liked it, especially alongside the creamy lobster dip with tomatoes and harissa, and the buttery shrimp pil pil, with lots of tasty little spears of asparagus.

I was saving myself for my first lobster roll, which we grabbed up the street in an unremarkable spot. It was pretty mediocre, so I won’t go on about it. But after eating, we stopped into Reddins, a speakeasy that channels PEI’s Prohibition history in a dark, intimate third-floor bar with vintage furniture, good jazz, and whimsical cocktails. Our excellent bartender, AB, told us the space had once been a pharmacy where folks came during Prohibition to get their “medicine” — drugstores could legally dispense alcohol by prescription. We tried a few of the signature cocktails, and the one that stood out was the Pink Canary, with vodka, rose, lychee, citrus, and rosé bubbles, served in a small bathtub. Yup, you heard that right. It was sweet and awfully fun to sip.

Tip: You need a secret password to get in when you buzz from downstairs. You can get it online, or just do as we did and ask the hostess next door for help.

In the pouring rain, we made our way to nearby Victoria Row for breakfast at local roaster Receiver Coffee. Fuel for the day included strong coffee, a particularly good cup of Earl Grey cream tea, and the Ham Slam, a big fluffy cheddar biscuit layered with a runny fried egg, Black Forest ham, Swiss, and Dijon mayo.

We swung by the shellfish festival (more on that later) but the rain wasn’t welcoming, so we got back in the car and drove out to tiny and charming Victoria-by-the-Sea. When I say tiny, I mean it: The town is half a square mile, with a population under 200. Despite the town’s size, Landmark Oyster House, set there in an old general store with pretty green shingles and a steep gabled roof, thrives.

Our friendly waiter (everyone is abundantly friendly on PEI) suggested Raspberry Point oysters to start. They hit the spot: medium-sized, briny, and sweet, served with lemon wedges and freshly grated horseradish, which is now how I think every oyster should be eaten. We also tried the scallop dog, with buttery sweet scallops, bacon jam, red pepper aioli, and pickled shallots nestled in a toasted bun. It came alongside a very good, eggy potato salad.

After seeing the cheery lighthouse and visiting a couple of little gift shops, we popped into Island Chocolates, a family-run shop and café where bars and truffles are hand-crafted, often using local ingredients like haskap, a berry that tastes somewhere between a blueberry and raspberry. That fruity haskap truffle had a nice thick shell of milk chocolate.

Sun out? Check. We spent the afternoon at the festival and got a substantial fix of oysters and clams. The lobster rolls here were stuffed with unadorned lobster meat, then melted butter from a gigantic vat was ladled over the top.

For dinner, both our bartender and waiter at Slaymaker recommended North Shore Canteen in French River, a local haunt for sure. (A slew of chefs from the shellfish festival were two tables down from us.) The menu, which changes with the current haul, hit on the day’s best ingredients: halibut, striped bass, the aforementioned shellfish, beef, and potatoes. We opted for a very generous portion of local beef tartare, amazingly tasty with capers, roasted garlic, and freshly grated Parmesan, served with Covered Bridge potato chips. We wanted to try more PEI beef and opted for a juicy hanger steak with chimichurri and black garlic, which showcased it well. Dessert was a must: parsnip cake drizzled with caramel sauce for the win.

It was time for me to check Green Gables off my bucket list. This is an article about where to eat, so suffice it to say that if you’re a fan, this is 100 percent worth a visit to see the house, wander the Haunted Wood and Lover’s Lane, and taste some nonalcoholic raspberry cordial (IYKYK).

All that walking made me hungry, which was good because this was a much anticipated two-lunch day.

First stop: Blue Mussel Café, a bright and very welcoming, beloved PEI restaurant set just back from the water in Rustico Harbor. I think it’s obvious what to order, and for good reason: These are excellent mussels — plump, fresh, and brought to the table piled high in a large stainless steel bowl. You can have them prepared with rosemary and lemon or beer and wine. I’d rate them equally, but I did like the hit of rosemary. Melted butter comes in a small ramekin on the side; I used it to dip each mussel, and my husband poured it all over the top. I didn’t have it, but the other signature, seafood chowder, looked popular. It’s made with haddock, salmon, scallops, mussels, and PEI potatoes, and served with a giant biscuit. Noted for my next visit.

We hightailed it to our next meal because I had yet to have the perfect lobster roll. Richard’s Fresh Seafood in Covehead Wharf delivered. This is one of the island’s longest-running fish shacks, where you can savor fish and chips and beer on the deck overlooking the fishing boats, or camp out on the nearby beach under the lighthouse with a lobster roll. no mistake: This is the quintessential lobster roll. It was an exercise in abundance, packed with sweet lobster meat that managed to be chunky and fine, bound with lemon and chive mayo and tiny bits of onion, all stuffed in a buttery toasted bun. It came with crunchy coleslaw, crispy fries, and a paper cup of ketchup. There are other menu items, but this lobster roll alone is worth the trip to PEI.

For our final dinner, we drove back toward North Rustico Harbor to Rustico Cannery, which opened this past spring. The airy, modern space has giant windows and a big deck that takes in super sunset views.

I needed greens, and Rustico delivered. We had crisp romaine hearts with a creamy, spicy charred jalapeño dressing, lardons, Parmesan, and sourdough crunchies. My husband hit the jackpot with his dinner: panko crusted, pan-fried haddock with pickled beet remoulade, jalapeño relish, confit potatoes, and coleslaw.

A final note: Many places are seasonal, so check if they’re open if you’re visiting in cooler months.

All-inclusive escapes have never looked — or tasted — so good

Today guests expect more than a Michelin-starred restaurant. They want to get into the kitchen and out in the field.

No more generic resort food. These culinary-savvy properties bring a distinct sense of place to the all-inclusive experience.

Where to go to rest, relax, recharge, and eat well while doing it

Or, how to stop worrying and learn to love the all-inclusive

#6530. Mamdani and Hochul Visit Queens Night Market to Get Out the Vote

Zohran Mamdani wanted to share with the governor, but the vendor at the Taiwanese Yummy tent wasn’t having it. Cheng Liu insisted the New York mayor try his own bowl of beef noodle soup—the chef’s way.

Instead of trying a bite from Governor Kathy Hochul, Mamdani watched and waited as Liu arranged slippery, wide noodles underneath pickled mustard greens, herbs, and slices of succulent brisket that had been cooked for eight hours, all ladled with a delicate broth. Mamdami started to dig in with his chopsticks when Liu rushed over to spoon in a generous amount of homemade chili oil.

“The mayor is not scared of spicy food,” Liu said via his son’s translation. “We wanted to give him Taiwanese cuisine.”

At the Queens Night Market, Mamdani and Hochul struck an unusual pair: a New York mayor and governor who get along.

Three days before Election Day, the political allies arrived at Flushing Meadows Corona Park in a motorcade of black SUVs to pose for photos and get out the vote for the Democratic party. Hochul has made the city part of her final push in a re-election campaign against Republican Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive endorsed by President Donald Trump.

In a joint interview with Hochul, Mamdani told Bon Appétit that he was showing up for the governor because she was showing up for immigrant New Yorkers. Earlier this year, Hochul signed legislation to ban local and state law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration operations, and to stop police at all levels from covering their face when interacting with the public.

“The governor has stood up and called for public safety to actually be public safety and not just be an assistance and an accompaniment of ICE,” Mamdani said. “That has been part of what makes people feel like they can be part of this city.”

The mayor also mentioned that the Queens Night Market was a favorite with constituents because of the price. Every dish is capped at $6. Hochul, running on affordability, points to her expansion of free school lunch statewide. “As a mom, this is personal,” she said. “I made a lot of peanut butter and jelly sandwiches over the years for kids.”

Representing different generations and factions of their party, Mamdani and Hochul recognize what they stand to gain together. Mamdani needed Hochul to expand free childcare and greenlight plans for a second-home tax. Hochul needs the enthusiasm of the Democratic Socialist mayor’s voting bloc.

Hochul said she and Mamdani are aligned on lowering the cost of living and supporting the small business owners that make the food and nightlife scene so special.

“It’s a rare day in New York for this kind of relationship,” Hochul said, “but when we talk to each other, we don’t disagree on these issues.”

The pair of politicians approached the night market in a coordinated operation that included advance teams, extra security, and business casual ’fits: Hochul in jeans, Mamdani tie-less in a quarter-zip. The mayor—who has made his appetite a key part of his public identity—appeared less stiff in his interactions with food vendors, but Hochul gamely grabbed chopsticks and posed for selfies.

John Wang, who launched the Queens Night Market in 2015, said politicians are a regular presence here. “Every election season, they come out,” Wang said. “Even if they’ve never been here before, they’re like, ‘Yeahhh! I love the Queens Night Market.’” He said some (2020 presidential candidate Andrew Yang, for instance) get feted like Mamdani, and others (N.Y. Sen. Chuck Schumer) draw a tamer response. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez used to come a lot, Wang said, and would always get swarmed by supporters.

For the last market of the season, which fell on Halloween, Mamdani might as well have been a member of BTS. Vendors and visitors alike stared slackjawed, squealed, and uttered “oh my God!”

A young man named Asad showed up in a Mamdani costume with no idea he would meet the mayor, let alone pose for photos that brought him to tears.“This is Bruce Blakeman’s nightmare!” the mayor said of his Mamdani double.

“It was surreal, emotional a little bit,” said Asad, who declined to share his last name. Asad said he was born in Karachi, Pakistan, became a U.S. citizen in 2022, and voted for Mamdani after moving to New York from Florida.

At the Ella Spice stand, Akera Phillip represents Grenada with breadfruit croquettes, fried cou-cou, and to-go pouches of sorrel. Phillip, who named her business after her grandmother, felt “elated” and “blessed” to serve her food to the leaders of the state and the city.

“As a small island girl, it just made me feel big,” she said.

Akera Phillip holds breadfruit croquettes.

At the Epis by Steve tent, Hochul told Steve Lahens she could handle “Buffalo spicy,” a nod to her hometown, rather than admit to any trouble with his Haitian pikliz. Lahens and his wife fixed up plates of griot (fried pork) with diri djondjon (black rice) and makawoni au graten, a Caribbean mac and cheese he makes with bell peppers, “evaporated milk and a few little things I can’t talk about.”

Lahens said he was born in Haiti but came to the U.S. in 1988. A workplace injury pushed him toward cooking, “and it changed my life, for the better.” He began cooking out of his house but now works out of the Mangrove shared kitchen at the Flatbush Central Caribbean Marketplace. He was excited to hobnob with the governor and the mayor, but Lahens also said New York small businesses need more help.

“The rent could be lower so people like me could get a spot,” Lahens said. “Right now I’m stuck in catering. I love it, too, but my whole plan and goal is to get a storefront.”

#6529. “Nearly Everybody Had Given Up” – Scientists Finally Solve a 60-Year Chemistry Mystery

After more than six decades of failed attempts, chemists have achieved a breakthrough involving a class of molecules long considered too unstable to isolate.

Chemists have succeeded in isolating a group of molecules that researchers have struggled to capture for more than 60 years. Known as oxoboranes, these compounds contain an unusual triple bond between boron and oxygen, a combination long considered too unstable to isolate in a lasting form.

Researchers led by Professor Holger Braunschweig at the University of Würzburg have now developed a method that produces three surprisingly stable oxoboranes. Published in Nature Chemistry, the work was supported by computational research from Professor Ashwini K. Phukan’s team at Tezpur University in India.

The breakthrough began when Würzburg doctoral students Lukas Lubczyk and Christian Markl independently reacted a compound called a diboracumulene with different ketones, chemicals commonly used in organic synthesis. Instead of the anticipated products, they obtained unusual orange or yellow solids. The reactions had unexpectedly produced oxoboranes as their main products.

“The discovery was a pleasant surprise. I never thought the diboracumulene would react the way it did, let alone with multiple different, simple substrates. And when Christian came to me with his compound, I knew we were onto something,” says Lukas Lubczyk.

Boron has a strong tendency to avoid forming triple bonds, making these molecules particularly difficult to synthesize. Braunschweig has spent more than 15 years investigating this type of chemical bonding. His team created the first molecule containing a boron-boron triple bond in 2012, followed by the first neutral molecule with a boron-carbon triple bond in 2025. Organic oxoboranes represented the remaining challenge involving triple bonds between boron and other elements in the first row of the periodic table’s p-block.

Chemists have pursued oxoboranes since at least the early 1960s. Although previous experiments detected or trapped them under extreme conditions, inferred their presence from chemical reactions, or produced related derivatives, researchers had been unable to isolate stable examples.

“Nearly everybody in the field had given up on oxoboranes, as they were thought to be just too unstable to be isolated. So we were stunned to see them spontaneously form in these reactions and stick around long enough that we could study them,” says Holger Braunschweig.

The successful preparation of three oxoboranes suggests that the new approach could provide access to additional members of this difficult-to-synthesize molecular family. The researchers are now investigating whether the method can be extended to produce other elusive compounds involving elements across the periodic table.

Reference: “Synthesis and isolation of stable oxoboranes” by Lukas Lubczyk, Christian Markl, Mudit Jain, Sourav Kar, Thomas Kupfer, Rian D. Dewhurst, Ashwini K. Phukan and Holger Braunschweig, 27 October 2026, Nature Chemistry. DOI: 10.1038/s41557-026-02272-w

The work was funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG), the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) and the Department of Science & Technology (DST) of India.

#6528. This Gamma-Ray Burst Wasn't Dim, It Was Just Misunderstood

Every photon that reaches us tells us something about the Universe. Most of them come from the Sun and are well-understood. But others aren't so easily understood.

The highest energy photons are gamma photons, and they reach us in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). They were first detected by accident in the 1960s by a satellite watching for covert nuclear weapons tests, an unnatural, Earthly source of gamma radiation. Now we've detected large numbers of GRBs with satellites dedicated to sensing them.

GRBs are extremely energetic events in the Universe, second only to the Big Bang. In only a few seconds, they can release as much energy as our Sun will across its nearly 10 billion years of fusion. They're the calling cards of supernovae, when the core of a massive star collapses in on itself at the end of its life, leaving behind a neutron star or a black hole.

GRBs are rare, but they're not difficult to detect, due to their extreme bursts of energy. So despite being rare, they're regularly detected in distant galaxies. A typical GRB from a supernova lasts about 20 or 30 seconds, followed by an afterglow with stages of declining energy. A GRB's energy is in its jets, which are ultrarelativistic beams of plasma and radiation that approach the speed of light.

This artist's illustration shows two jets from a GRB emitted in opposite directions. The jets lose energy and fade into longer wavelengths as they travel through the surrounding medium. Image Credit: By NASA/Swift/Mary Pat Hrybyk-Keith and John Jones - http://imagine.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/features/news/10sep08.html [1]Transferred from en.wikipedia to Commons by TheDJ using CommonsHelper., Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=8807284

The GRB is followed by an x-ray phase, then an optical phase, then a radio phase, as the jet decelerates into the surrounding medium, losing energy in stages. (Another class of GRBs, short GRBs, are separate and have a different source.)

On March 10, 2026, NASAâs Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope detected a GRB with an unusual light signature.

This one, named GRB 260310A, had an initial flash of gamma-rays that lasted almost one minute, releasing a relatively small amount of energy. Then, in another twist, its visible light afterglow gradually brightened over the course of a few hours. The optical light was brighter than the supernova's host galaxy. If that wasn't unusual enough, after its initial x-ray flash, the x-ray afterglow also brightened again, and remained visible for months.

In astronomy and astrophysics, outliers always attract attention because they have something new to tell us. GRB 260310A was no different. An international group of researchers studied the burst to try and understand its unusual signature.

Their results are in research titled "An Extremely Bright Slow-rising Afterglow from an Off-axis Jet in GRB 260310A," published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. The lead author is Yu-Han Yang, a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Physics at the University of Rome Tor Vergata. As the title says, the GRB strange signal is related to our viewing angle.

âWe see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,â said co-author Roberto Ricci, who led the radio observations. âWe could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder.â

To understand them, GRBs have to be observed across multiple wavelengths. Once the Fermi Gamma-Ray Telescope detected GRB 260310A, it sent out alerts for quick follow-up observations. NASAâs Chandra X-ray Observatory, ESAâs XMM-Newton, the China/ESA Einstein Probe mission, the Large Binocular Telescope, and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array all contributed. The Calar Alto Observatory in Spain also contributed observations confirming that a supernova was behind the GRB.

"We present a multiwavelength study of GRB 260310A, a nearby long-duration gamma-ray burst (GRB) at z â 0.153 associated with a broad-lined Type Ic supernova," the authors write. "Despite its modest prompt gamma-ray output, GRB 260310A exhibits one of the brightest afterglows ever observed in the X-ray, optical, and radio bands."

This figure compares GRB 260310A with a broader population of GRB afterglows. From top to bottom, the rows of panels compare x-ray flux and luminosity, then optical apparent magnitude and absolute magnitude, then radio flux density and radio luminosity. All panels show how GRB 260310A is different than the broader population and how it peaked later than others. Image Credit: Yu-Han Yang et al 2026 ApJL 1011 L22

Most GRBs are detected when one of its jets is pointed right at us. âMuch like a flashlight, the jet appears brightest when seen head-on," said lead author Yu-Han Yang. "Most of our models are calibrated using events seen from that same perspective. This burst gave us a chance to look beyond that glare."

GRB 260310A wasn't pointed at us, and that explains some of its unusual light pattern, especially its weaker initial gamma flash. But its later stages were among the brightest. Both its x-ray and optical afterglows ranked among the top 1% in brightness, and its radio brightness was among the top 5% of GRBs. âWe looked at it from a side angle," Yang said. "As the jet slowed down, its light became visible over a wider range of angles, allowing us to probe the jetâs shape, from its outer edges toward its inner core.â

Strangely, after about three weeks, the x-rays brightened again and stayed bright for about one week. Then, it gradually faded away. âThat was unexpected. At first, I thought another X-ray source was contaminating our observations. But the brightening really came from the afterglow,â said Yang, who coordinated the X-ray monitoring. âThis prompted us to explore a more complex jetâs shape.â

Only NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory has the angular resolution required to detect a contaminating source, and the researchers used some of its Director's Discretionary Time to examine GRB 260310A. Those observations ruled out a contaminating x-ray source.

This figure shows the Large Binocular Telescope's optical image of GRB 260310A's field in the left panel. The right panel shows the Chandra X-ray Observatory's image of the GRB. The cyan circle is the NuSTAR's Fast X-ray Transients observation, which helps show how Chandra has the power to see the source more clearly compared to other x-ray observatories. Its observations ruled out a contaminating x-ray source. Image Credit: Yu-Han Yang et al 2026 ApJL 1011 L22

So what's the overall explanation for GRB 260310A?

"We argue that the combination of weak prompt emission, hard peak energy, and late afterglow onset is naturally explained by a GRB jet viewed off-axis," the authors write in their research. The critical part is that it had two separate shocks.

"Our analysis of the broadband spectrum favors the presence of two emission components: a bright RS (reverse shock) dominating the radio and extending to the optical band, and an FS (forward shock) contributing to the optical and dominating in the X-rays," the researchers explain.

There are existing models of GRBs with two shock components, but they didn't match GRB 260310A. "However, as often occurs for bright GRB afterglows, none of our standard RS plus FS models..." could explain the GRB.

A different explanation matches the light from this GRB.

"Our long-term X-ray monitoring of the X-ray afterglow identifies a peculiar late-time rebrightening at â¼20â30 days, after a phase of rapid decay," the authors write. "This behavior is difficult to accommodate within a single FS model and may instead indicate a late episode of energy injection that refreshes the shock or additional structure in the outflow, such as a two-component jet."

While GRBs were initially seen as single-angle cones emanating outward from supernovae, that explanation hasn't held up. Two component jets with forward and reverse shocks more accurately explain complex light from some GRBs. In this model, the jet features a bright, inner core, and a dimmer outlying sheath.

This schematic shows a two-component jet model. It shows a central, compact jet surrounded by a wider, sheath-like jet. It also shows the Reverse Shock and Forward Shock. Image Credit: J.D. Myers (NASA).

A jet seen head-on like other GRBs is also ruled out, whereas a jet seen from the side, and having two components, can explain the observations. "A low-velocity jet seen (approximately) on-axis would not be able to combine the early peak and late rebrightening in a single jet model, whereas an off-axis two-component jet can accommodate both these peaks," the researchers explain.

The GRB's relative dimness compared to others is not because it's intrinsically less bright. It's because of our viewing angle. "We showed that viewing effects solve the apparent tension in the burstâs properties. The slow rise and delayed onset of its optical afterglow support the scenario of a jet seen off-axis," the authors write.

Understanding the viewing angle only explains some of this oddball GRB. It's unusual late re-brightening phase is also odd, even for a two-component jet.

"This late-time rebrightening represents a critical test for the two-component jet model," the researchers explain. "If interpreted as the emergence of a narrow jet core viewed further off-axis, it would imply extreme luminosities and energetics for an on-axis observer."

So what seemed like an unusually dim GRB, followed by an unexpected re-brightening, stems from our viewing angle.

âWhat appeared to us as an unremarkable GRB might have looked like a monster explosion to an observer looking straight down the jet's core,â notes Yang. âOur models suggest that the explosion packed roughly a billion years of the Sunâs energy output into a pencil-thin beam.â

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

#6527. NYC’s Hottest New Wine Bar Started With a DM Slide

An interview with the team behind El Camarón Peludo.

Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings.

Giovanni Cervantes and Tania Apolinar spent the last five years slinging tacos at breakneck pace to keep up with the lines at Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ramírez and rowdy World Cup crowds at Socceria. Now the duo is slowing things down a bit for their first full-service restaurant El Camarón Peludo, a playful wine and seafood spot in the West Village where guests linger over mariscos.

At the tiny, walk-in-only restaurant, the menu fuses Mexican seafood dishes with Spanish influences and excellent wine from around the world. For the project, Cervantes and Apolinar teamed up with chef Carlos Barrera, a Mexico City-born chef who has worked in Michelin-starred restaurants in Spain and hosted dozens of popular pop-ups around NYC. When I sat down with Cervantes and Apolinar, I planned to pick their brains about how and why they manage four wildly popular (and very different) New York City restaurants. Then I learned how much El Camarón Peludo was the result of fate: If it weren’t for space constraints, a tapas-fueled trip, and a social media superfan, the duo may have had an entirely different restaurant on their hands.

Pre Shift: Where did the idea for El Camarón Peludo come from?

Tania Apolinar: When we were looking at [the space], we considered making it a taqueria, but because of the [long shape of the restaurant], it wouldn’t have worked for that concept. We knew we wanted to do something different, focused on seafood and wine.

Giovanni Cervantes: I was in conversation with Carlos about this idea to serve mariscos in New York when we saw the space. We didn’t know [at the time], but we were setting up the basis of the menu because we were talking about what we like and what we miss a lot [from Mexico]. We also talked about [our past trips] to Europe. We were really interested in how to match [the style of European tapas and wine bars] with what we do, which is the Mexican approach.

How did you connect with Barrera for the project?

Cervantes: Carlos was one of the first clients that we ever had in Taqueria Ramírez. We met basically through that and through Instagram. He was always commenting a lot...

Cervantes: Exactly. Sending the flame emoji. Then soon enough, we find out that we were neighbors because he lives in Greenpoint, so we started seeing each other more often.

Apolinar: Then we did a pop-up with him serving his famous Trompo Negro, which is like al pastor with [a smoky black spice paste that is widely used in Yucatán and surrounding regions], and that was the first time we actually connected in a working setup. We’re really aligned and happy with the partnership.

Can you tell me about how you balance Mexican and Spanish influences on the menu?

Cervantes: When we found the space, we knew it was the perfect setup to try something different. Then we made a trip to Europe and a trip to Mexico. After we came back from Europe, I think I was feeling very “Europeanized.” I remember having a conversation with Tanya and Carlos about making it even more Spanish, and both of them were like, “What?” And I’m glad they [pushed back], because we definitely found the right balance.

Apolinar: We’re talking about Mexican and Spanish, but in the end, it’s about the seafood and the freshness, the product that we really want to stand out. That’s why [we serve a] very simple gambas a la plancha, and the carpaccio has that approach as well, but then other more Mexican classics [like tostadas topped with tuna or aguachile] have more sauces and all of that.

Cervantes: And it’s not just the food. The influence that we took from different parts of Europe is the setup, the vibe, the size of the plates, the type of space. We want the space to feel cozy and friendly.

How is the service different from your other spots?

Cervantes: At Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ramírez, it’s all about efficiency. Making it right, as fast as you can, and getting people in and out of the place. It’s nonstop volume. The consistency is awesome over there, and that’s [how we] measure that we’re making it right. Here it’s different. It’s more about the experience of the space and the music and the wine. [Our staff are] with these people for an hour or two, so you try to make it personal in a way. It feels different when you have that much time to see how people are enjoying the experience and transporting people to that world through what we’re doing. That’s comforting to me.

Now that you have four different restaurants around the city, how do you balance your time between them?

Cervantes: For Taqueria Ramírez, the very first one, we can sleep very well because almost everybody on the staff has been there since we opened. I’m just mentioning that because it’s all about building the right team because you can only be in one place at a time. Then at Carnitas, our partners [Yvon de Tassigny and Kari Boden] are really great and the plan was for them to be the day to day operators from the beginning. So right now we’re between El Cameron Peludo and Socceria because they’re the new babies and there’s a lot of work to do there.

Tania: It’s tiring, but at the end of the day, I’ve been enjoying it a lot. It’s nonstop but it feels rewarding to see the point of view of customers and make people feel happy and connect to them.

#6526. A Mysterious Explosion in Space Just Did Something Scientists Didn’t Expect

An explosion that initially appeared unremarkable in gamma rays went on to produce one of the brightest afterglows astronomers have recorded in the past 20 years. Its visible light became brighter than its host galaxy, and its X-ray emission unexpectedly intensified again weeks later.

An international research team believes the extraordinary behavior can be explained by the direction of the explosion’s powerful jet. Rather than pointing directly toward Earth, the jet was viewed from an angle that initially concealed its most energetic region. The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, suggest that some exceptionally powerful stellar explosions may be difficult to recognize from their initial gamma-ray flashes alone.

NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope detected the event, designated GRB 260310A, on March 10, 2026. Its initial burst of gamma rays lasted approximately 53 seconds and appeared to release relatively little energy. Over the following hours, however, its visible afterglow steadily grew brighter before eventually fading.

The contrast became even more pronounced at other wavelengths. Compared with samples of previously observed gamma-ray bursts, the event’s X-ray and optical afterglows ranked among the brightest 1%, while its radio emission placed it among the brightest 5%. Approximately three weeks after the explosion, the X-ray afterglow brightened again, remaining unusually luminous for more than a week and detectable for months.

“We see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,” says co-author Roberto Ricci, who led the radio observations. “We could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder.”

Gamma-ray bursts are among the most energetic explosions in the universe. Many occur when massive stars collapse and launch narrow jets of matter traveling at nearly the speed of light. As these jets collide with surrounding gas, they generate afterglows that can be detected in X-rays, visible light, and radio waves.

Astronomers typically observe the brightest gamma-ray flashes when a jet points almost directly at Earth. GRB 260310A appears to have been different. Its relatively weak initial emission, followed by an exceptionally bright afterglow, is consistent with a jet viewed from outside its most intensely beamed region.

“Much like a flashlight, the jet appears brightest when seen head-on. Most of our models are calibrated using events seen from that same perspective. This burst gave us a chance to look beyond that glare,” explains Yu-Han Yang, a postdoctoral scholar and lead author of the study.

The researchers propose that the explosion produced a jet with a narrow, highly energetic core surrounded by a wider, slower outflow. From Earth’s viewing angle, the broader outer regions would dominate the early afterglow, while much of the core’s radiation would initially be directed elsewhere.

As the jet slowed, its emission became visible across a wider range of angles. Radiation from the energetic core could then reach Earth, potentially explaining the delayed increase in X-ray brightness. This structured jet model offers a possible explanation for the unusual observations, although the precise configuration remains uncertain.

“We looked at it from a side angle. As the jet slowed down, its light became visible over a wider range of angles, allowing us to probe the jet’s shape, from its outer edges toward its inner core.”

The delayed X-ray brightening was particularly difficult to explain. “That was unexpected. At first, I thought another X-ray source was contaminating our observations. But the brightening really came from the afterglow,” recalls Yang, who coordinated the X-ray monitoring. “This prompted us to explore a more complex jet’s shape.”

To investigate the event, the international team, led by the ERC-funded BHianca group at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, combined observations from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, ESA’s XMM-Newton, the Einstein Probe mission, the Large Binocular Telescope, and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array. Additional observations from Calar Alto Observatory detected the signature of a supernova, confirming that the gamma-ray burst accompanied the death of a massive star.

The team’s models indicate that the jet’s central region may have carried vastly more energy than the initial gamma-ray measurements suggested. “What appeared to us as an unremarkable GRB might have looked like a monster explosion to an observer looking straight down the jet’s core,” notes Yang. “Our models suggest that the explosion packed roughly a billion years of the Sun’s energy output into a pencil-thin beam.”

The findings also point toward a population of stellar explosions that conventional gamma-ray observations may overlook. As powerful new sky surveys, including those conducted by the Vera Rubin Observatory, expand their coverage, astronomers expect to identify more afterglows from jets that are not directed toward Earth. Such detections could help establish how frequently collapsing massive stars produce relativistic jets and how those jets escape through the stars’ outer layers.

“Gamma rays are not the most efficient route to spot these hidden jets: we find them once in a blue moon,” concludes Muskan Yadav, a graduate student who contributed to the study. “Upcoming surveys will pick up hundreds of them. Identifying them among millions of variable sources won’t be easy, but it’s a challenge I’m excited to take on.”

Reference: “An Extremely Bright Slow-rising Afterglow from an Off-axis Jet in GRB 260310A” by Yu-Han Yang, Roberto Ricci, Eleonora Troja, Muskan Yadav, Yi-Han Iris Yin, Rubén Sánchez-Ramírez, Brendan O’Connor, Niccolò Passaleva, Alberto J. Castro-Tirado, Hendrik van Eerten, Simone Dichiara, Vincenzo Galluzzi, Narjes Shahamat Dehsorkh, Iván Agudo, Jesús Aceituno, Malte Busmann, Maria D. Caballero-García, Emilio Fernández-García, Daniel Gruen, Maria Gritsevich, Sergiy Guziy, David Hiriart, You-Dong Hu, Martin Jelínek, Alexander Kutyrev, Alzbeta Malenakova, Filip Novotny, Ignacio Pérez-García, Shashi B. Pandey, Jorma Ryske, Alfredo Sota, Jan Strobl, Hira Waseem and Siyu Wu, 28 October 2026, The Astrophysical Journal Letters. DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/aea990
