#6525. A Classic Thanksgiving Menu With Make-Ahead Tips

The editors at Bon Appétit take Thanksgiving very seriously. We are, in fact, in the business of furnishing readers with rigorously tested dishes destined for your family’s annual holiday table (and hopefully—eventually!—the treasured recipe box). What we’ve learned over the years is that—no matter how adventurous a cook might be 364 days of the year—when it comes to T-Day, most people don’t really budge from their traditional mainstays.

People often crave a classic, tried-and-true holiday meal. Guests expect it. So we’re happy to share this menu of Thanksgiving favorites from our archives to get you to the Rockwellian holiday spread of your dreams. These are the dishes we wait all year for: roast turkey and gravy, mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, stuffing, cranberry sauce, buttery rolls, and pumpkin pie. Plus a few tips for making elements ahead.

You’d be hard-pressed to conjure up a more quintessential bird than our 2017 covergirl. This whole-roasted, beautifully burnished Thanksgiving turkey gets a straightforward dry brine, keeping the white meat succulent and juicy.

You can’t beat Andy Baraghani’s make-ahead gravy, which you can prepare up to four days ahead. Reheat it with a bit of stock to revive that perfectly silky texture.

This recipe, originally published as “Ultra-Creamy Mashed Potatoes” in our 2017 Thanksgiving spread, includes its own list of not-to-miss tips for superior mashed potatoes. They’re so good, in fact, they retroactively earned the mantle of BA’s Best. Make sure you know where you’ve stashed the ricer (or food mill).

My colleague Chris Morocco probably didn’t expect his 2016 recipe to become the gold standard for green bean casserole. Yet it’s held that title year after year. No canned cream of mushroom soup here—the savory sauce is totally D.I.Y. The French’s Crispy Fried Onions, however, aren’t going anywhere.

The people have spoken: Victoria Granof’s 2012 stuffing recipe gets virtually dog-eared every Thanksgiving. It’s minimalist but has everything you expect from stuffing (technically “dressing” as it’s cooked outside of the turkey in its own casserole dish), including the quintessential quartet of herbs: parsley, sage, rosemary, and thyme.

Making cranberry sauce is the first order of business on my Thanksgiving menu. I usually whip up a batch of Priya Krishna’s 2019 version the weekend before and feel an outsized sense of pride that I’ve managed to tick one thing off the long prep list. Her recipe is a great starting (or ending) point, but you can jazz it up with a cinnamon stick, star anise, or a few cranks of black pepper if you’d like. Or sub in brown sugar for white—the choice is yours!

Try not to fill up on these buttery treasures before The Big Meal. Originally published in the iconic Fannie Farmer Baking Book, we featured these as part of our 2012 Thanksgiving menu in print. You can bake them ahead of time, let them cool, and keep them in the freezer for reheating. Or, if you’re feeling a little adventurous, try their distant cousin, Salt Bread, for even more oohs and ahhs.

Is it even Thanksgiving without pumpkin pie? Rick Martinez’s 2016 rendition is as classic as they come, and it tastes even better the next day (if you’re lucky enough to have any leftovers… come to think of it, maybe just plan on making two?).

You don’t have to cook the whole menu on Thanksgiving morning. Here’s what you can get out of the way:

Remember to account for oven space on Thanksgiving itself: The green bean casserole still needs baking, the stuffing needs its final uncovered bake, and the rolls need warming.

Maple-glazed turkey, garlicky mashed potatoes, pumpkin chiffon pie, and more recipes worthy of your Thanksgiving table.

#6524. Beyond the Iconic Potato Dish at New NYC Restaurant Somssi

There’s plenty of creative dishes coming out of this West Village kitchen

You’ve probably heard of the Potato Potato Potato dish at Somssi, the newest restaurant from Na:eun Hospitality. The triple-layered potato dish is the most labor-intensive dish on the menu but has also become the most popular order, with the kitchen going through up to 100 pounds of potatoes each week. The whimsical, caviar-topped dish really encapsulates what the restaurant is trying to achieve: “We should have serious food, serious hospitality, but we shouldn’t take ourselves too seriously,” says managing partner Ahris Kim. Here’s how the Somssi kitchen preps to create the newly famous potato and plenty of other dishes before a night of service.

Yukon gold potatoes are put through a ricer to become a cream and butter-heavy puree that is set in molds in the freezer. After being toasted in breadcrumbs, the logs of potato are wrapped in russet potato ribbons before being fried up to order.

Next is the ox tongue, which is brined for just over 16 hours before being slow-cooked in herbs, aromatics, and beef tallow for four hours. Huge cuts of tongue are carefully scored so they will get a great sear when they hit the grill. It’s served on a romesco sauce with just a bit of wasabi on the side.

Finally, pork loin is coated in ground shrimp for a creative schnitzel that is reminiscent of shrimp toast. The schnitzel is topped with a sweet-and-sour plum sauce that balances out the thick, crispy fried exterior. Scallop crudo is made up of pressed scallops surrounded with a strawberry sauce and topped off with gooseberries and peppers.

Watch the team at Somssi create creative dishes like a triple-potato bite and a show-stopping grilled tongue dish in this episode of Mise En Place.

The PBS Nature film "Tiger Island" captures rare glimpses of tiger behavior, including a mother, father and cubs spending time together ‪—‬ a first for these usually solitary cats.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A male tiger approaches his cubs and greets them with a head-bobbing motion while their mother rests nearby. The surprising interaction, captured in the PBS Nature documentary "Tiger Island," a two-part series that follows two big-cat families across Nepal.

The footage marks the first time a tiger "family" has been documented spending time together, and it could challenge conventional assumptions about how the seemingly solitary cats behave around their young, said Dan O'Neill, a wildlife biologist and filmmaker who contributed to "Tiger Island." Previously, it was thought that tiger moms raise their cubs for up to two years without any help from the male tiger.

"It just shows that we really know nothing about them," O'Neill told Live Science. "And they're so much more complex than people realize."

That's just one of the scenes in Tiger Island that challenges our understanding of the tigers' solitary nature. In another scene, a female tiger cares for another tigress's cubs.

"We have these very rigid ideas of how these animals live," O'Neill told Live Science. But the natural world is "diverse and ever-changing," and tigers are no exception, he said.

The footage of the female caring for another tiger's cubs could offer clues about how mother tigers protect their young. Male tigers, like male lions, sometimes kill cubs ‪—‬ a behavior known as infanticide ‪—‬ particularly when a new male takes over a territory. Allowing another female tiger to care for cubs might help more cubs survive to adulthood, O'Neill suggested. Previous observations of female tigers have shown females helping to co-parent each other's cubs, but it's a rare event.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To capture these scenes, the crew used drones with powerful optical-zoom lenses and quiet propellers to observe the tigers in places that were difficult to access without disturbing the big cats. Traditional camera traps often capture animals along trails, leaving much of their private lives unseen. O'Neill noted that the drone propellers were quieter than the local bees where the filming took place, thus giving the crew candid views of the tigers as they went about their lives.

Though tigers (Panthera tigris) are solitary animals, they often live close to or share habitat with human communities. That means tigers sometimes attack people and kill livestock, O'Neill said. "It would be absolutely naive and wrong to suggest that they [attacks on people] don't happen," O'Neill said. As a result, conservation efforts must account for the circumstances in which people and big cats encounter one another, rather than treating human communities as separate from wildlife, he said.

The same issue affects other big cats. O'Neill, a researcher with the wild-cat conservation organization Panthera, has spent years studying jaguars, pumas and snow leopards. He said the popular image of these animals living in remote wilderness can obscure how closely they overlap with human lives.

For O'Neill, conservation requires more than studying the animals' behaviors or protecting their habitats. It also means helping people who bear the cost of living alongside these apex predators.

"Helping those people is how you help tiger conservation," he said.

In the U.S. "Tiger Island" Part Two airs on Wednesday, Oct. 28 at 12:30 am on the PBS channel.

#6522. This Ancient Meteorite Hints at Mars' Warm, Wet Past

Mars is the subject of an ongoing, decades-long effort to understand its past. Its potential ancient habitability drives that effort. More than 20 missions have been sent to its surface (though many didn't survive the entry and landing). Two are operating there currently, Curiosity and Perserverance, and multiple orbiters scan the planet's surface from above.

Clues to Mars' past are in its rock, and the more ancient a piece of rock, the deeper the clues it can contain about the planet's ancient past. Visiting Mars with rovers is only one way to access the planet's rock. Fortunately, some chunks of Mars have been sent to Earth. Violent impacts have sent chunks of Mars rock into space, where they've eventually found their way to Earth as meteorites.

A Martian meteorite named Black Beauty set the standard for ancient meteorites from Mars when it was found in 2011. Most meteorites are found in deserts or in snowy/icy areas simply because they're more easily seen, and Black Beauty (Northwest Africa 7034, or NWA 7034) was found by nomads in the Western Sahara. Portions of it are about 4.43 billion years old, and Mars is about 4.5, maybe 4.6 billion years old. So Black Beauty is extremely ancient.

The Sahara Desert has yielded other ancient Martian meteorites, including Teghaza 001 (Teg 001), found in Mali in 2022. New research uncovered some unusual properties in Teg 001, and they're presented in new research.

The research is titled "A Martian meteorite that formed â³4.1 billion years ago samples Marsâ early crust and mantle," and it's published in the journal Science. The lead author is Yang Liu from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology. Scientist Carl Agee, director and curator at the University of New Mexicoâs Institute of Meteoritics (IOM), also played a leading role in the work.

"This sample probably came from an environment on Mars that was more Earth-like." - Carl Agee, University of New Mexico.

(A) shows the largest of the eight pieces of Teg001. (B) shows a cut section of a smaller chunk. Image Credit: Yang Liu et al., A Martian meteorite that formed â³4.1 billion years ago samples Marsâ early crust and mantle. Science0,eadz5646DOI:10.1126/science.adz5646

Ancient meteorites are rare finds and they're extremely valuable scientifically.

"Martian meteorites provide a record of the planetâs geological history," the authors explain in their research. "However, most are geologically young samples that are not representative of Marsâ surface, which is dominated by ancient rocks."

Most meteorites are young just because of selection effects. Meteorites are launched into space by impacts, and that favours young rocks, which are stronger. So meteorites tend to come from younger, basaltic volcanic rocks. More ancient parts of Mars crust are weaker because they're fractured and brecciated by impacts. Some ancient rocks are also sedimentary or clay-bearing rock. These rocks are weaker and much less likely to survive an impact that can launch them into space.

Teghaza is one of the rare ancient Martian meteorites.

"We describe the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001 (Teg 001), a slowly cooled igneous rock that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago," the authors write. "Its composition, mineralogy, and texture are distinct from other Martian meteorites." Distinct from other Martian meteorites, but also similar to likewise ancient Black Beauty.

âI realized that this one was a little bit like Black Beauty, not exactly, but it resembled it in the oxygen isotope values,â Agee said in a press release. "I looked at it microscopically and found domains within it that had high levels of manganese oxide, a compound being looked for on Mars by the rovers as an indicator of environments conducive to life.â

MSL Curiosity found rock fractures in Gale Crater that were filled with material rich in MnO. It suggests, but doesn't prove, that the planet's atmosphere once had free oxygen and oxygen-rich groundwater. That's still being debated.

Lead author Yang Liu and other Caltech scientists used a dating technique to find the age of tiny zircon crystals in Teg 001. Zircon crystals are important finding the age of ancient rocks because they can survive geological processes. They also contain trace amounts of elements with long half-lives. This is how Liu determined that Teg 001 is 4.1 billion years old. "We conducted ten measurements of U and Pb isotopes, in six shocked zircon grains with different morphologies, to determine their U-Pb and Pb-Pb ages," the authors explain.

Though Black Beauty is also ancient, the pair of meteorites are quite different from one another.

âThere are a few parts to Black Beauty that are around that age, but that whole meteorite itself is a conglomeration of many different rock types. Teghaza 001 is just one unadulterated rock type, and it's 4.1 billion years or older, so that was a big surprise,â said Agee. âIt's the oldest Martian igneous rock ever found by a huge margin, but in addition to that, it seemed to have these clues in its composition that suggested it had been in an environment that had fluids and water coursing through it.â

Teghaza 001 was found in several chunks adding up to almost 800 grams. Unlike Black Beauty, which is a congolomeration of different chunks, Teg 001 is a single rock type. Image Credit: UNM.

The isotope Oxygen-18 indicated that it had interacted with water in the past, most likely on the Martian surface. "The high Î´ 18O value of Teg 001 probably reflects assimilation of Î´18O-rich crustal material that had interacted with surficial fluids, or direct reaction of the magma with high-Î´18O fluids," the authors write. That finding supports the hypothesis that Mars was once warm and wet, a hypothesis supported by a growing body of evidence.

âWe also had these anomalous oxygen isotopes, and these domains that had high manganese levels, Agee said. "All of that was consistent with it being from a time on Mars, from the very, very beginning when the Martian environment was different from the time in which most of the Martian meteorites that we see were formed and erupted a few 100 million years ago when Mars was a dry desert, just like it is now. This sample probably came from an environment on Mars that was more Earth-like.â

This image shows a cut section of Teg001, with some of its features and contents labelled. Pigeonite (PgT) is particularly relevant, because it hosts fluid-altered Magnesium. "The Mg-rich interiors of pigeonite have been heavily altered by reactions with a fluid phase," the authors write. Image Credit: Yang Liu et al., A Martian meteorite that formed â³4.1 billion years ago samples Marsâ early crust and mantle. Science0,eadz5646DOI:10.1126/science.adz5646

Mars' early, potentially more Earth-like time period is called the Pre-Noachian period. Planetary scientists struggle to paint a clear picture of the Pre-Noachian because it was so long ago, and geologica processes and weathering have erased much of the ancient. Some research shows that Mars may have had global oceans during this period, a stunning difference from the frigid, dessicated planet it is today.

It's possible that billions of years ago, Mars had a global ocean, as shown in this illustration. That could explain the aqueous alteration in Teg001. Image Credit: By Ittiz - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=7861829

It's possible that Mars still has some simple, extant life. If it does, that life is hiding somewhere underground where the last of the planet's ancient water might be sequestered, away from the harsh radiation on the surface. But if the emerging picture of an ancient, warm and wet Mars is true, that would be the Pre-Noachian.

âIf there was ever abundant life on Mars, on the surface, not sequestered away in some subsurface, that would be the time that you would be looking at, the Pre-Noachian period,â said Agee. âIt's the very earliest time, and that was when maybe Mars still had a magnetic field, and it was shielded from radiation, and there were surface waters. There was a denser atmosphere. If primitive life was abundant in Mars. That is the time that is most likely for it to have happened.â

Most Martian meteorites are much younger than Teg001, only a few hundred million years old. It likely came from a place no rover has visited, possibly from Mars' southern highlands. Remote sensing shows that that ancient region has a similar composition to Teg001.

âThis is just one single meteorite. It's like going out, going back in time and chipping off a hunk of an outcrop, 4 billion years ago on Mars, and then we have this example of what was actually happening,â said Agee. âThat is why it's such a valuable sample. Weâve never found one like this before. The most exciting part about this find is its age, plus the alteration in the meteorite that indicates it has been in what I would call an Earth-like environment, with fluids coursing over the surface and volcanoes creating hydrothermal systems. There are surface waters and so on. And that's all reflected in the way that the meteorite has been sort of altered from its original state.â

"The presence of aqueously altered minerals, combined with bulk and mineral-specific oxygen isotope measurements, indicate that Teg 001 experienced reactions with fluids enriched in 18O, before ejection into space by an impact," the authors summarize in their paper.

#6521. A Breakthrough in Magnetism Could Make Computer Chips Use Dramatically Less Energy

Researchers have overcome a longstanding obstacle that has prevented promising materials from being used in ultra-low-power computer chips.

A promising class of materials could help dramatically reduce the electricity needed for computing, but a persistent problem has kept them out of computer chips. When these materials are made thin enough for modern electronics, the electrical and magnetic properties that make them valuable can disappear.

Researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces ultrathin films of bismuth ferrite that retain their essential properties and develop an additional form of magnetism with potential advantages for future computing devices. The findings were published in Nature Materials.

Bismuth ferrite belongs to a class of materials called multiferroics, which have interconnected electrical and magnetic properties. Within their crystalline structures, positive and negative charges are displaced in opposite directions, creating electrical polarization. Applying a small voltage can reverse that polarization, allowing information to be stored as binary data (ones and zeros). Because the electrical and magnetic states are linked, the stored information could also be read magnetically, potentially enabling memory and logic devices that consume far less power.

The obstacle is a phenomenon known as the “dead layer” effect. When multiferroic films become extremely thin, their atomic structures and chemical environments can change enough to disrupt their functionality. At the same time, internal electric fields can destabilize their polarization. Together, these effects can eliminate the ferroelectric and magnetic behavior needed for electronic applications.

The Brown team addressed both problems by carefully engineering the layers surrounding the bismuth ferrite. First, they grew the material on dysprosium scandate, a rare earth-based crystalline substrate with a smaller lattice spacing than bismuth ferrite. The mismatch places the film under compressive strain, helping preserve the atomic arrangement required for its electrical and magnetic properties.

The researchers also incorporated a metallic layer that screens unwanted electric fields, preventing them from destabilizing the film’s polarization. With both effects controlled, bismuth ferrite remained functional even at thicknesses of only a few angstroms. An angstrom measures approximately four billionths of an inch.

“We’ve established that we can get rid of the dead layer,” said Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. “We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want — down to a few angstroms — and it’s still ferroelectric, and it’s still magnetic.”

Beyond preserving the material’s original properties, the engineered structure enhanced its magnetic behavior. The researchers demonstrated that the thin film exhibits altermagnetism, a magnetic state with characteristics that could overcome some limitations of conventional magnetic materials.

“Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out,” Caretta said. “The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds — they can be fast, densely integrated, and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout.”

These characteristics could eventually support faster, more densely packed electronic components while reducing energy consumption. Although the researchers have demonstrated the material’s properties rather than a finished computing device, the technique addresses a major barrier to incorporating multiferroics into practical chips, particularly as artificial intelligence increases demand for computing power.

“We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials,” Caretta said. “The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that’s useful — and sometimes even better than what nature gives us.”

Reference: “Altermagnetic signatures and topological textures in ultrathin multiferroic BiFeO3” by Geo Fratian, Maya Ramesh, Xinyan Li, Evangelos Golias, Yousra Nahas, Sebastian Maria Ulrich Schultheis, Julian Skolaut, Marti Checa, Arundhati Ghosal, Evan Krysko, Paul Malinowski, Brendan D. Faeth, Jan Priessnitz, F. C. Fobasso Mbognou, Atsushi Hariki, Kosuke Sakurai, Mizuki Furo, Shashank Kumar Ojha, Morgan Congdon, Shiyu Zhou, Alexander Qualls, Kai Litzius, Christoph Klewe, Peter Meisenheimer, Jan Kuneš, Kyle Shen, Laurent Bellaiche, Libor Šmejkal, Darrell G. Schlom, Yimo Han, Sergei Prokhorenko, Ramamoorthy Ramesh, Paul Stevenson, Angela Wittmann and Lucas Caretta, 28 October 2026, Nature Materials. DOI: 10.1038/s41563-026-02786-1

The research was supported by the U.S. Army Research Office (W911NF-21-2-0162), the National Science Foundation (DMR-2039380, OIA-2327352) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-AC02-05CH11231).

Based on Topological Vortex Theory (TVT), altermagnetism should be regarded as an experimental clue toward geometric magnetic ordering, rather than a mature chip-ready solution. The notion that “engineering structures enable materials to outperform their natural states” represents a direction that human science has always pursued; however, researchers should further interrogate the topology, symmetry, and transport mechanisms, instead of mechanically adopting the performance promises found in mainstream narratives:

(1) Interrogate the geometric origin: Does this altermagnetic response arise from lattice symmetry, strain fields, or interfacial topological defects? Do not remain at the superficial level of describing merely “strong” or “weak” signals. (2) Distinguish between bulk materials and thin films: The potential properties already exist in the bulk material, while thin-film engineering merely “manifests” them. It is necessary to analyze which boundary conditions and symmetries are altered by the engineered structure. (3) Focus on the readout mechanism: Does the so-called “strong electrical signal” originate from the anomalous Hall effect, spin Hall effect, magnetoresistance, or other geometric transport effects? This is key to judging its true applicability. (4) Evaluate the speed advantage: One must consider dynamic time scales, damping, energy consumption, and thermal stability, rather than drawing conclusions solely based on the analogy that “antiferromagnets are faster.” (5) Be wary of overhyped claims: The increasing demand for AI computing power does not automatically imply that such materials can be integrated into practical chips; process compatibility and the difficulty of device integration must still be carefully assessed.

Mainstream physics frequently makes the leap from material properties to device performance; in contrast, the TVT framework demands that we ground our understanding in geometric structures, topological constraints, and observable mechanisms.

#6520. Queen's University Belfast Students Find Neptune's Elusive Trojan Asteroids

An international team led by researchers at Queen's University Belfast has made a discovery that has eluded astronomers for decades. Beginning in 1906, telescope observations revealed a population of asteroids leading and trailing Jupiter, which came to be known as the "Trojan" and "Greek" populations. Since then, astronomers have discovered similar "families" orbiting Saturn and Uranus, but not Neptune. Thanks to the Queen's-led team, the mystery of the missing Trojans has now been resolved!

As detailed in a paper that appeared in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, the team found these distant icy bodies by analyzing data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the next-generation telescope perched high atop the Andes in Chile. Thanks to Rubin's sharp optics and ability to rapidly survey the night sky (the fastest of any ground-based telescope), the team identified two asteroids and a candidate as permanent members of Neptune's trailing Trojans.

The team was led by Dr. Meg Schwamb, an astronomer and lecturer at the Astrophysics Research Centre, Queen's University Belfast (QUB). She was joined by researchers from the Instituto de Astronomia, GeofÃ­sica e CiÃªncias AtmosfÃ©ricas (IAG), the Planetary Science Institute (PSI), the DiRAC Institute, the Michigan Institute for Data and AI in Society (MIDAS), JHUAPL, the NSF's NOIRLAB, and multiple universities worldwide.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory's LSST survey will help scientists create a census of Solar System objects. Credit: Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA H.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory combines the resolution of its 8.4-meter Simony Survey Telescope with the LSST Camera, the largest digital camera ever built. Having commenced operations in June 2025, Rubin is currently conducting the largest survey of the southern sky - the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). At the same time, it is mapping the northern sky to create an ultra-wide, ultra-high-definition time-lapse record of the cosmos.

Through these surveys, Rubin will provide new insight into the mysteries of the cosmos, including Dark Matter and Dark Energy. It will map the Milky Way and its faint satellite galaxies, detect transient phenomena (supernovae, variable stars, rogue planets, etc.) and create an inventory of objects in the Solar System. This last objective was what drew Schwamb and her team to analyze data from Rubin's early test observations last year.

After combining this massive trove of data, the team identified the objects as primordial members of the elusive trailing Neptune Trojan population. "Early data from Rubin Observatory is already expanding our knowledge of the solar system's 'small bodies,' including asteroids, comets, and other minor planets," Schwamb explained in a QUB press release. "And these early observations have provided our clearest view yet of Neptune's trailing Trojan cloud."

A rendering of the inner Solar System showing the asteroids discovered by Rubin in light teal. Known asteroids are dark blue. Credit: NSFâDOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NSF NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R/NASA/Goddard/ESA/Gaia/DPAC

Previously, astronomers struggled to find Neptune's Trojan populations because of the difficulty of spotting such distant, faint objects as they moved across the night sky. For the past ten years, the Trojans have been crowded in a region of the sky that placed them in front of the Milky Way's center (relative to Earth-based observers), an extremely dense and bright part of the night sky that obscured any tiny light sources in the foreground. Said Schwamb:

The Trailing Cloud has now begun to move out of this region of sky and combined with the Rubin Observatory's unmatched depth and sky coverage, we've been able to double the number of known objects in this population on long-lived orbits. These discoveries offer a glimpse of just how transformative Rubin's data will be, with even more exciting findings expected in the years ahead.

The Rubin Observatory obtained images of these objects using different filters, which allowed Dr. Schwamb and her team to show that the Trojans leading and trailing Neptune have similar surfaces. As Rubin continues the LSST survey over the next nine years, it is expected to discover tens to hundreds of Neptune Trojans in both its leading and trailing population, plus tens of thousands of icy bodies in the Trans-Neptunian Region and Kuiper Belt.

Further Reading: Queen's University, The Astrophysical Journal Letters**

#6519. Scientists Say This Medication Could Be the Next “Wonder Drug”

A diabetes medication may protect against heart attacks and strokes through an unexpected biological mechanism.

Two medications used in people with type 2 diabetes produced dramatically different results when scientists tested their ability to prevent dangerous blood clots. In mice with injured blood vessels, sotagliflozin reduced clot formation by approximately 60%, compared with just 5% to 10% for the widely prescribed drug empagliflozin.

Researchers at Michigan Medicine also found that sotagliflozin suppresses excessive platelet activity, a process that can block blood flow to the heart or brain. Published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation, the findings suggest a possible explanation for the drug’s ability to reduce heart attack and stroke risk beyond its effects on blood sugar.

Sotagliflozin, marketed as Inpefa, belongs to a group of medications called sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) inhibitors. These drugs interfere with proteins that transport glucose through the body. Common treatments such as empagliflozin (Jardiance) and dapagliflozin (Farxiga) primarily block SGLT2, a protein that helps the kidneys reabsorb glucose. Sotagliflozin acts on both SGLT2 and SGLT1, which is also present in other tissues.

Although SGLT2 inhibitors have established cardiovascular benefits, clinical trials have shown that sotagliflozin can also reduce ischemic events, including heart attacks and strokes. These occur when blood clots or other blockages restrict circulation. The researchers investigated whether the drug’s broader action on glucose transport proteins might help explain this protection.

“A drug that can both decrease the risk for diabetes along with the risk for having a heart attack or stroke could be a turning point in our ability safely treat this growing population in the US and abroad,” said Michael A. Holinstat, Ph.D., M.S., co-senior author and professor of pharmacology, internal medicine, and surgery at the University of Michigan Medical School.

Scientists compared sotagliflozin and empagliflozin using blood samples from healthy volunteers and people with type 2 diabetes. Sotagliflozin significantly reduced platelet activation and made platelets less likely to clump together. Empagliflozin produced little or no comparable effect.

Platelets normally help stop bleeding by gathering at damaged blood vessels. However, excessive activation can produce clots inside arteries, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke. Sotagliflozin’s ability to suppress this activity may contribute to its cardiovascular benefits.

“These experiments showed that sotagliflozin has a unique effect, and blocking SGLT2 alone is not enough to inhibit platelet aggregation,” said Eugene Chen, M.D., Ph.D., co-senior author and Frederick G. L. Huetwell Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.

“Sotagliflozin may offer additional protection against blood clots, potentially lowering the risk of heart attack and stroke.”

The researchers next investigated whether inhibiting SGLT1 alone could account for sotagliflozin’s effects. When they genetically removed SGLT1 from mouse platelets, blood clot formation decreased by approximately 40%. However, neither this genetic approach nor treatment with mizagliflozin, a drug that selectively blocks SGLT1, fully reproduced sotagliflozin’s results.

This suggests that other biological mechanisms contribute to the drug’s ability to prevent clot formation. One possibility involves SGLT1 in endothelial cells, which form the inner lining of blood vessels and interact with circulating platelets. Researchers have not yet established whether these cells contribute to sotagliflozin’s anti-clotting effects.

“Sotagliflozin appears to be in the sweet spot because compounds that have higher levels of SGLT1-selective inhibitors can cause gastrointestinal issues,” said Bertram Pitt, M.D., co-author and professor emeritus of internal medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.

“We think this could be a wonder drug with potential to offer benefit for many conditions.”

Sotagliflozin is FDA-approved to reduce certain cardiovascular risks in adults with heart failure and in adults with type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and additional cardiovascular risk factors. The researchers hope to investigate whether its effects on clotting could benefit patients with other conditions, including chronic kidney disease and atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm associated with increased stroke risk.

The laboratory and animal findings provide evidence that sotagliflozin affects clotting through mechanisms beyond conventional SGLT2 inhibition. However, further clinical research is needed to determine how much this platelet effect contributes to preventing cardiovascular events in humans and whether it can do so without increasing bleeding complications.

“The search for medications that reduce the risk of life-threatening blood clots without increasing the risk of bleeding has continued for decades,” Holinstat said.

“Sotagliflozin has now been demonstrated to serve both functions and may represent the next advancement in prevention of blood clots, heart failure and stroke in patients with and without diabetes.”

Reference: “SGLT1/2 inhibitor sotagliflozin, but not SGLT2-selective inhibitor empagliflozin, attenuates platelet activation and thrombosis” by Livia Stanger, Krista Goerger, Xu Zhang, Pooja Yalavarthi, Andrew Rickenberg, Adriana Yamaguchi, Mariane Flores Nascimento, Ashleigh Kilgore, Heeseo Kim, Xiaokang Wu, Yanhong Guo, Anna R. Dahlgren, Jifeng Zhang, Jordan A. Shavit, Bertram Pitt, Y. Eugene Chen and Michael Holinstat, 14 October 2026, The Journal of Clinical Investigation. DOI: 10.1172/JCI201899

A new study revealed that people who rely on AI for basic tasks like math problems became less motivated over time. In response, Live Science polled its readers to see if they agree with these findings.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Artificial intelligence (AI) tools like chatbots are becoming part of everyday life, helping people write messages, answer questions and learn new skills. While some of these processes may save people time, a new study reveals a possible new downside of consistently relying on AI assistance.

The research, presented at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco earlier this month, found that people who relied on AI assistance for tasks like math problems and reading comprehension were more likely to give up or struggle when the assistance was taken away. The findings suggest that leaning too heavily on AI could weaken people's motivation to push through challenges.

The research raises the question of what happens when people stop exercising their brains. So do you think AI is making you less motivated, or even "dumber," or is it simply making you more efficient? Vote in our poll, and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

#6517. What Could Split a Black Hole in Two?

We all know that black holes can collide. It has happened since black holes began to form, early in cosmic time. The result is always a clash that gives off gravitational waves and a giant bang. Since black holes have such strong gravity, it's almost impossible to imagine a way that any force could break one apart. Yet, that's the task that a group of scientists in Europe set for themselves.

In a study of possible mechanisms for black hole fragmentation, Francesco Sannino of the University of Naples Federico II in Italy and the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark, along with Giacomo Cacciapaglia (Laboratoire de Physique ThÃ©orique et Hautes Ãnergies) and Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, both from the Quantum Field Theory Center, conducted a series of calculations showing that under the right conditions, a black hole could split up into two black holes. It's an unusual possibility, to say the least, but the team has calculated what needs to happen if such an event were to occur.

The two pieces would have to stay apart, according to Sannino. "The two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate," he said. If such a split-up could happen, the event horizon of the black hole would form a trouser-like shape as the split-up proceeded. Essentially, it would form two legs of a pair of pants, which is why the team called it a "pair-of-pants topology."

That's one possibility for what happens if/when a black hole splits into pieces. No one has seen such an event (yet), so it's still largely theoretical. There's one major impediment, however. That's called entropy, the measure of how many different microscopic ways a physical system can be arranged while still appearing the same from the outside. For example, a rock's shape can remain solid and static until some outside force changes it, such as heating. In the case of an ordinary, non-rotating black hole, breaking it into two pieces would reduce its entropy and make the process thermodynamically unlikely.

The black hole at the centre of M87. It has a measured spin, so theoretically, if conditions were right, it could break apart, according to a new study. Credit: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration

However, let's say we have a rotating black hole, spinning very rapidly. According to the team, such a system could break up into two pieces. However, they have to separate quickly, or risk falling back together. So, it turns out it could happen if both black holes have to keep rotating as fast as they possibly can (or close to it). But what would cause the split to occur? The answer lies in the rotation. It alters the relationship between black hole mass, its angular momentum as it spins, and entropy. It's possible that change could lead to the black hole fragmenting. If so, then the next steps are for the black hole "twins" to move apart and retain the momentum and speed of the original.

Focusing just on black holes, it seems pretty unlikely that such events have happened, but they don't want to say it's never happened. According to Sannino, the possibility is there, but in specific cases. "We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einsteinâs theory, and we are working to quantify this," he explained. "We expect small primordial black holes to be more prone to splitting than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may detect a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT can search for signals from tiny black-hole fragments that might form during mergers."

When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies

#6516. Depression Symptoms Improved in Just 48 Hours After a Single Psychedelic Dose

A single dose of psilocybin produced rapid antidepressant effects in a small Swedish clinical trial, with improvements lasting for weeks.

A single dose of psilocybin, the psychedelic compound found in magic mushrooms, produced rapid improvements in depression symptoms in a small Swedish clinical trial. After six weeks, 53% of participants who received psilocybin were in remission, compared with just 6% of those given a placebo.

Some participants reported improvements within two days, and the antidepressant effects persisted for more than three months in self-reported assessments. The findings come from Sweden’s first randomized, double-blind trial of psilocybin for depression, conducted by researchers at Karolinska Institutet and published in JAMA Network Open.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are among the most widely prescribed treatments for depression, but they can take several weeks to work, cause unwanted side effects, and provide insufficient relief for some patients. Previous research has suggested that psilocybin may act more quickly, although much of that work has focused on treatment-resistant depression or depression associated with cancer.

The new phase 2 trial investigated whether psilocybin could also help people with more common forms of recurrent depression. Researchers enrolled 35 adults between the ages of 20 and 65 who had moderate to severe symptoms. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either 25 milligrams of psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin used as an active placebo because it produces noticeable physical sensations.

Both groups received psychotherapeutic support across five sessions before, during, and after treatment. During the dosing session, participants wore eye masks, listened to music through headphones, and were encouraged to direct their attention inward.

Researchers measured depression severity using the MADRS (Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale), with assessments conducted by clinicians who did not know which treatment each participant had received.

Eight days after treatment, depression scores had fallen by an average of 9.7 points in the psilocybin group, compared with 2.4 points in the placebo group. The 7.3-point difference was statistically significant and considered clinically meaningful. The advantage remained evident at assessments conducted 15 and 42 days after treatment, while participants’ own ratings indicated improvement as early as the second day.

“Our results suggest that psilocybin can provide rapid, clinically meaningful improvement in depression and may serve as an alternative to standard treatment when fast symptom reduction is important,” says lead author Hampus Yngwe, consultant psychiatrist and PhD student at the Department of Clinical Neuroscience, Karolinska Institutet.

Although the initial results favored psilocybin, the difference between the groups was no longer statistically confirmed after one year. At that point, 53% of participants in the psilocybin group remained in remission, but many people who had received the placebo had also recovered.

“However, the long-term effects are uncertain. Repeated treatments may be needed to prevent relapse. This needs to be investigated in larger studies.”

The findings suggest that a single supervised dose may provide relatively rapid symptom relief for some patients, but the small trial cannot establish how consistently those benefits will last or whether additional doses would improve long-term outcomes.

Psilocybin was generally well tolerated, with most reported side effects being mild or moderate and temporary. However, two participants who received the psychedelic experienced severe, persistent anxiety that required medical attention.

“It is important to emphasize that the treatment is not risk-free and that some patients may need extra support,” says Johan Lundberg, professor at the Department of Clinical Neuroscience and the Centre for Psychiatry Research, Karolinska Institutet, who led the study.

Another limitation involved the difficulty of keeping participants unaware of their assigned treatment. Psychedelics produce distinctive psychological effects, and almost everyone in the trial correctly guessed whether they had received psilocybin or the placebo. Such awareness can influence expectations and make it harder to determine how much improvement comes from the drug itself.

“We want to understand how factors such as treatment expectations and lack of blinding affect the results, as previous studies may have exaggerated the treatment effects,” says Hampus Yngwe.

Researchers are now turning to biological measurements collected during the trial to investigate how psilocybin might influence depression. Their next analyses will examine PET brain scans alongside blood and cerebrospinal fluid samples obtained before and after treatment.

One area of interest is synaptic density, which reflects the number of connections through which nerve cells communicate. Depression has been associated with disrupted communication between brain regions, while preclinical studies suggest that psychedelics may promote the growth of synaptic connections. Whether comparable changes occur in people receiving psilocybin remains an open question.

“Research suggests that the interaction between parts of the brain is impaired in depression and that this may be linked to changes in the connections between nerve cells, known as synapses. In preclinical studies, psychedelics have been shown to stimulate synaptic growth. We therefore want to investigate whether psilocybin alters synaptic density in the brain,” concludes Hampus Yngwe.

#6512. Scientists Discover a Common Treatment for Chronic Tendon Pain May Not Actually Work

A major clinical trial is challenging the effectiveness of commonly used injections for chronic Achilles tendon pain.

A widely used injection treatment for chronic Achilles tendon pain may offer little lasting relief, according to a clinical trial published in The BMJ. Researchers found that high-volume injections, including those containing corticosteroids, did not significantly improve pain or physical function compared with a sham procedure after one year. The findings challenge the routine use of injections for a condition that can persist for years and interfere with everyday movement.

Achilles tendinopathy causes pain, stiffness, and swelling in the tendon that connects the calf muscles to the heel. Approximately 6% of people experience the condition during their lifetime, and although exercise-based rehabilitation is the recommended treatment, up to 44% of patients do not recover. Many consequently explore other options, including injections intended to reduce pain and improve tendon function.

To investigate whether these treatments provide meaningful benefits, researchers conducted a randomized clinical trial involving 192 adults with midportion Achilles tendinopathy in Melbourne, Australia, between December 2019 and July 2022. Participants were 49 years old on average, and their symptoms had persisted for a median of two years.

The researchers divided participants into three groups receiving either a sham injection (64), a high-volume injection without corticosteroid (63), or a high-volume injection containing corticosteroid (65). The active injections delivered saline and local anesthetic around the affected tendon, with corticosteroid added in one group. Everyone also received the same exercise program, education, and guidance on modifying physical activity.

The primary measure was pain and disability after 52 weeks, assessed using the Victoria Institute of Sport Assessment-Achilles scale (0-100, where 100 is no pain or disability). Participants began the trial with an average score of 48.7, indicating substantial symptoms and functional limitations.

At the one-year follow-up, researchers obtained results from 181 participants (94%). Neither high-volume injection treatment produced a clear improvement in pain or disability compared with the sham procedure. The two active injection approaches also showed no meaningful difference in their overall outcomes.

Injections without corticosteroid failed to outperform the placebo at any assessment point. Adding corticosteroid produced small improvements after six weeks, but these benefits were short-lived. By 26 weeks, participants who received corticosteroid had worse outcomes than those given high volume injections without the drug.

An economic analysis found that corticosteroid-containing injections were less costly and generated more quality-adjusted life-years than sham treatment. However, the overall clinical results did not justify their routine use. No serious adverse events related to the trial treatments were reported.

The researchers acknowledged several limitations. Many participants were recruited through social media, which could affect how well the findings apply to other patient populations. Clinicians administering the injections also knew which treatment they were providing, and some observed differences may have resulted from chance.

Despite these uncertainties, the authors concluded that the evidence “should prompt clinicians to reconsider the rationale for using these injections in people with Achilles tendinopathy.”

In a linked editorial, John Orchard of the University of Sydney cautioned that corticosteroids are neither universally beneficial nor inherently inappropriate. Their use should depend on the patient’s circumstances, particularly when immediate symptom relief takes priority over longer-term outcomes (where short-term needs predominate over longer-term needs). He emphasized that patients should never be told corticosteroid injections will fix or cure tendinopathy.

“All clinicians recommending or performing corticosteroid injections for tendinopathy need to understand this trade-off and make every effort to explain the broader overview to the patient as part of the informed consent process,” he concluded.

Reference: “Efficacy and cost effectiveness of high volume injections with and without corticosteroid compared with sham for midportion Achilles tendinopathy (Inject trial): randomised controlled trial” by Peter Malliaras, David Connell, Anders Ploug Boesen, Rebecca S Kearney, Hylton B Menz, Dylan Morrissey, Shannon E Munteanu, Karin Gravare Silbernagel, Martin Underwood, Andrew Forbes and Terry P Haines, 28 October 2026, BMJ. DOI: 10.1136/bmj-2026-100807

#6511. Hera Probe Sees Asteroid Pair Separately for First Time

Planetary defense is a growing concern among the scientific community, as efforts have been made to design and implement missions meant to deflect incoming threats to the Earth well in advance. In 2022, NASA intentionally collided the Double Asteroid Redirection test (DART) planetary defense spacecraft into the smaller asteroid of the binary asteroid, Didymos and Dimorphos, with the latter being the smaller one. While the goal was to ascertain if deflecting an asteroid is feasible, how did this influence the geological characteristics of Dimorphos, and what can it teach us about planetary defense missions?

This is the task of a brave robotic explorer known as Hera, which is a spacecraft mission led by the European Space Agency (ESA) in cooperation with NASA and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Hera recently sent back its first image of Didymos and Dimorphos, which orbit each other as they orbit the Sun, with the image revealing the two asteroids separated, as opposed to seeing a single dot. This comes after Hera was launched in October 2024 and is now about 1,280 kilometers (795 miles) from the well-known binary asteroid, the latter of which is about 197 million kilometers (122 million miles) from Earth. While the larger Didymos is estimated to be 780 meters (2,559 feet) in diameter, the much smaller Dimorphos is estimated to be about 151 meters (495 feet) across.

âFor the very first time we are seeing through Heraâs own eyes the very double asteroid system that the mission was designed and built for,â said Ian Carnelli, who is the ESA Head of the Systems Department and the Hera mission manager. âOur views will much grow sharper as Hera comes closer. We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos â the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action â on 25 November [2026].â

As noted, the goal of the Hera mission will be to conduct follow-up observations and data collection for NASAâs DART planetary defense mission. For this mission, the DART spacecraft intentionally impacted Dimorphos with the goal of ascertaining whether impacting an object could deflect it away from impacting Earth. The intentional impact occurred in September 2022 at 6.1 km/s (3.8 mi/s), resulting in not only slowing Dimorphosâ orbit around Didymos by 32 to 33 minutes, with the initial goal being at least 73 seconds. Thus, the mission was deemed a resounding success, and the researchers even observed an ejecta plume from the surface of Dimorphos as far as 10,000 kilometers (6,214 miles) into space.

Aristic rendering of Hera approaching Dimorphos. (Credit: ESA-Science Office)

Along with conducting observational analyses of the post-collision Dimorphos surface, Hera will also deploy two shoebox-sixed CubeSats named Milani and Juventas since Hera canât fly that close to the surface. While Milaniâs task is to perform a close-up mineralogical analysis of the DART impact site, Juventas will be tasked with using ground-penetrating radar to peer about 100 meters (328 feet) beneath Dimorphosâ surface to ascertain whether its interior is solid rock or a loose rubble pile which has been proposed by researchers.

As noted, planetary defense is rapidly becoming a growing concern among not only the scientific community, but governments worldwide. This is primarily driven by our growing awareness of the number of asteroids in our solar system that cross Earthâs orbital path, but also the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor that blew out windows and injured more than 1,500 people, primarily from broken glass. But with this concern comes how to address, and a combination of NASAâs DART and Hera missions are providing key insights into how to deflect potential asteroid impactors that could cause widespread death and destruction if one impacts Earth.

What new insights into Didymos and Dimorphos will Hera and other space missions make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

The promise of AI automation to fix the administrative problems facing universities is a fallacy. These systems will only increase the burdens of already-struggling institutions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Universities are at a critical point as students and faculty embrace the use of AI. Already, universities like Harvard are introducing courses that feature an AI avatar as an "instructor."

The promises AI offers higher education are familiar: an increase in efficiency as a consequence of less administration, more teaching coverage, better feedback and smarter assessment. But introducing artificial intelligence (AI) systems in an attempt to fix these problems is not the answer. If anything, AI systems will magnify and speed up the bureaucracy that is driving universities' decline.

In practice, the more likely outcome is darker: AI will not simply sweep away the bureaucratic machinery of universities; it will give that machinery a new regime of AI compliance — more policies, more forms, more trackers, more oversight roles and more work downloaded onto faculty who are already stretched thin.

The danger is not that AI will destroy universities but that universities will use AI to preserve the very processes that make them dysfunctional. If this happens, we might see faculty spending less time on research, less time on teaching, and more time on activities that do not directly contribute to the production of knowledge and education of students.

This is already evident in the existing assessment system in the U.K., but shades are creeping into systems elsewhere, providing a window into the future for U.S institutions. A single piece of student work may pass through a plagiarism-detection platform, a grading interface, a moderation spreadsheet for faculty to share feedback, a grade-transfer system, and an exam-board record. Each stage generates its own logins, deadlines, exception rules and audit trails. None of this is inherently malicious. Anonymous marking, moderation, appeals, accessibility and academic integrity are legitimate concerns. But when each concern is implemented as a separate system, the combined effect is administrative incoherence.

In essence, faculty become the human interface between incompatible platforms, spending their time reconciling grades and chasing missing evidence rather than teaching. While this example pertains to U.K. universities, the trend to expand the administrative staff extends to North America. AI simply introduces a new opportunity to increase administration.

AI could, in principle, solve this. It could integrate systems, automate routine reporting, draft feedback, identify inconsistencies and remove duplicate data entry. Yet the institutional incentive is rarely to remove work; it is to make work visible. A university that automates a broken workflow does not necessarily simplify it. It may simply produce faster reports about the broken workflow, more sophisticated dashboards and more elaborate evidence of compliance. The bureaucratic impulse survives by changing its vocabulary: risk management, assurance, transparency, governance, responsible innovation.

At least one possible outcome is that universities will create AI-use policies, require module-level AI statements, mandate disclosure forms, introduce approved-tool lists and establish review committees. Faculty will be asked to redesign assessments, monitor suspected misuse, document their decisions, complete training, and explain their approach to students. Much of this labor will be invisible. It will appear not as a new job title but as an additional expectation attached to teaching.

When something goes wrong, the academic is exposed; when the system works, the institution claims the credit. That asymmetry is corrosive.

That asymmetry is corrosive. It teaches committed staff that careful judgment is not valued as expertise but rather as a compliance risk to be managed, and the consequences will fall unevenly. Experienced faculty, after voicing their concern to no avail, may leave, retire early or disengage. Early-career academics, already precarious because they don't have tenure, will have the least power to resist. Students will receive less of the resource that matters most: sustained intellectual attention.

One possible outcome is that universities will encourage the development of faculty AI avatars and cut hours and employment. The institution will then justify hiring more ‪—‬ not fewer ‪—‬ compliance and "educational enhancement" staff to manage and maintain these AI avatars, negating the idea of efficiency and cost savings. In this scenario, bureaucracy will expand to manage the problems created by its own expansion while undercutting quality for the students who are paying high tuition fees. One might need to hire staff for oversight of these avatars, administrators and lawyers to manage licensing agreements, quality control staff in case things go wrong, and IT teams for integrating them into learning platforms and websites.

There is an alternative to the administrative tasks. AI should be governed by a simple institutional rule: no new compliance requirement without the removal of an equivalent existing burden. If a university requires assessment redesign to accommodate AI, or the introduction of new technology, it should provide protected time, technical support and a single integrated platform. If it expects faculty to manage AI use, it must give them clear institutional backing rather than leaving them to improvise. And critically, it should show how the technology makes work more efficient before rolling it out across the board.

But the deeper issue is not technology but institutional purpose. A university exists — or should exist — to cultivate understanding, judgment and intellectual independence. If its systems consume faculty time, fragment the student experience, and reward documentation over learning, then AI becomes another instrument of managerial self-preservation. The question is not whether universities can adopt AI. It is whether they can resist using AI to automate their own absurdities.

If they cannot, the outcome will be an educational system that looks progressively sophisticated while becoming increasingly hollow ‪—‬ full of monitoring, low on trust; rich in measuring, poor in teaching; obsessed with compliance, indifferent to the people who make education possible; overly procedural sans intellectual life. It will become an audited theater of learning not worth students' time.

#6508. Einstein’s Equations Reveal an Unusual New Way Space-Time Can Transfer Energy

Einstein’s equations suggest that gravity may be capable of a process resembling the one behind powerful solar explosions. In a new theoretical study, physicists show how gravitational field structures can change their connections and transfer energy into matter. They call this process “gravitational reconnection.”

Luca Comisso of Columbia University and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile describe the discovery in Physical Review D. Their work reveals a mathematical connection between gravity and the behavior of plasmas, electrically charged gases found in stars and throughout space.

In plasmas, magnetic field lines can become stretched and twisted until they rearrange through a process called “magnetic reconnection.” This releases stored magnetic energy and drives powerful events such as solar flares.

“Magnetic reconnection is when these field lines, in some specific configuration, break and reattach in a different configuration,” Comisso said. “When they break and reconnect, they release energy.” He added, “It takes energy from the magnetic field and gives it to the particles in the plasma, producing explosions, energetic events.”

Gravity operates differently because Einstein’s theory describes space-time as a four-dimensional structure rather than three-dimensional space.

“Because space-time is four-dimensional rather than three-dimensional, gravity involves something like field ‘sheets’ rather than field lines,” explained Comisso. “Adding one dimension to a line gives you a plane. You can think of it as putting many lines together to form a ‘sheet.’”

These sheets are mathematical structures, not physical surfaces. The researchers found that when the conditions preserving their connections break down, the sheets can reconnect, allowing energy to transfer from the gravitational field into matter.

The researchers uncovered this behavior by expressing Einstein’s equations using different mathematical variables, revealing similarities with equations that describe plasmas. Their study builds on earlier research with Maricarmen A. Winkler that identified previously unrecognized constraints on how space-time can evolve.

“Einstein’s equations contain constraints on how space-time can evolve that are not immediately apparent,” said Asenjo. “By revealing these hidden new properties, we can begin to understand the fundamental rules governing how this gravitational reconnection process behaves.”

“Some implications are hidden in the equations, and they are not straightforward to capture just by looking at them,” Comisso said. “You need to rewrite them in a different way, and then you can exploit that behavior.”

One potential application involves merging black holes, where extreme gravity severely distorts space-time. Scientists rely on powerful computer simulations to predict the gravitational waves produced by these collisions, which detectors such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) are designed to measure.

The newly identified constraints could help researchers determine how gravitational fields must behave without calculating every detail of their evolution.

“It helps us predict some patterns of the space-time,” Comisso said. “Even without doing the full calculation, we know that space-time needs to behave in a certain way, that it needs to satisfy those constraints.”

Gravitational reconnection remains a theoretical discovery. Researchers must now investigate whether it occurs in astrophysical environments, how much energy it could transfer, and whether it might produce detectable signatures in gravitational waves.

Reference: “Reconnection of gravitational fields” by Luca Comisso and Felipe A. Asenjo, 28 October 2026, Physical Review D. DOI: 10.1103/lmqy-pf9k

The research was supported by the National Science Foundation and NASA.

#6507. Space Outposts Beyond the Moon May Rely on Planetary AI

NASA plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 for the first time since Apollo 17 in 1972. But the famed agency has no intention of stopping there, as they plan to establish a permanent human presence on the Moon through a slow and meticulous process involving power, resource extraction, and habitat technologies. However, with the soaring use of artificial intelligence (AI) in our everyday lives, how could this emerging technology be used to identify new landing sites for future outposts on the Moon and possibly Mars?

Now, a team of researchers from The Ohio State University might have contributed to how AI can be used for future space outposts. As discussed in a recent study presented at the 58th Annual Meeting of the Division for Planetary Sciences (DPS 58) of the American Astronomical Society, the researchers introduced how a novel AI model could be used to both identify safe landing sites and develop a human outpost strategy at those landing sites. The model is called LUMINA, which is an agentic AI framework designed to help mission planners evaluate safe landing sites on the lunar surface, specifically focusing on key resources like water ice, along with potential scientific value.

To identify prime landing sites, LUMINA doesnât just rely on orbital images. It incorporates a myriad of lunar surface data, including topography and terrain hazards, scientific value, geology, surface properties, and even comparing the candidate landing sites to each other. As a result, LUMINA demonstrates a keen ability to identify landing sites across the lunar surface that could maximize mission success and effectiveness for both human habitation and science. But the researchers donât want to limit LUMINA to the Moon, as they envision LUMINA contributing to other planetary bodies, specifically Mars.

âAI systems are going to become critical tools for space exploration that will help humans analyze the millions of images and datasets that future missions will require,â said Gokce Inal, who is a PhD candidate in Civil Environmental and Geodetic Engineering at The Ohio State University and lead author of the study. âThis work is meant to serve as a bridge between those two worlds, AI and planetary science.â

LUMINA is built upon previous research by this same group called the Large Language-and-Vision Assistant for Lunar Exploration (LLaVA-LE), which demonstrated its ability to analyze and describe orbital images of the lunar surface. The LLaVA-LE model is currently available on arXiv, was recently presented at the CVPR2026 AI4Space Workshop in June 2026 and can be found on GitHub.

As noted, NASA has ambitious plans to establish a permanent human presence on the lunar surface with the long-term goal of sending humans to Mars. Developing the necessary technologies to accomplish both goals is part of NASAâs Moon to Mars Architecture, which is a constantly evolving strategic framework designed to develop and test vital technologies that will allow humans to work and live on the Moon that can then be used for human missions to the Red Planet. These technologies include power systems, transportation, habitation & life support, robotics & construction, in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), communications, and more. The question then becomes how can AI, and specifically the LUMINA model, be used to further develop these technologies?

âNASAâs Artemis program creates important opportunities for our research,â said Inal. âAs new lunar data becomes available, their results can improve systems like ours and better support future mission planning.â

Of the technologies listed above, ISRU plays a crucial role in using local and available resources for crew use and survival. This includes water ice for drinking, bathing, fuel, and even oxygen from electrolysis, and using the lunar regolith to potentially grow plants and for construction. Also known as âliving off the landâ, ISRU aims to reduce, and potentially eliminate, the need for resupplies from Earth. Essentially, it wants to create a self-sustaining system exactly like life on Earth.

How will LUMINA help plan future space outposts on the Moon and Mars in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6506. This Unusual Spider’s Genome Is Roughly 50% Larger Than a Human’s

Scientists have sequenced the unusually large genome of a trapdoor spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert, uncovering surprising features of its DNA.

A spider no bigger than a quarter has a genome roughly 50% larger than the human genome. Known as Aptostichus stephencolberti, this elusive trapdoor spider lives beneath California’s coastal dunes and carries 4.6 billion DNA base pairs. Researchers at the University of California, Davis, have now sequenced its genome, uncovering features that could help explain how spider DNA has evolved.

“At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it’s not the largest genome among the spiders, but it’s significant,” said Jason Bond, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology. The research, published in the Journal of Heredity, marks the first time scientists have sequenced the genome of a species in this spider family.

The spider’s enormous genome is not packed with an unusually large number of genes. Instead, approximately 77% consists of repetitive DNA sequences, stretches of genetic material copied many times throughout the genome. Its DNA is organized into 52 chromosomes, compared with the 46 chromosomes typically found in human body cells.

Another feature involves telomeres, protective structures at the ends of chromosomes. Spiders lack the conventional telomere repeat sequences found in many other animals, a difference that may help explain why their chromosomes evolve more rapidly than those of vertebrates.

“It lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal Tree of Life,” Bond said.

A. stephencolberti lives in coastal sand dunes between the San Francisco Bay Area and Monterey, often sharing beaches with people who never realize the spiders are there. Females spend their entire lives inside underground burrows lined with silk and concealed beneath hinged, camouflaged doors. They detect vibrations from approaching prey and rapidly emerge to capture unsuspecting insects and other small animals.

Although these spiders use venom to subdue their prey, they are not dangerous to humans. According to Bond, among the more than 50,000 known spider species, only about 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to people.

The genome sequencing is part of the California Conservation Genomics project, a state-funded initiative developing genetic resources to support wildlife conservation. Because trapdoor spiders rarely travel far from their burrows, populations can become genetically isolated when their habitats are separated. Examining their DNA could help scientists identify distinct populations that may need protection.

“We Californians love our beaches and trapdoor spiders share them with us,” Bond said. “We’re hoping to understand how things like climate change, fire and urbanization might be impacting the genetic diversity of species.”

The spider’s limited coastal range makes it particularly vulnerable to environmental changes. Rising sea levels threaten the dunes where it lives, while invasive species place additional pressure on its habitat. “They’re going to be incredibly sensitive to sea-level rise, but they’re also very sensitive to invasive species,” Bond said.

The species has an unusual connection to comedian Stephen Colbert. In 2008, after learning that Bond had named another trapdoor spider after musician Neil Young, Colbert demanded similar recognition. He made his case during the “Who’s Not Honoring Me Now?” segment of his former Comedy Central program, “The Colbert Report.”

Bond granted the request, naming the species Aptostichus stephencolberti (the “t” in Colbert is silent). The spider’s oversized genome now provides an unexpected scientific distinction for an animal named after a comedian known for playing an exaggerated, self-important television pundit.

Beyond conservation and evolutionary research, spider genomes may help scientists investigate venom compounds with potential medical or agricultural applications. Some molecules found in spider venoms are being studied for their possible use in pain relief, while others could offer new approaches to controlling agricultural pests.

The full range of these substances remains largely unexplored, and the newly sequenced genome could provide a foundation for further investigations.

“We don’t really know what’s out there in terms of untapped natural product diversity for venoms,” Bond said.

Reference: “Reference genome of the Californian trapdoor spider Aptostichus stephencolberti Bond 2008 (Araneae: Mygalomorphae: Euctenizidae)” by Stephen Richards, Emma Jochim, Lacie Newton, James Starrett, Ruta Sahasrabudhe, Oanh Nguyen, Eric Beraut, Colin Fairbairn, Samuel Sacco, William Seligmann, Merly Escalona, Robert D Cooper, H Bradley Shaffer, Erin Toffelmier and Jason E Bond, 8 September 2026, Journal of Heredity. DOI: 10.1093/jhered/esag069

This research was supported by the California Conservation Genomics Project, with funding provided to the University of California by the state of California, State Budget Act of 2019 and by the National Science Foundation.
