#6505. Doctors Just Completed the First Spinal Cord Transplant. Experts Aren’t Sure It Should’ve Happened.

Surgeons in Russia fixed a broken spinal cord with a transplanted segment using polymer glue, but experts fear the patient may end up worse off.

The history of medicine is filled with firsts, and those pioneering attempts are often met with criticism and skepticism. On December 3, 1967, South African surgeon Christiaan Barnard performed the world’s first human-to-human heart transplant, and the daring procedure filled the world with fascination and apprehension. Although Barnard’s famous medical intervention came with its own bevy of controversies, especially the politics of organ transplantation in an apartheid state, the science backing heart-to-heart transplants was sound (in fact, just three days later, surgeons at Stanford University Hospital performed the first heart transplant in the U.S.).

The same cannot necessarily be said for the world’s first human-to-human spinal cord transplant, which took place earlier this month at the Sklifosovsky Institute for Emergency Medicine in Moscow, Russia. According to New Scientist, the operation was carried out by Chinese surgeon Xiaoping Ren, who replaced a damaged segment of a patient’s spinal cord with a corresponding segment provided by a brain-dead donor.

While details about the procedure are limited (including its level of success), Ren says the operation involved polyethylene glycol (PEG), a kind of biological glue that was used to fuse the donor’s spinal cord to the recipient’s. Some evidence suggests that PEG can play an important role in spinal cord repair, but the glue hasn’t been used at this scale before.

“A unique surgical procedure, which lasted 12 hours, was performed at the Sklifosovsky Institute of Emergency Care,” Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said in a translated press statement on the hospital’s website. “The patient, who was facing complete immobility, now has a chance to recover. He is now feeling well.”

Ren has long championed spinal cord transplantation, and in 2021 he co-authored a paper that made the case for it and walked through how the procedure might work. One of his co-authors was Sergio Canavero, who had previously pitched human head transplants (an idea that was likely a bit too Frankensteinian for the U.S. medical community). As for the spinal cord transplant, some surgical experts remain skeptical about the procedure’s ethics, its effectiveness, and its toll on the patient’s well-being.

“I’m concerned for the patient’s safety as they likely will be much worse off after this procedure, given the need to recover from a substantial surgery, with very little benefit,” Melissa Andrews, a spinal cord specialist at the University of Southampton, told New Scientist.

Of course, the need for such a procedure is immense. Millions of people worldwide live with debilitating spinal cord injuries, and Ren’s “fusion” technique could help restore their mobility and improve their quality of life. Animal studies have also shown some hopeful signs. Earlier this year, researchers led by Michael Lebenstein-Gumovski published a study in PLOS One reporting that three paralyzed pigs were walking on all four legs 60 days after treatment with a polyethylene glycol-chitosan glue. (Lebenstein-Gumovski also works at the Sklifosovsky Institute, though he wasn’t involved in the spinal cord transplant.) However, as New Atlas notes, that study differs from a transplant in one key way: It involved freshly severed spinal cords, not ones that had already adapted to extensive nerve damage.

For now, the medical world will have to wait for the full results to learn whether spinal cord transplants are truly possible, or whether they remain frustratingly out of reach.

#6504. Ceres' Water Ice Can Mask Massive Surface Salt Deposits

The dwarf planet Ceres is arguably one of the most overlooked and underappreciated planetary objects in the entire solar system. This could be because while Ceres has the same dwarf planet designation as Pluto, Ceres is largely considered an âasteroidâ since it resides the in main asteroid belt. However, along with being the largest object in the main asteroid belt, Ceresâ mass comprises between 25 to 30 percent of all the mass of the entire main asteroid belt. Despite its lack of recognition, Ceresâ interior is layered like most rocky planets, including Pluto, and its surface displays evidence of past water ice activity (also called cryovolcanism) with several âbright spotsâ, which are highly reflective salt deposits. But what can these salt deposits teach scientists about Ceresâ formation and evolution?

Now, a pair of researchers from the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) might have inched our way to better understanding a connection between Ceresâ water ice activity and surface salt deposits. As discussed in findings published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets (JGR: Planets), the researcher presented evidence that past data might have been incorrect regarding the amount of salt deposits previously observed by NASAâs Dawn spacecraft, which explored Ceres from 2015 to 2018.

For the study, researchers used a combination of Dawn spacecraft data and a series of computer models to examine the evolution of surface water ice and salt deposits on Ceresâ surface. The primary motivation behind the study was to fill a longstanding knowledge gap regarding observational results of surface water ice and salt deposits versus whatâs actually happening. Specifically, this study focused on the transition of water ice to salt deposits through evaporation (scientifically called sublimation) and whether data collected from Dawn accurately estimated the amount of water ice and salt.

In the end, the researchers found that the salt deposits might be hidden by the water ice deposits theyâre mixed with, with the salt deposits potentially existing in larger amounts than previously hypothesized, estimated to be between 30 to 50 percent greater. Additionally, they found that landslides (scientifically called mass wasting) contribute to more surface ice being exposed, which then evaporate, leaving behind the salty bright spots observed by Dawn. They note some water ice deposits could have been observed by Dawn that could have been recently exposed from landslides.

âWe proposed a qualitative model of long-term surface evolution of Ceres' salty ices based on observations that is akin to thermal segregation [sorting] on icy satellites,â the study notes. âIce in deposits with salts sublimates more readily and may move to colder areas, resulting in a feedback that creates compositional differences between colder, icy surfaces and warmer, salt-richer regions. Ongoing replenishment of ice at the optical [visible] surface is required to reconcile multiple detections with geologically negligible lifetimes of ice. The finding resolves an existing paradox about how salt-rich deposits arise in the Ceres near-surface; they are likely not initially salt-rich but instead result from enrichment of salt at the optical surface by sublimation of salty ices.â

Essentially, the salt-water ice deposits are sorted based on heat and evaporation, the salt within water ice mixture causes the water ice to evaporate faster, leaving behind the salt deposits. This creates a feedback loop that results in different mixture amounts and types among separate water ice and salt deposits. Additionally, the surface water ice is exposed from landslides, adding to this evaporation feedback loop. Finally, the study fills a longstanding misunderstanding between how salt deposits are formed and evolve, in that they donât start out with heavy amounts of salt. Instead, they start out with low amounts of salt but have their salt contents increase from the evaporation of water ice that also contains salt.

What new insights into Ceresâ salt deposits and water ice will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6503. Scientists Create a Tiny Electronic Device That Can Learn Like the Human Brain

A breakthrough in brain-inspired electronics could lead to devices that process information and learn without relying on conventional computing architectures.

A single nanoscale electronic component can perform three different jobs, switching electrical current, storing information through resistance, and remembering past electrical activity through changes in capacitance. Researchers in Germany have demonstrated this versatility using unusual oxide materials, opening a possible path toward computer hardware that processes information and adapts more like the human brain.

Today’s artificial intelligence systems can consume enormous amounts of electricity, particularly during the training of large models. One reason researchers are exploring alternative hardware is that conventional computers typically separate memory from computation, requiring information to move between them. The brain operates differently. Its neurons communicate through synapses, connections that can change in response to repeated or intense signals. This ability to adapt, known as neuroplasticity, helps the brain learn from experience.

A research team at the University of Würzburg, working within the Würzburg and Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat, has developed electronic components that reproduce several important behaviors of neurons and synapses. Their approach uses complex oxides, materials whose electrical properties can be adjusted to support different functions within the same system.

The devices rely on two materials: lanthanum aluminate (LaAlO₃, or LAO for short) and strontium titanate (SrTiO₃, or STO for short). Both are electrical insulators individually, but when brought together, they form an extremely thin conductive layer at their interface. This layer, called a quasi-two-dimensional electron gas, allows electrons to move through a region confined to the boundary between the materials.

By carefully patterning the interface, researchers can create microscopic conductive pathways, sometimes described as “electron highways.” Electrical current can displace oxygen atoms within the structure, altering its resistance. These changes allow the device to be “trained” through electrical stimulation, providing a physical mechanism for storing information about previous activity.

Using this material platform, the Würzburg researchers created components that can act as a transistor, a memristor, or a memcapacitor. A transistor controls current flow, while a memristor stores information through changes in electrical resistance. A memcapacitor behaves differently: its ability to store electrical charge depends on its previous electrical state.

The researchers demonstrated that a single nanoscale component can provide any of these three functions depending on how it is connected electrically. This versatility could simplify the design of artificial neural networks built directly into electronic hardware.

“What makes our platform so exciting is that we can realize very different functions using the same material system. This brings us closer to hardware that not only computes but can also learn directly within the component and temporarily store information,” says Soumen Pradhan, a postdoctoral researcher at the Chair of Technical Physics in Würzburg.

“Brain-inspired computing” seeks to reproduce some of the brain’s information processing and learning mechanisms in electronic circuits. Rather than continually transferring data between separate processing and memory units, these systems aim to combine computation, information storage, and adaptation within individual components.

“Complex oxides are an especially exciting field for us because they combine many electronic properties in a single material platform. That is precisely what makes them so interesting for a new generation of energy-efficient and adaptable computer hardware,” says Ralph Claessen, spokesperson at JMU Würzburg for the Würzburg–Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat and a co-author of the study.

One potential application is health monitoring. Wearable devices incorporating this type of adaptive electronics might eventually analyze physiological signals directly, without requiring separate computing hardware for every processing task.

Such “self-learning” sensors could potentially track heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood oxygen saturation, or blood glucose while adapting their responses to incoming data. Processing signals locally could also reduce the energy required to transfer information to external systems.

For now, these possibilities remain long-term goals. The research demonstrates the underlying electronic functions rather than a complete artificial intelligence system or medical sensor. Further development will be needed to establish whether the technology can deliver practical improvements in energy consumption, reliability, and performance.

Reference: “Oxide interface-based polymorphic electronic devices for neuromorphic computing” by Soumen Pradhan, Kirill Miller, Fabian Hartmann, Merit Spring, Judith Gabel, Berengar Leikert, Silke Kuhn, Martin Kamp, Victor Lopez-Richard, Michael Sing, Ralph Claessen and Sven Höfling, 9 April 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-71642-2

A woman's unexplained abdominal pain led doctors to a diagnosis that has only been documented a few hundred times over the past 400 years.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 42-year-old woman in Somaliland, Africa

The symptoms: The woman went to the hospital after having three years of chronic, dull pain in her lower abdomen, as well as a growing sense of heaviness in her abdomen that had worsened in recent months.

When doctors reviewed her medical history, they learned that, three years earlier, she had experienced a number of symptoms that seemed to indicate a pregnancy. She recalled her abdomen growing over time and feeling "fetal movements," her doctors noted in a report of the case. Then, the movements stopped, the abdominal growth halted, and the enlargement gradually subsided. She had not sought medical care during or after this apparent pregnancy.

What happened next: When doctors physically examined the woman's abdomen, they found a hard, irregular mass that extended to her belly button and barely moved when they touched it. Blood tests showed mild anemia, meaning she had fewer healthy red blood cells than normal. Her white blood cell count and kidney and liver tests were normal, and a pregnancy test was negative.

An ultrasound revealed a calcified mass and an empty uterus. Calcification is a buildup of calcium that hardens tissue into a solid mass.

To get a better look at the mass, which occupied the woman's lower abdomen and pelvis, the doctors ordered an advanced CT scan to create a 3D model. The imaging revealed that the mass contained clearly identifiable fetal skeletal structures, including a skull, a spinal column, ribs, and arm and leg bones. The mass measured roughly 7 by 5 inches (18 by 13 centimeters).

The diagnosis: Doctors concluded that the woman had a lithopedion, or "stone baby." The term comes from the Greek words "lithos," meaning stone, and "paidion," meaning child.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a typical pregnancy, an egg is fertilized in a fallopian tube — the structure between the ovaries and the womb — and then travels into the uterus, where it implants in the uterine lining. By contrast, lithopedions most often start as abdominal pregnancies,‬ a type of ectopic pregnancy in which the embryo instead implants on the lining of the abdominal cavity.

There, the embryo shares the space with organs like the stomach, kidneys and appendix. These misplaced pregnancies are almost never viable and are highly life-threatening for the mother. Because the placenta attaches directly to delicate abdominal organs and blood vessels, these carry a severe risk of catastrophic internal bleeding.

If the fetus dies at a developmental stage when it is too large for the mother's body to naturally break down and absorb, her immune system can sometimes treat the retained tissue as a foreign object. To protect the mother from inflammatory complications and infection, the body progressively deposits calcium over the fetal remains, creating a protective casing. In this case, the calcified fetus likely accounted for the woman's chronic abdominal pain and increasing sense of heaviness, her doctors concluded.

The treatment: The doctors performed abdominal surgery to completely remove the calcified fetal mass from the woman's pelvis.

The day after surgery, she developed a mild fever and nausea, but both resolved with treatment. She remained stable and improved during her hospital stay before being discharged in good condition.

Follow-up visits over the next six months showed she had healed well, with a complete resolution of her abdominal pain.

What makes this case unique: Only about 340 cases of lithopedion have been documented in the medical literature over the past 400 years, with the earliest documented in 1582.

This woman's case stands out because she was 42 years old, while many recent cases have been diagnosed in postmenopausal women. (Women typically experience menopause around 51 to 52 years old.) In these cases, the initial ectopic pregnancy occurred during the woman's childbearing years, but she unknowingly carried the calcified remains for decades before developing symptoms. For example, a 74-year old woman from India carried her "stone baby" for more than three decades. By contrast, the woman's recent case was caught after only three years.

The case also highlights the challenges of maternal healthcare in resource-limited settings such as Somaliland, where a lack of access to routine prenatal care and early pregnancy scans can lead to delayed diagnoses. That said, the successful use of advanced 3D imaging and complete surgical recovery demonstrate that excellent outcomes are possible even in these constrained environments, the doctors noted.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

#6500. Martian Polar Crater Ice Shifts with Seasonal Frost

The planet Mars shares many landforms and weather patterns with the Earth, including changing seasons, volcanoes, canyons, dust storms and dust devils, and water ice. But one feature that Earth and Mars share among the eight planets in our solar system are polar ice caps. Both are one of each planetâs striking features, but the major difference is while Earthâs polar ice caps are both comprised of water, Marsâ north polar ice cap is only comprised of water while its southern polar ice cap is carbon dioxide. The reasons for this are determined by altitude, but Marsâ northern polar ice cap is one of the most studied regions primarily due to its water ice composition. But how does the north polar ice cap water ice change with the seasons compared to Earth, and what can this teach scientists about Marsâ climate history?

Now, an international team of researchers might have shed new light on this conundrum. As discussed in a recent study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, the researchers challenged our understanding of ice deposits in Marsâ northern polar ice cap region. The primary motivation behind this study was to fill a longstanding knowledge gap regarding the seasonal changes in Martian polar ice deposits, specifically focusing on craters. The researchers note that better understanding seasonal changes in polar ice cap deposits could help gain insights into long-term climate changes on the Red Planet.

For the study, the researchers analyzed images of 36 craters within the northern polar ice cap region of Mars. The images were obtained from NASAâs Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera between 2006 and 2025. This time period is also referred to as Mars Years (MY) 28â38 since one year on Mars is 668 Earth days. The goal of the study was to identify how polar ice deposits on crater floors changed with seasons, specifically whether the deposits increased or decreased in size based on winter or summer months, respectively.

In the end, the researchers found that 32 of the 36 craters exhibited changes in bright deposits, broadly indicating ice deposits are expanding and shrinking with the seasons. Of the remaining four craters, the researchers didnât observe changes in brightness. The researchers note that seasonal frost deposits on the outside of each crater could be responsible for the changes in brightness.

âNot all craters exhibit changes in frost coverage from one Mars year to the next,â the study notes. âFor a given Mars year, only a subset of craters show altered frost conditions relative to previous years, while others maintain similar or nearly identical frost extents. This spatial heterogeneity suggests that seasonal frost cycles and interannual mass balance are localized processes rather than cap-wide phenomena. Local topography, crater geometry, and microclimatic conditions likely modulate energy balance and vapor transport, leading to crater-specific responses to broader climatic forcing.â

Essentially, the researchers found the changes in crater ice deposits are triggered by local climate changes, as opposed to being triggered by larger climate changes. The reason why understanding Marsâ climate changes is important is to help pin down specific triggers, whether itâs seasonal or related to other factors. For example, Mars experiences much larger climate changes on grander scales compared to Earth due to the Red Planetâs planetary tilt having much larger swings than Earth. However, as this study demonstrates, local climates are still capable of delivering their own changes disconnected from the larger climate picture. This study identifies seasonal changes in polar ice deposits while providing motivation for future modeling work that could help expand our understanding of localized climates on Mars.

What new insights into Mars polar crater ice will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6498. Scientists Finally Identify Mysterious Creature Nearly 90 Years After It Was First Found

A millipede first collected nearly 90 years ago in South Australia has finally been identified as a new species, challenging assumptions about where its moisture-loving relatives can survive. Named Colobothrix deckeri, the species belongs to the family Dalodesmidae, which typically inhabits damp environments. Yet its original collection site receives just 400 to 500 millimeters (15.7 to 19.7 inches) of annual rainfall, making it the first member of its family recorded from such a dry region of Australia.

The new species also possesses an unusual microscopic feature. Mature males in Dalodesmidae and certain other millipede families have tiny, ball-shaped structures on their legs called sphaerotrichomes, normally topped by a long, pointed bristle known as a seta. In C. deckeri, that bristle is reduced to a short, blunt rod. This distinctive anatomy inspired the new genus name Colobothrix, meaning “stunted hair.”

The discovery began with a specimen collected in 1936 on South Australia’s lower Yorke Peninsula. It remained unidentified in the South Australian Museum (SAMA) until 2015, when German researcher Peter Decker encountered it while examining borrowed museum specimens for his doctoral research on a different millipede family, Paradoxosomatidae.

Recognizing that the animal belonged to Dalodesmidae, Decker sent photographs of its microscopic features to Australian millipede specialist Robert Mesibov. The specimen provided the first evidence that this family occurred in dry South Australia. Mesibov searched the original collection area in 2016 and 2017, but neither expedition located another specimen. He later named the species in Decker’s honor, publishing the description in the peer-reviewed, open-access journal ZooKeys.

Unknown to the researchers at the time, additional specimens had already been collected about 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of the original location. In 2010, arachnologists Michael Rix and Danilo Harms were surveying spiders and leaf-litter invertebrates on Kangaroo Island when they discovered a remarkable new assassin spider species in the island’s relatively wet northwestern region. Their collections also included several unidentified millipedes, which were deposited in the Western Australian Museum (WAM).

The island’s devastating 2020 bushfires later destroyed the original collection site, raising fears that the rare assassin spider might be approaching extinction. During a follow-up survey in 2021, arachnologist Jessica Marsh found the spider at additional locations several kilometers (a few miles) away. Her collections of other invertebrates also contained specimens of the unidentified millipede.

In early 2026, Mesibov discovered the Western Australian Museum’s millipede record online and contacted curator Mark Harvey. Close-up photographs supplied by Harvey confirmed that the Kangaroo Island specimens belonged to the same species collected on the Yorke Peninsula in 1936.

Mesibov subsequently visited Kangaroo Island and successfully located living specimens near the earlier collection sites. “Third time lucky!” said Mesibov. “I found the new millipede alive and well this year at relatively wet sites not far from its 2010 and 2021 localities.”

He collected several specimens for the formal species description and future genetic research. The specimens collected in 1936, 2021, and 2026 are now housed at the South Australian Museum.

Although C. deckeri has been confirmed on Kangaroo Island, researchers still do not know whether it survives at its original Yorke Peninsula location. That mainland site receives considerably less rainfall than the species’ known habitats in northwestern Kangaroo Island.

Mesibov suspects that the peninsula’s underlying limestone could provide a possible explanation for how the millipede survives in such a dry environment.

“The 1936 locality is underlain by limestone,” said Mesibov, “and the rock is broken where it is exposed at the ground surface. I wonder if the species survives in small voids in this bedrock, as a relict from wetter periods in South Australia’s past. That might explain why I couldn’t find it in 2016 and 2017, and how it could persist in such a dry climate.”

Reference: “Two new millipede genera and species from Kangaroo Island, South Australia (Polydesmida, Dalodesmidae, Spirostreptida, Cambalidae)” by Robert Mesibov, 23 October 2026, ZooKeys. DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1295.214938

#6497. New Research Resolves the Mystery Behind Van Gogh's The Starry Night

Starry Night, the iconic painting by legendary Impressionist Vincent Van Gogh, has inspired debate among art historians and astronomers for decades. Was the painting something that Van Gogh was spontaneously inspired to create in the early morning hours in July 1889, or did it present a realistic depiction of the night sky over Saint-RÃ©my (where he painted it)? According to a recent study conducted jointly by South Korean telescope manufacturer SLLAB and the School of Space Research at Kyung Hee University, it's the latter.

For over a century and a half, scholars focused primarily on religious and symbolic interpretations of the painting. It was not until the mid-1980s that studies were presented that analyzed its astronomical aspects. These were conducted by UCLA art historian Albert Boime (1984) and Harvard astronomer Charles Whitney (1986), who examined celestial correspondences and proposed constellation identifications based on a mid-June date. However, the two reached conflicting conclusions, and no studies since have examined the painting using observational geometry.

The study, presented in Scientific Reports (a Nature journal), instead narrows the dates on which a crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades star cluster (which appear closely together in the painting) fell within Van Gogh's field of view. The study's first author, Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, CEO of SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University's School of Space Research, has spent years building telescopes and observing the night sky and was inspired to weigh in on the debate.

(a)The stars in The Starry Night (1889) overlaid by the real stars after matching for size, orientation, and position; red dashed lines show the residual differences. (b) The stars in CafÃ© Terrace at Night (1888), left, and the stars around the Summer Triangle. Credit: Kim et al., Scientific Reports

"To an observational astronomer, the cluster of stars in The Starry Night is the Hyades in Taurus," he said. "But the moment I read the earlier studies explaining it as Aries, I heard the painting calling to me." The research builds on Kim's previous book (released in 2025) and began with two field trips to France in 2019 to gather additional evidence and add quantitative data. Traditionally, the painting was dated to June 18th, 1889, based on a letter Van Gogh wrote to his brother, Leo.

However, on that date, the Moon was in its waning gibbous phase, which does not match the slender crescent in the painting. On July 22nd, the Moon was a crescent, and the Hyades cluster would have been seen rising in the east alongside Venus (placing it in the Taurus constellation). In the past, that date was thought to be one when Van Gogh experienced one of his seizures, but cross-analysis of the original French and Dutch letters and the details mentioned in both suggests his seizure began in late July.

Using on-site photographs taken in Arles, the team verified Van Gogh's field of view overlooking the RhÃ´ne River. Afterward, they traveled to Saint-RÃ©my, where they located the spot where Van Gogh drew the landscape in preparation for his painting. They then conducted a statistical shape analysis to confirm that the five central stars in the painting corresponded to the Hyades cluster, which matched even more closely in the pen drawing Van Gogh made after he finished the painting.

These results suggest that the sky in the painting was based on actual observation rather than pure impressionist feeling. The methods employed could also be extended to other historical night paintings, leading to collaborative efforts between astronomers and art historians. The team has already used the same method on another of Van Gogh's famous creations that features stars in the sky - CafÃ© Terrace at Night (painted in 1888) - and found a possible match to the Summer Triangle asterism.

"I hope this work prompts a renewed, multidisciplinary look at the sequence and working methods of the Saint-RÃ©my paintings, and at Van Gogh's movements that summer," Kim said. "Our conversation with Van Gogh's other skies is still ongoing. We plan to tell those stories one by one."

#6495. Scientists Discover That a Giant Bird Thought Extinct for Thousands of Years Never Actually Disappeared

Ancient DNA analysis has challenged a 150-year-old belief about a giant bird thought to have disappeared after the last Ice Age.

For more than 150 years, scientists believed that enormous crane bones found in European caves belonged to a giant bird species that disappeared after the last Ice Age. Now, ancient DNA has overturned that identification, revealing that the supposedly extinct bird was actually a larger version of a species still living in Europe today.

Researchers at Bournemouth University (BU) found that the fossils attributed to Grus primigenia belonged to the common crane. Their findings also raise questions about whether other prehistoric birds classified as extinct species were simply larger forms of birds that survive today.

The mystery began in the 19th century when French biologist Alphonse Milne-Edwards examined unusually large crane bones discovered in caves in southern France. Believing they represented a distinct species, he named the bird Grus primigenia. The remains dated to the end of the last Ice Age and were long considered evidence of an extinct giant crane.

To investigate the bird’s identity, a team led by Dr. John Stewart, Professor of Evolutionary Paleoecology at BU, analyzed ancient DNA from 18 crane bones recovered across England, Wales, France, Germany, and the Balearic Islands. Working with the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, Sweden, the researchers used genetic evidence to determine which species the bones belonged to.

“Previous studies had merely used the size and shape of the bones to attempt to understand these large birds. The use of DNA analysis has given us a more accurate picture of what they represent,” Stewart explained.

The genetic findings indicate that the oversized fossils belonged to common cranes rather than a separate extinct species. Stewart believes differences in body size between male and female cranes may have contributed to the original misidentification.

“We suspected that these large cranes were not extinct and instead represented larger, modern European common cranes. We believe that the reason for the mistaken identity was that cranes have large males and smaller females, and we think this contributed to previous speculation that there were two different species: the living, common crane we see today and the extinct, larger species,” Stewart said.

Although the DNA evidence clarifies the birds’ identity, it leaves another question unanswered: Why were some prehistoric common cranes considerably larger than those living today?

“The challenge going forward is to investigate the reason for the cranes decrease in size. Wetland drainage and human land use changes are what we suspect, but more work is needed to resolve that,” Stewart said.

The researchers plan to investigate whether changes in wetland habitats and human land use contributed to the reduction in crane body size. These remain possible explanations rather than established causes.

The findings suggest that some prehistoric bird species identified primarily through fossil measurements may need to be reconsidered. Differences in bone size do not necessarily indicate separate species, and ancient DNA could help determine whether other supposedly extinct birds were actually larger or smaller populations of surviving species.

“While it is true that many species of birds are vulnerable to human actions today, it may be that we have overestimated the number of extinctions in the past,” Stewart said.

“Some of these may instead represent size changes to living species,” he concluded.

Reference: “Ancient DNA study resolves the taxonomic status of the extinct large Palaearctic crane Grus primigenia Milne-Edwards, 1871 (Aves: Gruiformes: Gruidae)” by John R. Stewart, Rebecca Rickard, Sheila Hamilton-Dyer, Keith Dobney, Veronique Laroulandie, Josep Antoni Alcover, Joan Femenias-Gual, Nadja Pöllath, Erik Ersmark, Bodil Cronholm, Per G. P. Ericson and Love Dalén, 1 October 2026, Royal Society Open Science. DOI: 10.1098/rsos.260699

Paleoproteomic analysis of fossils from northern China reveals that Denisovans had a distinctive physical appearance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The enigmatic and now-extinct Denisovans of China shared traits with Neanderthals, modern humans and Homo erectus, according to a new study that looked at ancient proteins and fossils. But the Denisovans also had several unique skull traits and genetic variants that made them a distinctive ancient human group, according to the researchers ‪—‬ and these traits have now revealed a new face for a Denisovan man.

In the study, published Oct. 21 in the journal Nature, researchers analyzed Denisovan skulls from the archaeological site of Xujiayao in northern China. The Denisovans were a group of ancient humans who lived in Asia and disappeared around 30,000 years ago. This human relative was first identified in 2010 from the DNA of a finger bone discovered in a cave in Siberia.

The Xujiayao bones and teeth were excavated in the late 1970s, long before scientists knew about the existence of Denisovans, and were initially thought to be either Neanderthals or archaic Homo sapiens due to the shape of the fossils and their age: 138,000 to 199,000 years old.

But recent advances in paleoproteomics ‪—‬ the study of bone and tooth proteins that persist longer than DNA ‪—‬ have helped researchers identify Denisovan individuals due to specific genetic variants that differentiate them from other ancient human groups.

In the new study, researchers used paleoproteomic analysis on 20 remains from Xujaiyao and determined that all of them were from Denisovans. This determination then allowed the researchers to study the skull bones closely and figure out what Denisovans might have looked like.

The Xujiayao skulls had some features similar to H. erectus, the researchers wrote, including a low and wide braincase and thick cranial bones. But they also had anatomical features more similar to those of Neanderthals and modern humans, particularly in their bicuspids (the teeth between the canines and molars). The researchers also identified some unique Denisovan cranial traits. The back of the skull, for example, was more vertical and less rounded than in Neanderthals or modern humans.

Armed with a better understanding of Denisovan skull shape from the Xujiayao fossils, the researchers compared them with East Asian Denisovan remains that some experts have assigned to other species, such as Homo juluensis and Homo longi. But the researchers identified similarities that may preclude splitting Denisovans into different species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This unique combination of morphological traits, distinct from H. erectus, modern humans and Neanderthal-lineage hominins, supports the assignment of most members of East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo as Denisovans," they wrote in the study. This means that Denisovans may have been one human lineage that adapted to diverse ecological zones across Asia over hundreds of thousands of years.

"It is still possible that there are some other lineages that existed in East Asia during the time Denisovans are known to have existed," study co-author Qiaomei Fu, director of the Ancient DNA Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Live Science in an email.

"We know from DNA that Denisovans were a very varied group genetically, which split early into different populations," Chris Stringer, a paleoanthropologist at the Natural History Museum in London who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email. "These could have developed a lot of morphological variation, which may well surprise us as the sample of fossils grows."

The researchers also produced a new reconstruction of what a Denisovan man might have looked like. A previous DNA study suggested that Denisovans likely had dark skin, brown hair and brown eyes. The new reconstruction shows the Denisovan looking directly at the viewer, with his low, wide braincase mostly obscured by dark hair flowing back from his massive brow ridge. There are clear similarities between the Denisovan man and Neanderthals as well as modern humans, but the Denisovan has a distinct visage all his own.

Xing, S., Wu, Z., Shao, Q., Ge, J., Bennett, E. A., Rao, H., Lin, S., Zhao, Y., Liu, F., Liu, Y., Zhou, K., Feng, X., Jiangzuo, Q., & Fu, Q. (2026). The proteome of Middle Pleistocene Xujiayao and common Denisovan morphology. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11132-z

#6492. Researchers May Have Solved a Puzzling Contradiction in the Ryugu Sample

The Solar System's asteroids are sometimes referred to as fossils because they preserve evidence of the conditions when the Solar System formed. Asteroids are critically different than their planetary counterparts. On the rocky planets, the rock itself has been subjected to billions of years of change. On Earth, tectonic plates have melted rocks, exposure to water has altered its mineral content, and pressure deep inside the Earth has transformed its crystalline structure. Cosmic and solar radiation has also driven fundamental changes on some worlds, and across Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, a mixture of these factors have altered the rock.

But asteroids and the parent bodies they came from haven't been subjected to all of these forces. In many ways, they remain unchanged from the early days of the Solar System, 4.5 billion years ago. They haven't remained completely unchanged; that would be next to impossible. But their ancient state and what it can teach us about the Solar System's history is why we've sent missions to collect samples and return them to Earth.

In 2020, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA)Hayabusa 2 successfully completed its sampling mission to asteroid Ryugu and returned its precious sample to Earth. Almost six years after its arrival on Earth, the Ryugu sample is still generating valuable scientific results, as researchers examine its mineralogical and chemical composition.

The newest results are in research titled "Pervasive poorly crystalline Mg-rich hydrous silicate material in C-type asteroid matrices." It's published in Nature Communications Earth and Environment, and the lead author is Reon Okumura from the Division of Geosciences and Civil Engineering at Kanazawa University, Japan.

Ryugu and other carbonaceous chondrites present an apparent contradiction. It involves aqueous alteration, where contact with water creates mineralogical and chemical changes in rocks and minerals. Aqueous alteration isn't a rare action that happens only in space environments; it's common on Earth. The best-known example is how clay forms from common silicate rocks in Earth's crust, from exposure to water. It's basically how soil is created.

A JAXA official successfully retrieving the 16 kg capsule that it contained a sample from the asteroid Ryugu. (Courtesy: JAXA)

There's obviously no soil on Ryugu, but there is aqueous alteration. "C-type asteroid-derived samples, including Ryugu and carbonaceous chondrites, consist primarily of fine-grained matrices of magnesium-rich hydrous silicates formed by aqueous alteration," the paper states.

The contradiction stems from the matrix of minerals in the asteroid. There seems to be two components, each altered under a different set of aqueous conditions. That implies that Ryugu's interior matrix is patchy, which is highly improbable. An asteroid can be clumpy on a macroscale, but how can it have two components in the same mineral matrix? That's been a nagging question in cosmochemistry: how can aqueous alteration happen to some of the matrix while leaving some of it more intact?

The authors write that Ryugu's matrix is "commonly interpreted as mixtures of serpentine- and saponite-like phyllosilicates..." Serpentine and saponite are both found on Earth, where they're created when rock is aqueously altered. But despite the fact that they're generally interpreted to be these substances, "their mineralogical characteristics do not fully correspond to these well-crystalline terrestrial layered silicates."

To dig into this apparent contradiction, the researchers used the SPring-8 synchrotron radiation facility and the Photon Factory High Energy Accelerator, both in Japan. Both of these research facilities use powerful x-rays to look deeply into the Ryugu sample.

They found the expected serpentine and saponite, but they also identified something else: poorly crystalline magnesium silicate hydrate (M-S-H).

âWhat makes M-S-H particularly interesting is that it can accommodate a wide range of magnesium-to-silicon ratios,â said study corresponding author Keisuke Fukushi of Kanazawa University. âThis flexibility may be key to understanding how water-rock interactions proceeded without erasing pre-existing chemical differences within their parent asteroids.â

The composition of most materials remains stable when subjected to the same aqueous conditions. But previous research and lab work shows that M-S-H is a bit of an oddball: it can exist in the same aqueous conditions and have different magnesium to silicon ratios. So this work suggests that M-S-H is the initial starting point, and that if it formed into serpentine and saponite phases, the presence of M-S-H can explain the two different outcomes without necessarily requiring a different aqueous alteration for each one.

This illustration helps explain the findings. The previous interpretation on the left shows tighly packed grains of serpentine and saponite, with the parallel lines representing their orderly crystal structure. The alternating blue and green lines in some grains represent interleaves of serpentine and saponite layers in the same crystal. There's almost no empty space between grains. The image on the right shows the new model, with a background of poorly crystalline M-S-H, making up the bulk of the matrix. In this model, serpentine and saponite are a minor part of the matrix, and are poorly-formed intrusions. Image Credit: Keisuke FUKUSHI, Kanazawa University (2026)

The study says something not only about Ryugu, but about carbonaceous chondrites. Much of their matrices could be poorly crystalline M-S-H. If this material precipitated first and then was transformed later, the different compositions of clay-like minerals found in the matrix could have arisen without a separate, distinct water environment for different regions of the parent asteroid.

"Assuming its initial precipitation and subsequent mineralogical transformations, a wide range of compositional variation can be produced without requiring separate aqueous conditions for each local composition," the authors write. "This framework provides a physicochemical basis for explaining the compositional variability and associated phyllosilicate diversity of C-type chondritic matrices within a parent-body alteration scenario."

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) is developing a reputation for successful sampling missions, one of the most difficult type of missions to complete. The original Hayabusa mission, though plagued with difficulties, still managed to return a small sample from asteroid Itokawa in 2010. Hayabusa 2 was a complete success, as this research shows. And at this moment, JAXA's Martian Moons eXplorer mission is on its way to collect a sample from Phobos, the largest of Mars' two moons.

That sample should be on Earth five years from now. What questions will it answer?

#6491. Human Bodies Are Producing Two Billion Tons of CO2 a Year

A new study reveals that the amount of carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism has increased dramatically over three decades.

The carbon dioxide produced by human bodies as they convert food into energy increased by 74% over three decades, according to a University of Bath-led study. By 2015, the global total had reached an estimated 2.05 billion metric tons (2.26 billion U.S. tons) annually, highlighting a substantial component of the Earth’s carbon cycle that scientists had not previously quantified on this scale.

Unlike emissions from burning fossil fuels, the CO2 humans exhale largely comes from carbon recently absorbed from the atmosphere by plants and transferred through food. Burning coal, oil, and natural gas releases carbon that has been stored underground for millions of years, adding it to the active carbon cycle.

Published in The Lancet Planetary Health, the study found that annual CO2 production from human metabolism rose from 1.18 billion metric tons (1.30 billion U.S. tons) in 1985 to 2.05 billion metric tons (2.26 billion U.S. tons) in 2015. More than 60% of that increase was attributable to population growth rather than a substantial rise in the amount produced by each individual.

To estimate global emissions from metabolism, the researchers analyzed thousands of real-world measurements of CO2 production in people ranging from infants to older adults. They combined these findings with worldwide population and body weight data to calculate how human metabolic activity changed over time.

Professor Javier Gonzalez, who led the research at the University of Bath’s Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism, explained:

“We all produce carbon dioxide simply by turning food into energy, but until now we haven’t had a good idea how much that adds up to worldwide.

“What we’ve found is that the increase is mainly because there are more of us. This gives scientists one more piece of the puzzle when working out where carbon comes from and where it goes. Ultimately, this information can help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be.”

Human metabolism contributes to the continuous movement of carbon through the environment, particularly in densely populated cities. Accounting for that activity could help researchers develop more accurate carbon budgets and better assess the effects of strategies designed to reduce emissions.

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not suggest people should exercise less, change their diets, or attempt to reduce the carbon dioxide they breathe out. The purpose is to improve scientific measurements of carbon movement, not identify respiration as a contributor to fossil fuel emissions.

Gonzalez stressed the distinction: “The important thing is that the carbon dioxide we breathe out is not the same as burning fossil fuels. We’re not saying that breathing is driving climate change.

“What this study does is give us a much clearer picture of how much CO2 people produce around the world, and how that is changing as the population grows. This understanding can help improve the accuracy predictions of carbon reduction programs.”

Reference: “Accounting for global carbon dioxide production from human metabolism between 1985 and 2015: a modelling study” by Javier T Gonzalez, Lorenzo Lolli, Bruno Spellanzon, Greg Atkinson, Ed Maunder, Alfonso Moreno-Cabañas, Jariya Buniam, Dylan Thompson, James Betts, Philip N Ainslie, Heliodoro Alemán-Mateo, Linda Bandini, Ellen E Blaak, Carlijn V C Bouten, Pascal Bovet, Soren Brage, Regina Casper, Prasangi Dabare, Barry W Fudge, Melanie Gillingham, Annalies H Goris, Michael Gurven, Hinke Haisma, Marije B Hoos, Noorjehan Joonas, Peter Katzmarzyk, Misaka Kimura, Sai Krupa Das, Pulani Lanerolle, Christel L Larsson, Marie Löf, Aviva Must, Marian Neuhouser, Theresa A Nicklas, Robert M Ojiambo, Kirsi H Pietilainen, Susan B Racette, Eric Ravussin, Leanne M Redman, John J Reilly, Susan Roberts, Luis B Sardinha, Analiza M Silva, Srishti Sinha, Anders M Sjödin, Eric Stice, Samuel S Urlacher, Edgar A Van Mil, Jeanine A Verbunt, Jonathan C K Wells, Tsukasa Yoshida, Xueying Zhang, Alexia Murphy-Alford, Cornelia U Loechl, Amy Luke, Michele Novaes Ravelli, Herman Pontzer, Jennifer Rood, Hiroyuki Sagayama, Dale A Schoeller, Klaas R Westerterp, William W Wong, Yosuke Yamada and John Speakman, 26 October 2026, The Lancet Planetary Health. #6487. The JWST May Have Found Where Heavy Black Hole Seeds Formed

Astrophysicists think that the supermassive black holes (SMBH) we see in the modern Universe are the result of a long drawn-out process. That process is referred to as the hierarchical black hole mergers framework. It explains how some SMBH can reach such staggering masses. Some of the most massive appear to have billions of solar masses.

The idea is that these SMBH start out as seeds, and those seeds are stellar-mass black holes. Two processes create them. One is when massive stars between about 8 and 50 solar masses reach the end of their lives of fusion. They either explode as supernovae, and their cores collapse, forming black holes, or they collapse directly into black holes. The other is when two neutron stars merge.

In between stellar mass black holes and SMBH are intermediate mass black holes (IMBH.) These black holes range in mass from about 100 solar masses to 100,000 solar masses. The observational evidence for IMBHs is still thin, but it's persistent.

A 2024 paper focused on Omega Centauri, a globular cluster on the outskirts of the Milky Way, as the site of an IMBH. A group of fast-moving stars in the center of Omega Centauri can only be explained by the presence of an IMBH with about 8,200 solar masses, according to that work.

Gravitational waves from a black hole merger are also evidence of an IMBH. A 2020 paper presented the only direct evidence of an IMBH when the waves showed that two black holes, with 85 and 66 solar masses, merged to create an IMBH with about 142 solar masses.

But what are the birthplaces of these IMBH? Some must have formed in the early Universe to act as seeds for the SMBH we see today.

Research titled "Massive star clusters detected by JWST as natural birth places to form intermediate-mass black holes" may have the answer. It's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics, and the lead author is Viola Bocchi. Bocchi is from the Sapienza University of Rome.

"The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a population of dense stellar systems at high redshifts, including the âCosmic Gemsâ arc (zââ¼â10.2) and the âFirefly Sparkleâ (zââ¼â8.3). With masses in the range 105 Mââ107 Mâ and half-mass radii in the range â¼0.4â15 pc, these systems are ideally suited to form intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via collision-based models," the authors write.

The Cosmic Gems arc is a gravitationally lensed galaxy, and the JWST observed its light when the Universe was only about 460 million years old. The JWST found five dense star clusters there.

The Cosmic Gems was first discovered by the Hubble during its Reionization Lensing Cluster Survey (RELICS) and was identified as a powerful source of radiation during the Epoch of Reionization. In 2024, the JWST took another look and found the five Young Massive Clusters (YMC), the first discovery of such ancient clusters.

The Firefly Sparkle is another gravitationally lensed early galaxies, imaged only about 600 million years after the Big Bang. The JWST found 10 YMCs in the Firefly Sparkle.

This image shows the Firefly Sparkle galaxy, where the JWST found 10 YMCs. It also shows a pair of companion galaxies. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Chris Willott (National Research Council Canada), Lamiya Mowla (Wellesley College), Kartheik Iyer (Columbia University)

This research shows that not only were all these YMCs sources of ionizing radiation, they may have been the birthplaces of IMBH.

Due to the density in these YMCs, n-body simulations weren't viable. Instead, the researchers used a model based on runaway collisions and mass-loss by stellar winds to estimate the resulting IMBH masses. They then validated these results against direct N-body simulations of compact star clusters.

"With masses in the range 105 Mââ107 Mâ and half-mass radii in the range â¼0.4â15 pc, these systems are ideally suited to form intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via collision-based models," the authors write. "Our estimates yield typical IMBH masses in the range â¼102 Mâ to â¼4âÃâ103 Mâ, implying typical formation efficiencies on the few percent level."

The clusters in the Cosmic Gems yieled the heaviest IMBH, with masses ranging from 1600â2700 Mâ. "The extreme compactness of the Cosmic Gems clusters (Rhââ¼â1 pc) facilitates the formation of black hole seeds with high masses of 1600â2700 Mâ," the authors write. Rh â¼â1 pc is the radius of the sphere that contains half of the clusterâs total mass and measures how compact a cluster is.

"The low metallicity (Zââ²â0.02âZâ) is a critical factor for retaining the seed mass despite stellar winds," the authors write.

These young clusters also have low metallicities because not enough stars have lived and died in them to generate higher metallicity. Their low metallicity played a critical role in forming IMBH. Low metallicity limits mass-loss due to stellar winds, and that let the objects keep growing.

The results from the Firefly Sparkle are different. "In contrast to the Cosmic Gems, these clusters exhibit significantly larger radii (Rhââ¼â4âââ6 pc) for typically lower total masses (105âââ106âMâ)," the authors write. That creates cores that are less massive, limiting the potential for the runaway collision process to create IMBH. The black hole masses in Firefly Sparkle range 1.8âÃâ102âââ8.1âÃâ102âMâ. That's about 180 to 810 Mâ, which represents the lower boundary for IMBH masses.

This artist's illustration shows what the Firefly Sparkle galaxy looked like about 600 million years after the big bang if it wasnât stretched and distorted by gravitational lensing. This illustration is based on images and data from NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Ralf Crawford (STScI). Science: Lamiya Mowla (Wellesley College), Guillaume Desprez (Saint Mary's University)

Overall, the lower range for IMBH masses in this work (~100 solar mases) is comparable to black holes formed by massive Population III stars, the Universe's hypothetical first stars, which were likely extremely massive. But, "the upper bound extends significantly higher, allowing the most massive clusters to produce objects firmly in the âheavy seedâ regime," the authors write. "Forming such heavy seeds is highly beneficial to form SMBHs at high redshift."

These results aren't observational in the sense that the JWST didn't observe any IMBH. But they do show a plausible environment where IMBH could form and potentially lead to the SMBH we see in the centers of galaxies like ours.

These results could also explain the JWST's Little Red Dots. Their spectra are often interpreted as being powered by SMBH. "Our results suggest that dense massive star clusters could provide possible massive seeds from which the SMBHs in the LRDs may have grown," the researchers write.

The researchers state some caveats, based on some acknowledged weaknesses in their work. Many properties of these clusters are unknown, including their rotation and their internal structure, which could change the outcomes and lower the IMBH masses.

The initial mass function also isn't known, but it could be top-heavy. "This possibility, along with a possible primordial mass segregation, would favor the formation of massive IMBHs, though we did not explore it here in detail," the authors explain.

Researchers will no doubt dig deeper into these young massive clusters and try to fill in some of the blanks that remain. But this research shows that they could be the source of the heavy seed IMBH that eventually form SMBH.

"Our results suggest that these dense, metal-poor clusters are viable factories for heavy seeds that are capable of growing into the supermassive black holes observed in the early Universe," the authors conlude. .

#6486. Scientists Discover a New Type of Depression That Common Antidepressants May Miss

For some people with hard-to-treat depression, the body’s internal clock may help explain why standard antidepressants fall short.

University of Sydney researchers have identified a proposed subtype called “circadian depression,” marked by disrupted sleep and daily rhythms. It accounted for nearly a quarter of participants in a study of more than 10,000 Australians with severe, recurrent or persistent depression.

The findings, published in the British Journal of Psychiatry, suggest that recognizing this pattern could help clinicians identify people who may benefit from treatments targeting the body clock earlier in their care.

“Our research has identified circadian depression as a new subtype, affecting around a quarter of people in our study into those with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression,” said first author Dr. Emiliana Tonini, from the university’s Brain and Mind Centre.

Using clinical and genetic information from the nationwide Australian Genetics of Depression Study, the researchers classified nearly 25 percent (2,604 participants) as having circadian depression. Its features included seasonal episodes, sleeping longer when depressed, waking up exhausted, and a tendency to stay up late.

These symptoms point toward the circadian system, the body’s internal 24-hour timekeeping network that regulates sleep and wakefulness. The researchers identified genetic characteristics of the subtype that could help explain why treatments aimed at other brain pathways are less effective.

Participants with circadian depression were more likely to have developed depression earlier in life and experienced more severe symptoms (such as mania and higher levels of suicidal thoughts). They also had greater genetic susceptibility to inflammatory and cardiovascular conditions and major neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD.

“Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them,” Tonini said.

SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) and SNRIs (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are commonly offered as initial treatments for depression. People with the circadian subtype reported less benefit and more side effects from these medications.

The researchers suggest that this group may respond better to behavioral and medical therapies targeting the brain circuits involved in circadian rhythms. Options include light therapy, melatonin, and antidepressants that act on melatonin pathways.

Co-senior author Dr. Jacob Crouse, from the Brain and Mind Centre, said, “Because circadian depression is linked to people’s internal body clock, treatments targeting the circadian rhythm, such as light therapy and melatonin, may be much more relevant, and clinicians should reach for these much earlier in people with this presentation.

“For those who find that antidepressants are not working for them, it is important to speak to your clinician for advice about your individual circumstances.”

For young people, identifying this pattern early could help avoid unsuccessful initial treatments and additional side effects, according to Professor Ian Hickie, Co-Director of the Brain and Mind Centre and a clinical psychiatrist.

“We really want young people to receive the most appropriate treatment early in their course of illness.

“Most young people will be offered SSRIs first up, but for at least a quarter there are better circadian-focused medical and behavioral options to help treat and manage their condition.”

Reference: “Clinical and genetic correlates of a circadian subtype of depression in the Australian Genetics of Depression Study” by Emiliana Tonini, Jacob J. Crouse, Mirim Shin, Joanne S. Carpenter, Brittany L. Mitchell, Enda M. Byrne, Penelope A. Lind, Scott D. Gordon, Richard Parker, Samuel J. Hockey, Timothy To, Andrew Shim, Alex Hill, Anna Treneman, Elizabeth Scott, Jan Scott, Kathleen R. Merikangas, Naomi R. Wray, Nicholas G. Martin, Sarah E. Medland and Ian B. Hickie, 20 October 2026, The British Journal of Psychiatry. DOI: 10.1192/bjp.2026.10798

The Australian Genetics of Depression Study was primarily funded by grant 1086683 from the National Medical Health and Research Council (NHMRC) of Australia. This work was further supported by philanthropic donations from families who are affected by mental illness (who would like to be left anonymous) awarded to Dr. Mirim Shin. #6483. Why Are Men Twice As Likely To Develop Parkinson’s? Scientists Discover a Hidden Clue in the Brain

Scientists have identified sex-specific differences in gene activity within brain cells that may help explain why Parkinson’s disease affects men more frequently than women.

Men are 1.5 to 2 times more likely than women to develop Parkinson’s disease, yet the biological reasons remain poorly understood. New research suggests that differences in gene activity within the brain’s support cells may help explain why the condition affects the sexes differently.

The findings, presented at the Federation of European Neuroscience Societies (FENS) Forum 2026, are based on brain tissue from 73 people with Parkinson’s disease (28 women and 45 men) and 24 people without the condition (9 women and 15 men). Researchers examined five brain regions, identifying cellular changes shared by both sexes as well as distinct patterns in men and women.

The strongest differences appeared in two types of glial cells, which support and protect neurons. In astrocytes, gene activity related to mitochondria, the structures that produce cellular energy, differed between sexes. In oligodendrocytes, researchers identified differences involving genes responsible for producing and maintaining myelin, the protective coating surrounding nerve fibers. These patterns appeared across the brain regions studied.

Professor Julia Schulze-Hentrich of Saarland University in Germany, who led the research, explained: “We looked at differences in gene expression individually in all cells of the brain – neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia – in healthy brains and in PD brains in men and women. We studied five brain regions and found that PD causes common changes in the brain, regardless of sex. All these cells in the five regions, showed signs of being under stress. They switched on proteins that help damaged proteins fold correctly, called ‘chaperones’. However, we also found important differences between men and women in gene activity in some cells and some brain regions.”

“This shows that PD triggers some shared ‘stress responses’ in everyone’s brain cells, but also there are differences between men and women at the cellular level, especially in how the brain ‘support’ cells manage energy and protect nerve connections. Our findings help to explain why symptoms and disease progression in Parkinson’s differ between men and women. Eventually, they may lead to more personalized treatments rather than treating all patients with PD as biologically identical,” said Prof. Schulze-Hentrich.

Parkinson’s disease causes progressive brain damage and affects approximately 9.4 million people worldwide. About 90% of cases are thought to involve a combination of genetic variation and environmental or lifestyle influences. Men not only develop the disease more frequently but also tend to experience faster cognitive decline and worsening difficulties with everyday activities.

“The higher prevalence of Parkinson’s disease in men suggests that sex-dependent biology may influence vulnerability. Therefore, studying sex differences may help identifying disease mechanisms that would be hidden in analyses that pool men and women together,” said Prof. Schulze-Hentrich, who is affiliated with Saarland University’s Center for Gender-Specific Biology and Medicine (CGMB).

The investigation builds on an earlier study involving 71 agricultural workers with early Parkinson’s and 147 healthy participants. Researchers found changes in DNA methylation across 69 genomic regions in women with Parkinson’s, compared with just two in men. DNA methylation regulates gene activity without altering the underlying DNA sequence, functioning much like a dimmer switch.

“These findings suggested that a person’s genetic makeup influences these DNA methylation changes, and that interaction with environmental exposures, such as to pesticides, may also contribute to the development of Parkinson’s disease,” Prof. Schulze-Hentrich said.

The new study extended this work by examining gene expression in individual types of brain cells. Although it identified differences associated with biological sex, it did not establish that those differences directly cause the higher rate of Parkinson’s in men.

The study’s relatively small sample size limits its conclusions, and larger investigations are needed. The findings also reinforce the need to examine men and women separately in Parkinson’s research, which has historically focused heavily on neurons and male subjects.

“Most importantly, our results indicate that it is crucial to recognize that biology varies between the sexes in PD research and that, wherever possible, researchers should analyze data separately in males and females instead of pooling everyone together. This is crucial to see whether an association, effect or outcome differs by sex. It also helps identify gaps in evidence because many studies still underreport or pool sex-specific outcomes.

“For patients, the main benefit is more personalized care, as sex-specific analysis can help clinicians predict which symptoms are more likely, monitor problems earlier, and choose treatments that fit a patient’s risk profile better.”

A new German research initiative aims to investigate how sex-related differences in glial cells affect neurological disease.

“Investigating how male- and female-specific glial responses shape vulnerability, progression and treatment response is rarely done in a systematic and coordinated way. Therefore, the German Research Foundation (DFG) Priority Programme ‘SEX and GLIA’ starting in the autumn of 2026 will bring together physiologists with functional geneticists and computational biologists to uncover a largely hidden layer of sex-biased biology that previous studies often ignored,” Prof. Schulze-Hentrich concluded.

Professor Christina Dalla of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, Greece, who chairs the FENS Forum communication committee and was not involved in the research, highlighted how the findings build on earlier investigations of environmental exposures.

“Although we have known for some time that there are higher rates of Parkinson’s disease in men than in women, it is interesting to see how Professor Schulze-Hentrich and her colleagues have built on their earlier work studying the impact of pesticides on agricultural workers to investigate the changes that occur at the cellular level and to understand the mechanisms underlying the development of Parkinson’s disease.

“Their findings show that although some changes in genetic activity are the same in both sexes, there are others that only occur in men, or in women. This is an important finding because it shows that there are differences in glial cells, the ‘support’ cells in the brain that are associated with the onset of the disease, and that these could interact with other factors such as sex, hormones, or social or environmental exposures.”

A new study with data from mice and human tissues suggests that, in ulcerative colitis, immune cells in the gut might make pain-sensing nerves hypersensitive.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

People with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) experience gut pain that can be severe, and it doesn't always go away when their inflammation is under control and their colonoscopy looks normal. Now, in a new laboratory study, researchers found a previously unknown pain pathway that may explain this phenomenon.

The findings, published Oct. 23 in the journal Science Immunology, also point to a potential way to block that pain.

"Inflammation in the gut has always been thought of like a fire: the sensory nerves alarm because of the smoke and the heat, and when the fire is put out the alarm should stop," said study co-author Dr. Heng Xu, a physician at Ninth People's Hospital in Shanghai. Xu and his colleagues set out to try to isolate what could be causing the pain even when there's no visible "fire" or "smoke."

"What we found is that the tissue itself changes consistency," Xu told Live Science in an email. "It becomes stiff and less elastic, a bit like a scar, and that stiffness alone keeps triggering the alarm even after the fire is out."

In ulcerative colitis, the most common form of IBD, inflammation causes ulcers in the gut, as well as symptoms like bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramping. Several medications can help quell this inflammation, but that doesn't necessarily eliminate patients' pain. The researchers wondered if immune cells that live in the gut might contribute to that ongoing pain.

They zoomed in on a protein called Piezo1; in immune cells, it's known to play a role in inflammation, and in neurons, it contributes to pain signals. The team looked at whether this protein's activity changed in the context of colitis.

"We started with sequencing data that reads cells one at a time, from the gut tissue of patients with ulcerative colitis and from mice with the disease," Xu said. "One cell type stood out: an immune cell that lives permanently in the gut wall, rather than arriving from the bloodstream when there's trouble." The quantity of these cells was higher in colitis than in healthy guts, and the cells carried more Piezo1 than the other cells analyzed.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"They sit touching the nerve endings," Xu added.

In several experiments with lab mice with colitis, the team used a probe to press on the gut tissue and measure how hard it was. This showed that, compared with healthy mice, the gut was stiffer in two models of disease: one with visible inflammation and another with almost none.

They also measured pain levels in both sets of mice. "In mice with almost no visible gut inflammation, the pain was still there, which is why a colonoscopy can look normal while the patient hurts," Xu said.

They then looked at Piezo1 in both sets of mice. The protein sits in the immune-cell membrane, and when the stiffened tissue around it is pulled or squeezed, it's as if a button were pressed and a channel opens, Xu said. This sets off a chain reaction that leads to pain, Xu said.

That's because calcium ions rush into the cell via the channel, and that surge sends a protein called NF-kB from the cell's interior fluid into its nucleus — the control center where DNA is stored. There, NF-kB plugs into a gene, ordering the cell to manufacture nerve growth factor (NGF) that then exits the immune cell.

This NGF, which is known to amplify pain signals in the body, interacts with nearby pain-sensing neurons. These nerve endings grow denser and become hypersensitive, which makes ordinary gut activity painful, the study suggests.

This newly described mechanism could help explain why ulcerative colitis patients can sometimes contend with pain even when their colonoscopies look normal.

The researchers used chemicals as on-off switches for Piezo1 in immune cells, opening the channel with one and closing it with another. As they did this, they tracked calcium signals and NGF production, and both rose and fell in step with the switch. This result suggests that Piezo1 activity is both necessary for this response and, on its own, enough to trigger it in these cells, Xu said.

Blocking this chain of events abolished the pain hypersensitivity in both sets of mice. The researchers tried completely removing the Piezo1 gene from the gut immune cells and found that this eliminated the pain. Removing the gene also caused no problems in healthy mice, they noted.

The study was "well controlled," said Hongzhen Hu, the scientific director for the Mark Lebwohl Center for Neuroinflammation and Sensation at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, who was not involved in the research. Future research should address the chemical messengers that coordinate inflammation, called cytokines, and determine whether the same chain reaction occurs in human cells, he said in an email.

The mouse experiments also may not reflect long-term, chronic disease in patients, given the mice experienced symptoms only transiently, Xu said.

Xu and his colleagues are now aiming to develop a drug that can target Piezo1 to switch off gut pain locally without suppressing the entire immune system. This would be a more targeted treatment than current options, such as immunosuppressants or opioids.

Other scientists have explored using anti-NGF treatments for other chronic pain conditions but not for ulcerative colitis, Xu noted. Fully blocking NGF might have downsides, he said, since NGF also helps to maintain nerves.

So more work is needed to translate these findings into a treatment. But for now, the work sheds new light on how immune cells can detect a physical change — such as tissue becoming stiff — and convert it to a pain signal.

"For the pain field, that's a conceptual shift," Xu said.
