#6463. A Hidden Nanoscopic Effect Is Disrupting Some of the World’s Most Sensitive Sensors

Nanomechanical resonators are vital to precision sensing and emerging quantum technologies, but their extraordinary sensitivity comes with an unexpected vulnerability.

A nanomechanical device can lose much of its ability to sustain vibrations without ever touching another object. Researchers at EPFL have discovered that placing insulating materials just a few hundred nanometers from these tiny structures can dramatically increase energy loss, reducing their mechanical quality factor by as much as tenfold.

The findings, published in Nature Physics by scientists in the group of Tobias J. Kippenberg, identify a previously underappreciated limitation for ultrahigh-precision sensors and quantum technologies. The source of the problem is an electrical interaction that allows energy to escape across an otherwise empty gap.

The mechanism begins with static electric charges trapped inside a mechanical resonator. As the structure vibrates, those charges move with it, producing a changing electric field in the surrounding space. When an insulating material such as silicon dioxide or silicon nitride is nearby, the fluctuating field interacts with the material and causes energy to dissipate through its small electrical losses.

This process is related to “noncontact friction,” a phenomenon previously observed in atomic force microscopy. Although the surfaces never touch, mechanical energy is transferred away from the vibrating structure. The resulting damping lowers its quality factor, which measures how efficiently a resonator stores vibrational energy rather than losing it.

The researchers developed a theoretical model predicting that lower-frequency vibrations would experience greater energy losses. To test this, they studied silicon nitride strings suspended approximately 500 nanometers (0.00002 inches) above a dielectric layer. By measuring how quickly different vibrational modes decayed, they confirmed that the lowest-frequency modes suffered the strongest additional damping, consistent with the model.

A second experiment examined resonators designed for exceptionally high quality factors. The team positioned vibrating strings between photonic crystal cavities, with separations of only a few hundred nanometers (roughly 0.00001 inches). As the gaps narrowed, the quality factor declined sharply, sometimes falling by a factor of ten. The researchers also demonstrated that their modeling approach could reproduce the effects of trapped charges in these more complicated device geometries.

Nanomechanical resonators are microscopic vibrating components fabricated on chips, operating at frequencies from a few kilohertz to several gigahertz. Their sensitivity makes them useful for detecting extremely small changes in mass, force, temperature, and pressure. They also serve as components in radiofrequency filters and chip-based clocks. Advanced versions can even be used to prepare quantum states of comparatively large mechanical objects and investigate fundamental physics.

Many of these applications require resonators to operate extremely close to other structures, particularly when measuring motion or coupling mechanical vibrations to light and electrical systems. The EPFL results show that trapped charges and dielectric losses must be considered when designing such closely integrated devices, even when no physical contact occurs.

The same interaction could also have practical uses. By measuring how mechanical vibrations lose energy near insulating surfaces, researchers may be able to characterize electrical losses in thin films or develop controlled interactions between mechanical resonators and other electrical systems. Understanding these effects could help engineers preserve mechanical coherence while integrating increasingly sensitive resonators into complex quantum and sensing devices.

Reference: “Non-contact friction in ultracoherent nanomechanical resonators near dielectric materials” by Amirali Arabmoheghi, Alessio Zicoschi, Guillermo Arregui, Mohammad J. Bereyhi, Yi Xia, Nils J. Engelsen and Tobias J. Kippenberg, 7 July 2026, Nature Physics. DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03350-z

Funding: Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF)

#6462. 6 Places in the US Where Travelers Can Hunt, Fish, or Forage for Their Own Food

This article is part of a series of stories about hunting, fishing, and foraging experiences across North America.

My boyhood summers tasted like wild fruit and fish. When I gathered blueberries from the pine and oak woods around my father’s New Hampshire home, he would stir their purple sweetness into pancake batter. When I pulled brook trout from the waters of a long-abandoned granite quarry, I would sauté them in a cast iron skillet until delicate flesh flaked from translucent bone.

Mount Monadnock in New Hampshire, where the author learned how to forage and fish.

At twenty, I went vegan and quit fishing. For food, I looked to the grocery store and, seasonally, the garden. Though I still gathered the occasional handful of berries or chanterelles, I took little sustenance directly from wild nature.

Ten years later—my black-and-white dietary ethics shaken by the realities of agriculture and my body demanding a wider array of nutrients—I began a journey back to omnivory and the wild. I took up a fishing rod again. I paid more attention to mushrooms emerging from the forest floor. And I began learning to hunt.

Indigo milk caps, an edible wild mushroom

Picking portobello-like indigo milk caps, casting for trout or striped bass, or sitting at the base of a maple with rifle in hand as dawn brightened the frosty deer woods, I began to remember that the land is a source not only of beauty but also of food, that the earth feeds our bodies as well as our souls. Over the past two decades, I have gradually awakened to this continent’s vast diversity of wild edibles and to the deep meanings wild foodways still carry across cultures. Many of us, of course, have lost these practices. We have forgotten how to eat wild.

If you want to reconnect with the entire nature-to-plate experience, you need to get out there and harvest with your own hands. Even if you aren’t ready to dive into relearning ancient skills, across the country you can find opportunities to experience wild foods, each a gift flavored by local land and culture, each a chance to savor what a place tastes like, straight from the source.

Sochan gathering in Great Smoky Mountains National Park is a Cherokee tradition.

People have walked the Blue Ridge Mountains in search of edibles since the end of the last Ice Age. Of the tens of thousands of species that inhabit the region’s lush and astonishingly biodiverse forests today, a handful dominate Asheville’s vibrant foraging and culinary scene.

Ramps, or wild leeks, bring the earthy, garlicky promise of spring. Pawpaws, the continent’s largest edible native fruit, ripen in late summer and early fall, delivering a near-tropical blend of mango and banana to the tongue. And a bounty of edible fungi—from morels and black trumpets to lion’s mane, chanterelles, and chicken of the woods—fill mushroom hunters’ baskets in every season but winter.

Overharvesting, both legal and illegal, has triggered some restrictions. In Great Smoky Mountains National Park, for example, the collection of ramps has been forbidden since 2004 and daily mushroom harvest is limited to a pound per person. The prohibition on gathering ramps extends to the Eastern Band of Cherokee, though a recent agreement with the National Park Service permits several dozen members to gather sochan within park boundaries.

Outside the park, opportunities still abound for all. In the nearby Pisgah and Nantahala National Forests, for instance, you can gather up to three pounds (or one gallon) of ramps or mushrooms for personal use, though truffles and chaga are off limits. Even if you don’t see yourself setting off into the woods in search of dinner, or exploring foraging possibilities within Asheville itself, the area offers a cornucopia of ways to enjoy and learn about wild edibles.

A non-resident fishing license from D.C., Virginia, or Maryland lets you head out on your own.

Blue catfish are invasive to Chesapeake Bay and a predator of the ever-popular blue crab

Covering nearly 4,500 square miles, the Chesapeake Bay and its tidal tributaries are famous for blue crabs, beloved by locals and visitors alike. Though the bay still supplies a significant portion of the nation’s catch, blue crab numbers have been impacted by habitat loss, overharvest, and predation.

Among the crab’s predators are locally invasive blue catfish. Introduced to Virginia rivers decades ago, the fish have proved able to tolerate the saltier waters of the bay and are now outcompeting native species. To mitigate the negative impacts, diverse stakeholders—including scientists, government agencies, seafood producers, restaurants, and grocery stores—are working to build a thriving “River to Table” market.

In recent years, Virginia and Maryland have each recorded millions of pounds in annual commercial blue catfish harvest. Though consumers are advised to eat smaller fish or to trim away belly fat and dark meat to remove contaminants, blue catfish is increasingly popular table fare. Delicious fried, grilled, smoked, or blackened, it is available in a growing number of restaurants and grocery stores around the region.

You can also catch your own, with or without a fishing guide. In most tidal waters, neither state limits how many blue catfish recreational anglers can keep. If you go, be prepared for some big, hard-fighting fish. Blue cats regularly run 30-plus pounds and can get much larger.

Farmers Jeffry Bellcourt (standing) and Bob Libby harvest wild rice using traditional methods on Rice Lake in northern Minnesota.

Centuries ago, the Anishinaabe migrated from the Atlantic coast to the western Great Lakes region. At the heart of their migration stories is a prophecy telling them to travel west until they found the place where food grows on water. That food was manoomin, or wild rice, an annual grass that grows in shallow water. An important traditional food for multiple Indigenous nations, wild rice (psiŋ in Dakota) continues to carry deep cultural meaning and is central to food sovereignty efforts in the western Great Lakes region.

To harvest wild rice in late summer, two people work from a canoe, one navigating with a long forked pole, the other using a pair of smooth cedar sticks to gently bend tall stalks over the gunwales and tap the ripe grain loose. (Mechanized harvest has been banned in Minnesota since 1939.) Knowledge of when and how to harvest is passed down by other harvesters and comes with experience. Once dried and parched, grain must be separated from chaff. Though some people still use traditional methods, most finishing is now done mechanically.

Nutty and smoky, manoomin works any time of day, from rice and berries with maple syrup for breakfast to a hearty stew for dinner. Natural wild rice grains are a mix of earthy hues and cook in 20 minutes or less. In contrast, “paddy” or “cultivated” variants grown in Minnesota and California are glossy black and take much longer. Minnesota law requires clear labeling to distinguish the two.

Though Minnesota residents and nonresidents alike can purchase a wild rice license, harvesting and processing is a complex process. For Tribal communities, it is also an ancient and ongoing relationship. For those new to ricing, learning from experienced harvesters or attending a Tribal-led camp or educational event is a respectful place to begin. Visitors can also support Tribal communities by purchasing manoomin directly from them.

Restaurants across Pensacola, Florida offer fishermen the option to cook their catch.

Harbor Docks combines fishing trips with restaurant preparation.

Dubbed the “Gloucester of the Gulf,” the commercial fishing hub of Pensacola, Florida, anchored a late 19th- and early 20th-century fishery that hauled in millions of pounds of red snapper each year. After World War II, recreational fishing surged as well. The pressure, combined with bycatch from shrimp trawlers, proved too much: between 1950 and 1990, red snapper numbers plunged. Since the 1990s, federal managers have capped the annual catch, split it between commercial and recreational fishermen, and limited anglers to two fish per day.

Sweet, mild, and firm, red snapper can be roasted as Snapper Veracruzana, fried as snapper bites, baked whole with Thai seasonings, or grilled with lemon sauce. You’ll find it at seafood markets along the Florida panhandle and Alabama coast. You’ll also find it at restaurants, many of which will cook your catch. Snapper season peaks in summer but often runs into fall.

Many snapper are released because they’re undersized, out of season, or over the two-fish limit. When anglers reel up a snapper from deep water, the fish’s swim bladder often expands, leaving it unable to swim back down. To keep released fish alive, Florida Sea Grant’s Return ’Em Right program urges anglers to use descending devices, which return fish quickly to depth, and offers free devices to those who complete an online course. In recent years, federal rules have also required anglers to carry them.

State and federal laws ban nearly all sale of wild game in the US, but federal rules allow USDA inspection and then sale of some non-native species, including axis deer.

In the 1860s, the British colony of Hong Kong gave the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi eight axis deer. The beautiful spotted animals, native to India, were released on the island of Molokaʻi. In the absence of predators, they multiplied swiftly. In 1959 and 1960, nine deer were relocated to Maui. There, too, numbers soared.

Alongside other large herbivores, none of which are native to Hawaiʻi, axis deer have devastated crops and stripped hillsides of drought-stressed vegetation, allowing rain to erode soil and sweep it into wetlands and onto coral reefs, harming critical habitats. To accelerate deer control measures, Hawaiʻi has issued more than two dozen emergency proclamations in recent years.

Many families hunt deer and prize the meat, especially on Molokaʻi, but hunting alone hasn’t kept numbers in check. So islanders have turned to an unconventional solution: commercial harvest. State and federal laws ban nearly all sale of wild game in the US, but federal rules allow USDA inspection and then sale of some non-native species, including axis deer. In 2007, Molokaʻi hunter Desmund Manaba became the first in Hawaiʻi to win approval to harvest axis deer and sell the meat. In 2012, Maui County backed a harvesting cooperative of its own.

Today, shooters working for Maui Nui Venison take deer from private ranches each night. Fresh or processed into snack sticks, most of the meat is sold. A portion is distributed for free to local families through the company’s Holo ʻAi program, which the company links to Hawaiʻi’s long tradition of food-sharing and which helped ensure food security during the COVID-19 pandemic and after the devastating 2023 wildfires.

Prickly pear fruit can be eaten raw or squeezed into juice.

Visitors to Arizona's Sonoran Desert can purchase wild foods gathered by O’odham harvesters.

The word “desert” may conjure ideas of emptiness, barrenness, a lack of life. Sitting on the eastern edge of the Sonoran Desert, Tucson, Arizona, dispels all such notions. Designated as a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy in 2015, Tucson boasts both the longest continuous agricultural history of any city in the United States and a rich set of wild foods traditions.

Among other plants, cacti are on the menu. For millennia, Tohono O’odham people have gathered food from—and maintained vital relationships with—multiple species, following a calendar set by the desert’s two rainy seasons. From late summer into fall, during and after the summer rains, people harvest prickly pear fruit, which can be eaten raw or squeezed into juice. In spring, after the winter rains, harvesters pluck cholla buds. Reminiscent of lemony asparagus tips, they can be cooked and eaten fresh or dried for later use.

In June, before the summer rains return, people gather saguaro fruit, knocking it from towering cacti with a kuipad, a long pole made of saguaro ribs, then dry the protein-rich seeds and make jam from the fruit. They also make syrup, fermenting some into wine for the rain ceremony that marks the O’odham New Year.

Foraging is prohibited in Saguaro National Park, with exceptions for O’odham harvesting traditions. Though gathering is legal on private land with permission, participating in guided harvests and walks is an ideal place to begin. You can also purchase foods gathered by O’odham harvesters.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

A new program aims to help scientists figure out how the ingredients of the universe formed early galaxies, which lit up the cosmos after a "dark age."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists are getting a new glimpse of how the first galaxies came to be. In a stunning new simulation, researchers charted the aftermath of the universe's "dark age," including the appearance of the first galaxies that began to shine about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

Lumina, the program behind the simulation, catalogs 2 billion years of cosmic time and represents a decent chunk of the 13.8 billion-year-old history of our universe. The results were published Monday (Oct. 26) in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

"Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," study co-author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT, said in a statement. "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation."

A video published alongside the paper shows what the scientists saw. The team zoomed in on an area roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide to learn more about how the ingredients of space create galaxies.

This section of the Lumina simulation shows the gas temperature in different parts of the early universe, with redder areas showing active galaxy clusters.

In the earliest years of our universe, a fog of neutral hydrogen atoms gradually built up, blocking out the light of the first stars. The hydrogen served as a "shroud" and didn't make light visible until galaxies began to form. This ancient, enshrouded period is known as the Cosmic Dark Age.

The video begins in the middle of this epoch, at roughly 45 million years after the Big Bang. Zooming in on one small part of the simulated universe, it slowly reveals a gassy halo giving way to young galaxies shining brightly within it. Included in the calculations are dark matter, stars, gas and radiation — all contributing to the reemergence of cosmic light.

"We see this is where the first galaxies form," first author Oliver Zier, a former postdoctoral researcher and computational astrophysicist at MIT who is now at Harvard University, said in the statement. "And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Lumina aims to show off two phenomena key to the young universe's history: hydrogen reionization and helium reionization — a first for a program of its kind. Reionization describes how the intergalactic medium, or the area between galaxies, changed from neutral hydrogen to negatively charged ions.

Hydrogen reionization took place when ultraviolet light from young stars and galaxies hit the hydrogen, removing negatively charged electrons from the hydrogen molecules — a process that also allowed light to shine through the fog. Helium reionization happened when supermassive black holes, which have a lot of energy, broke apart neutral helium molecules.

The team said the simulation could eventually be used to validate telescope observations of the early universe, especially those focused on mapping many galaxies at the same time.

Zier, O., Smith, A., Shen, X., Liu, R., Kannan, R., Koehler, S. M., Springel, V., Pakmor, R., Vogelsberger, M., Bulichi, T., & Hernquist, L. (2026). Introducing the lumina project: large-volume radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of the epochs of hydrogen and helium reionization. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 552(4). https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stag1469

#6459. In Southeast Alaska, Connecting With My Indigenous Roots Through Salmon Fishing

This article is part of a series of stories about hunting, fishing, and foraging experiences across North America.

As the fish on the end of my line ferociously attempts to swim away from our boat, I can tell from the forcible tug that it's a prized Chinook salmon. I stay steady and let the fish (known as a king in Alaska for its large size) tire itself out before calmly reeling it in, following the advice of the expert guide standing alongside me. He hoists my catch into our North River cabin cruiser, and I meet my worthy opponent: a plump, silver-blue salmon with black speckles, weighing in around 15 pounds. As I take a moment to catch my breath and admire the scenery around me—pristine waters reflecting the blue sky above, dense forests, coastal cliffs—I realize my Indigenous ancestors likely fished this exact spot centuries before me.

A decade ago, I returned to my birthplace of Ketchikan in Southeast Alaska to reconnect with my Tlingit heritage, having only recently learned of my Alaska Native ancestry and found my Indigenous family members. I felt inspired by our tribe’s rich culture, especially after hearing stories about it from my brother, but at the same time I felt unmoored and unsure of my place within it, as someone who had grown up in Minnesota, far from my tribe’s ancestral homelands. I have since returned several times, but on this recent trip to Alaska’s Inside Passage, salmon fishing was making me feel like I belonged.

Steamboat Bay Fishing Club on Noyes Island in Southeast Alaska

The adventure began long before I arrived at Steamboat Bay Fishing Club on remote Noyes Island, where unadulterated, old-growth forest stretches right up to the edges of its serene shoreline. To get there from Ketchikan, I hopped a floatplane for a 45-minute flight over Tongass National Forest—the planet’s largest intact temperate rainforest—before being dropped off at the lodge’s private dock.

Certified by Alaska Green Adventure for its sustainability efforts, the luxury resort has operated on the island since 2013 and hosts a max of 24 guests. Typical three-night stays include guided fishing, curated chef’s dinners, rejuvenating massages, nature walks, and late-night storytelling and stargazing around the fire pit. Throughout my visit, I spied bald eagles, orcas, humpback whales, sea otters, and sea lions. The stay was unlike anything I’ve ever encountered before.

It’s still an awe-inspiring experience for Haida-Tsimshian fisherman and artist Everett Athorp, who has served as a fishing guide at Steamboat Bay since it opened. “I’m amazed by the beauty of the place,” he says. “There’s nothing like getting out on the water on a beautiful day and seeing the sunrise and all the wildlife. I can’t picture myself doing anything else—I just love the freedom of being out on the water.”

Athorp’s easygoing, unassuming demeanor belies his decades-long experience and expertise, which are rooted in the knowledge passed down by his Indigenous ancestors. Regulars who return to the resort every summer request to hit the water with him, eager to hear his stories of growing up in Alaska and to learn about the significance of fishing for the state’s 229 federally recognized tribal nations.

“Salmon are so important to Alaska Native culture,” says Athorp, who lives in nearby Klawook on Prince of Wales Island. “Fishing is a livelihood and a way of life here. I’ll tell my guests about the old ways people fished, using traps and wooden halibut hooks. I hope they come away with a respect for the salmon, the fishery, and the land—and an appreciation for the opportunity to be here, even if it’s a slow fishing day.”

In Alaska, fishing isn’t just a hobby—it’s a means of survival, especially for the state’s vast rural population, who depend on subsistence hunting and fishing to feed their families. Dating back millennia, Alaska Native communities have stewarded and sustainably harvested wild salmon runs, building smokehouses and summer fish camps (many of which are still in use). Oral histories, formline artwork, and traditional dances all honor the role of salmon as not only a vital food source but also an important cultural symbol; my Tlingit tribe considers salmon to be sacred beings representing abundance, renewal, and life itself.

Steamboat Bay’s main lodge is dotted with artistic homages to salmon and other important animals, including carved paddles, bentwood boxes, and a massive carved Western cedar panel perched above the fireplace. It’s all made by Athorp, who is also an accomplished carver. The craft is another important cultural component of his Haida-Tsimshian heritage, and his creations are an act of resistance and cultural preservation—carrying on the work of his grandfather, Jones Yeltatzie.

Haida-Tsimshian fisherman and artist Everett Athorp holds one of his works

“My grandfather went to Mt. Edgecumbe boarding school in Sitka, so he had to [teach himself the artistic method] when he was a kid,” says Athorp. The institution was established by the Bureau of Indian Affairs in the 1940s to offer a high school education for rural Alaska Native students, who historically were restricted from learning about their cultures. “Because he was self-taught, [his technique] was a little rough. Looking back at it now, he was trying to keep the tradition alive.” Today, Athorp is the one passing those skills on to both Native and non-Native aspiring artists.

Out on the water, I find myself settling into a rhythm as the hours pass. In some ways, it feels familiar, given that I grew up fishing Minnesota’s lakes for walleye, sunfish, and other freshwater species. But those Midwestern summers couldn’t have prepared me for quintessential Alaska fishing experiences like fighting a king salmon, hooking a barn-door halibut (so named for its size), or watching in disbelief as a sea lion snatches my hard-won catch right off the line.

But as any seasoned angler knows, fishing is never just about fishing. Much of the day is devoted to seemingly ancillary activities like shooting the breeze with my boatmates. We become fast friends, and I learn that although this trip holds particular significance for me, they too seem to have found what they were seeking amid Alaska’s unadulterated beauty. All of us have been offered a taste of a time-honored Tlingit tradition, and it's here, floating out in uncharted waters as my ancestors once did, that I finally feel like I've found my place.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6457. A Day at Sea With the Octopus Fisherman of the Yucatán

This article is part of a series of stories about hunting, fishing, and foraging experiences across North America.

The turquoise, bathtub-warm water of the Yucatán is extra sudsy today. Our little skiff, known around here as an alijo, is bobbing like a toy as our captain gently tugs on a few lines descending into the water. “Paciencia,” he repeats, reaching for the next line, before a knowing draw confirms, still, no octopus.

We’re just a 20-minute boat ride from the sleepy town of Rio Lagartos, aboard the Yahilin, captained by 55-year-old Limberth Orlando Alcocer Diaz, who has been fishing since the age of eight. His parents were fishermen too; these waters provide supple mero, a white fish loved for ceviche, and juicy shrimp that Alcocer Diaz promises is some of the tastiest you’ll find in the region. But there is another catch unique to this coastline, and the reason I'm here today: the octopus maya.

The writer and local chefs join fisherman Limberth Orlando Alcocer Diaz aboard the Yahilin

A grilled octopus maya is prepared at Maroma, a Belmond Hotel, in Riviera Maya

“The octopus maya is a bit smaller than the kind you get from the Mediterranean—it looks beautiful on the plate,” says chef Cesar A. Landeo, who has joined me and Alcocer Diaz on board Yahilin. A bucket of bait crabs wiggle between us. Landeo is currently the executive chef at the luxury Maroma, a Belmond Hotel, located about three hours from Rio Lagartos by car and where I'm staying—the night prior, I'd enjoyed a wood-grilled octopus, sourced from these very waters. Another chef, Karla Encisco, who has worked for various Cancún hotels over the years and now acts as a hospitality consultant, is on the other side of me, sharing tips for cooking octopus in a dry-pot method that uses only the seawater released by the animal for steaming. We're all here with the same shared interest: to trace the seafood I was enjoying at Maroma to its source, and gain a better understanding of the divisive choice to eat them at all.

This part of Mexico has earned a reputation for its sustainable approach to octopus fishing—and to understand why, you need to set sail with someone like Alcocer Diaz. He is one of several hundred fishermen who use a unique artisanal method built off of just two long pieces of bamboo (known as “jimbas”), a few cords, and a live crab and maybe some lobster as bait. Some records show this style of fishing has existed for hundreds of years among the Maya, but it has been employed commercially for the last five or six decades. And it is built entirely around an understanding of the animal we’re searching for.

Live bait crabs are used to catch octopus using an artisanal fishing method unique to the Yucatán.

Known colloquially as both the four-eyed octopus, the petite octopus maya is recognizable by divers and fishermen for its “false eyes” that sit below the real ones. A coral red in color—at least, when it isn’t camouflaging—it also lives a pointed existence of roughly one year. As Alcocer Diaz explains, once females have laid their eggs in a cave, they will guard them diligently from predators, abandoning their need for food until, finally, once the eggs hatch, the mothers literally drop dead, famished and withered.

Alcocer Diaz mimics a thin, spindly tentacle with a finger to describe the ones he’s seen. “Not even scavengers will eat what’s left of them,” he says while threading his bait. It’s not much better for the males, who may mate several times during a season before their own demise, expiring after they’ve completed a summer of procreation. Octopus fishing here is only allowed from August 1 to December 15, and not a day later, to catch the cephalopods at the sweet spot of their lifespan, with enough time to repopulate.

It's also why the jimba method is key to the process: By tying a crab or a lobster’s torso to a line and launching it overboard, letting it dangle from the bamboo, only males will take the bait they encounter on the sea floor while the females remain on their starvation-inducing egg-watch. The males willingly wrap themselves around the shellfish, just as they would to feed normally, and when fishermen check a line and notice a pound or two of extra weight attached—“it just feels different,” Alcocer Diaz tells me in Spanish—they reel them in.

Two long bamboo poles, a few fishing lines, and live bait are the backbone of this method

An octopus maya, smaller than its Mediterranean or Pacific counterpart

“They are really intelligent,” says Alcocer Diaz with a sense of awe, mimicking how the octopuses he catch will simply walk off his fiberglass boat and back into the water if he doesn’t act quickly. His method is swift: a spike between the eyes for a sudden brain death, a method more recently popularized under the ethical Japanese process of ikejime.

The animal’s intellect is, of course, why some diners will turn down the chance to eat a perfectly grilled pulpo. It’s also the reason that Encisco, who is often tasked with preparing these eight-armed creatures, still can’t watch the documentary My Octopus Friend. Lando admits his wife raised the same concern when he left early this morning for our excursion. (“‘Fishing octopus?’ she said to me, ‘But aren’t they so smart?’”). Alcocer Diaz considers it as a fact in the cycle of life. Everything he does, from gassing up his boat to choosing which seafood to fish based on the weather or season, comes from an understanding of his place on the food chain: “I just want to feed my family,” he says. I'm hoping that, by the end of our expedition, I'll have an answer of my own.

Pelicans and seagulls watch passing fishing boats outside the town of Rio Lagartos, Mexico.

As pelicans circle our boat, used to seeing scraps of fish tossed off the side of the ajilos, I prod Alcocer Diaz for a greater mission, or calling, driving his choice to use this artisanal method, and his commitment to respecting the rules of the “veda,” the months when octopus fishing is banned in the region so that the population can regenerate for the next season. He talks about sustainability as crucial to maintaining his livelihood. Later, over a lunch of octopus ceviche at a portside restaurant in town, Alcocer Diaz's friend Wabi Martin Tabasco Marfil—another fisherman in the same co-op—breaks down the logic further for me: “If we fish everything today, what will be left tomorrow? If we take all the little fish, how will the big fish survive—and then, how will we get the big fish?” It's a needs-based understanding of sustainability.

Reinforcing this commitment among local fishermen is an ongoing effort—both on the part of the fishing cooperatives organized by workers in every single port, all the way up to the chefs who purchase their seafood to put on a menu, and, finally, the consumers who order it. This is how Pesca Con Futuro (Fishing for the Future), an organization connecting chefs with sustainable fishing collectives throughout Mexico, came to fruition. “In almost all cases, consumption shapes how food is produced,” says Citlali Gomez Lepe, the biologist who founded Pesca Con Futuro eight years ago. Today, the group helps chefs restaurants and hotels source shrimp from the Gulf of Mexico, red lobster from Baja California, and rainbow trout from Michoacan, to name just a few products, with over 60 fisheries involved.

“If consumers of fish and seafood in Mexico show a preference for [artisanal and sustainably sourced] products—and if the market transmits that signal all the way along the value chain to the fishers themselves—then those fishers who operate according to best sustainability practices will find allies at the end of the chain,” says Gomez Lepe. Both Encisco and Landeo source seafood via Pesca Con Futuro for the hotels they work with, as do familiar culinary names like Gabriela Camara and Javier Plasencia, among many dozens of other Mexican chefs who act as ambassadors.

Chef Cesar A. Landeo plates grilled octopus at Maroma, a Belmond Hotel

Fisherman Wabi Martin Tabasco Marfil fishes for octopus maya

“We realized chefs have a huge voice in what lands on the table,” Enciso says, when I ask why she got involved with Pesca Con Futuro. “For those of us who work in hotels, we can educate the people who come into their restaurants.”

On the Riviera Maya, where the scenic coastline is home to a smattering of hotels from 1,800-key all-inclusives to luxury brands like Belmond and local boutiques, the sheer number of diners here presents a challenge—or an opportunity for sustainability, depending on how you look at it. Enciso is an optimist about the power we each hold when we sit down for our lobster dinner on vacation—whether that's choosing to eat only in-season seafood, or asking where your crustacean was sourced. “There’s a phrase I love,” Enciso says. “Little people in little small places doing little things can change the world.”

A day on the water requires more patience than I’d expected. After two hours of lurching on the waves, and hopelessly tugging lines that lead Alcocer Diaz to shake his head in the negative, we decide to return back to shore. “On a good day, you can get 50 kilos of octopus,” says Alcocer Diaz—that's about 25 octopuses. But last season was fantastic, he says. “Some days we got 70-80 kilos.” Today, the weather was against us, with an approaching storm muddying the waters and making it difficult for our eight-armed friends to see the bait. Despite our best efforts, the only octopus we will see today is on our plates.

Back on land, we sit for lunch at El Perico Marinero and order the famous pulpo rojo, all of which has been purchased from the local fishing co-op. I have no complaints when it lands on the table. A special ceviche distinct to this part of the Yucatán, it features octopus that has been sliced, battered, and fried into crispy pieces before being tossed in lime juice with chopped onions and sliced jalapeños. Every tentacle is a crunchy delight. Circling us like the morning's pelicans are plates weighed down with more octopus prepared in other ways: sautéed in garlic and butter, or cooked in a tomato-rich sofrito “a la Mexicana.”

Hotels that work with programs like Pesca Con Futuro can offer local, sustainably sourced seafood to guests—an answer to diners who are increasingly interested in knowing where their seafood comes from.

Belmond Maroma is one of several hotels in the Yucatan that uses seafood from Pesca Con Futuro. Follow founder Citlaly Gomez Lepe's advice and always ask your hotel where their seafood comes from. “Your questions will detonate through the restaurant, chefs, and businesses, making them all ask themselves the same questions,” she says. “It triggers a chain reaction and signals that consumers care about this information.” You'll either learn something interesting about the food you are going to eat—and who caught it—or you may inspire a hotel to find better sources, knowing this matters to guests.

While joining fishermen for octopus excursions isn’t a common tourist experience, there are fishing collectives that are open to it. Ask your hotel about sustainable seafood experiences ahead of time, and see what can be arranged.

That said, dining on sustainable seafood here still isn't a given. As we pass plates of battered shrimp and sliced habanero swimming in lime, the fishermen commiserate over a growing number of hurdles. The demand for local sea cucumbers, which get exported to China, is too high to sustain; there is also an ongoing battle between artisanal fishermen and those who use shortsighted methods to turn a quick buck. Limberth speaks of divers from a neighboring state who hit the water late at night to fish during the seasonal bans Limberth vouches that, while diving just offshore, he has seen an increasing number of bleached rock caves underwater—usually the result of freediving fishermen, who squirt the chemical into an octopus hideout to send them fleeing for an easy catch. I can’t help but think of the octopus eggs left behind.

The impact of climate change also remains an ongoing issue. “When the water is warm enough to dive without a wetsuit, I know I won’t see octopuses the rest of the season. They go deeper. Way deeper,” Limberth says, pointing further out toward the continental shelf. Even then, studies have shown that the octopus maya is vulnerable to high water temperatures, dying once they hit 80 degrees.

As we watch the water lap against boats beside the boardwalk, I begin to understand why many of our conversations keep ending on the words “círculo de la vida”—the circle of life. The fishermen respect the vulnerabilities in an octopus's lifecycle; and yet, they must continue to fish, and protect their future ability to fish, so that they can sustain their families. After a day out at sea with Alcocer Diaz, I still can’t answer the existential quandary of whether or not to eat octopus, but I can appreciate how considered the creature is in their fishing method. On the flip side, I feel guilty for a months-prior omakase dinner in New York City that featured creamy octopus eggs, not understanding how precious they are.

Alcocer Diaz, meanwhile, is preoccupied that our fishing efforts were unsuccessful. So much so, that he motorbikes off at the end of lunch, returning with some achiote-rich rechado (a chili paste for cooking, and regional specialty) as a parting gift.

An ajilo (skiff) boat sets off on the water

A couple of days later, I sit with Landeo on the restaurant terrace of Maroma. The menu before me has a blue icon beside various dishes to indicate that the key ingredient has been sourced via Pesca Con Futuro—the chef hopes that, soon, all of his seafood will come through the collective.

“When I started working here on the Riviera Maya, I thought it was going to be like Disneyland in terms of ingredients,” Landeo says. “But there have been real challenges. The majority of hotels here are all-inclusive, so the product they use is different than what we offer.” He hopes that Pesca Con Futuro can continue to get the buy-in from chefs and hotels that it needs to expand even further—and that all begins with diners. “For me, Pesca Con Futuro just makes sense.”

We look out at the sloshing sea, struck by the stories the fisherman told us.“I also want my son to find a world better than the one I got,” he says. “And it's why I want to work responsibly.”

Maybe we aren’t so different from the octopuses, diligently guarding their offspring. It's all a bet on the future.

#6456. Neanderthal DNA still survives in our human family tree. What were our ancient relatives' relationships like?

Developing research suggests that ancient interbreeding wasn't random — it was socially patterned, directional and far more complicated than the headlines suggest.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Deep in a limestone cave on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, two very different sets of humans left behind nearly identical traces of their lives — similar stone tools, the remains of the same prey animals, the same types of seashells pierced and strung into ornaments. They may have been separated by thousands of years and may not have directly interacted. Yet the overlap between them was striking enough that researchers studying the site had to look twice.

The site, Üçağızlı II, offers one of the clearest examples of a conundrum that scientists have long wrestled with: Neanderthals and modern humans (Homo sapiens) didn't just collide and go their separate ways. They inhabited the same areas, and, as dozens of genetic studies have confirmed, had sex, across tens of thousands of years and on multiple continents. The DNA of nearly every person alive outside Africa today carries the proof: Roughly 2% of the non-African genome is Neanderthal.

And yet, there is not a single archaeological site that shows them living together. Knowing that modern humans and Neanderthals mated is not the same as understanding how it happened. Who approached whom? Were these interactions consensual? Were they the result of violence or trade alliances? Who raised these hybrid babies? And what does the genetic record tell us about the social lives of two different kinds of humans navigating each other's existence for the first time?

Some of the answers, it turns out, are written on the X chromosome — and they are stranger than expected.

The first high-coverage Neanderthal genome was sequenced in 2010, and for the next 15 years, researchers kept noticing something puzzling: Neanderthal DNA was less common from the X chromosomes in people alive today.

One of the two sex chromosomes in humans, the X chromosome represents about 5% of the DNA in cells. Most females carry a pair of X chromosomes in each cell, while most males have one X and one Y.

Everywhere else in our genome, traces of long-ago breeding between Neanderthals and modern humans showed up in roughly consistent proportions. But on the X chromosome, there was far less Neanderthal DNA.

In people today, the X chromosome (bottom right) has less Neanderthal DNA than the non-sex chromosomes do.

The leading explanation was negative selection — the idea that Neanderthal gene variants unique to the X chromosome were somehow incompatible with modern-human biology and had been gradually eliminated from the gene pool over thousands of generations. It was a reasonable hypothesis, given that incompatibilities elsewhere in the genome did lead to the weeding out of Neanderthal DNA on other chromosomes over time.

To understand why the negative selection explanation didn't explain the X chromosome data, however, it helps to know what different parts of the genome actually do. Some stretches of DNA are protein-coding regions; they contain the instructions for building proteins, the molecular machinery that does most of the work inside cells. Others are regulatory sequences that don't build proteins themselves but help control when and how much of a protein gets produced. And then there are still other stretches of DNA that don’t appear to code for proteins or directly regulate gene expression, though researchers suspect at least some have functions we don’t yet fully understand.

Alexander Platt, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, hypothesized that if the problem was that Neanderthal gene variants on the X chromosome were inherently harmful, modern-human X gene variants would have been advantageous in Neanderthals. As a result, X chromosomal DNA extracted from Neanderthal skeletons should show an excess of modern-human DNA in stretches of the genome where they'd provide measurable benefit. They reasoned that this excess would likely appear in protein-coding genes or the regulatory regions that control their expression, not noncoding DNA.

But that's not what they found. Instead, Neanderthal X chromosomes carried more modern-human DNA in the noncoding regions of the genome than in coding regions. This pattern didn't reflect selection for better gene variants. It was a signature of reproduction ‪—‬ a record of who was passing chromosomes to whom.

In a typical pregnancy, the mother contributes an X chromosome via the egg, and the father contributes either an X or a Y via the sperm cell. So, while an individual is guaranteed to inherit their mother's X, they don't necessarily carry their father's — males exclusively inherit their mother's X. That pattern differs from the other 22 pairs of chromosomes, which mothers and fathers contribute to equally. Across a population, then, two-thirds of X chromosomes are inherited from mothers and one-third from fathers.

This fact makes the X chromosome a particularly sensitive recorder of who was reproducing with whom.

Tracking the flow of X chromosomes can reveal trends in Neanderthal-human mating. If Neanderthal males paired with modern-human females more often than Neanderthal females paired with modern-human males, you'd see more modern-human X chromosomes flow into the Neanderthal gene pool.

X data suggests that when the two types of humans mated, the mother was usually a Homo sapiens.

When the team ran simulations to explore this idea, the data suggested what Platt described as a persistent, recurring mating preference: Males with more Neanderthal ancestry tended to reproduce with females with more modern-human ancestry. And this trend held across at least two distinct mating periods separated by around 200,000 years, said Platt.

This finding gave the researchers a new window into the timeline of mating between Neanderthals and modern humans. Platt's team identified at least two distinct pulses: one roughly 45,000 years ago, which produced the majority the Neanderthal DNA that lives on in non-African genomes today, and an earlier period over 200,000 years ago, whose genetic traces survived not in modern-human populations but in Neanderthals.

The pattern of Neanderthal males having offspring with H. sapiens females appears in both periods, separated by more than 150,000 years.

What the X chromosome data alone cannot say is why the pattern exists. It documents who reproduced with whom. It says nothing about who wanted whom.

That distinction matters, because the same genetic signature can emerge from very different causes, and some have nothing to do with sexual preference.

Rajiv McCoy, a geneticist at Johns Hopkins University, pointed out that biology alone could produce a genetic signal like this one. When closely related species interbreed, the success of a pregnancy can depend not just on whose genes are inherited but on which parent belongs to which group.

Even if Neanderthal genes work fine in a modern-human genetic background, hybrid pregnancies may simply have been more likely to succeed when the Neanderthal was the father rather than the mother. That's not because of either parent's sexual preferences, but because of how their respective biologies interacted in the womb, McCoy told Live Science.

Researchers have recently proposed a few mechanisms that fit neatly with this theory. One study suggests that Neanderthal red blood cells restricted fetuses' growth in the womb. Another proposed that Neanderthal mothers carrying hybrid offspring may have been more prone to preeclampsia, a life-threatening pregnancy complication. Nothing in the existing data definitively rules such causes, McCoy said.

Neanderthal males were more likely to produce hybrid offspring that contributed to our gene pool than were Neanderthal females.

In practice, the two explanations are hard to separate. "Our models have no way of distinguishing mating from mating that produces a viable and fertile offspring," McCoy said. If hybrid pregnancies failed more often when the mother was Neanderthal, the genetic record would look similar to a world where Neanderthal females mated less often with H. sapiens males. Sexual encounters that didn't result in offspring left no genetic trace.

For now, the question of what drove that bias — social preference, or biology — remains open. Whatever barriers existed between the groups, they clearly weren't absolute. Multiple distinct episodes of interbreeding over thousands of years, McCoy noted, is itself evidence that the fertility of hybrid individuals was "sufficiently intact to leave a lasting mark."

Bridget Alex, a researcher in human evolutionary biology at Harvard University who has spent her career reconstructing the timing and geography of Neanderthal-H. sapiens overlap, cautioned that all this is hampered by one fact: no direct archaeological evidence reveals how the two groups interacted.

"Despite a century and a half of Neanderthal research," she told Live Science, "no one's ever found a Neanderthal and Homo sapiens fossil in the same exact layer dated to the same exact period at the same exact site."

Instead, we have a regional and variable patchwork shaped by conditions that shifted over thousands of years and hundreds to thousands of miles.

Neanderthals inhabited a territory stretching from Siberia to Iberia to Southwest Asia between roughly 250,000 and 40,000 years ago. Modern humans were evolving in Africa during much of that span and came out repeatedly, in multiple waves, meeting Neanderthals in different times and places, with likely very different outcomes each time, Alex said.

"It's not like the Neanderthals living in what's now Spain could call up the ones in what's now Uzbekistan and be like, 'OK, what's our policy with modern humans? Do we kill them, have sex with them, ignore them?'" she said. "My assumption has always been that interactions would vary across time and space depending on the particular environmental conditions, social conditions, and just the whims of a particular group."

Grotte Mandrine contains artifacts from tens of thousands of years of Neanderthal occupation — and a single layer suggestive of Homo sapiens occupation.

At Grotte Mandrin, a cave in the Rhône Valley in southern France, archaeologists found one of the most illuminating records of what those encounters may have looked like. Ludovic Slimak, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Toulouse who has spent years excavating the site, described it as something genetics alone can't offer: "an extraordinarily precise archaeological sequence of Neanderthals and [Homo] sapiens occupying exactly the same place," he told Live Science in an email.

Neanderthal artifacts fill layer after layer of radiocarbon and luminescence dating up to about 57,000 years ago. And then, in one thin layer dated to between 56,800 and 51,700 years ago, there's a set of different stone tools and a single tooth that appear to belong to H. sapiens. Then, in layers immediately above, beginning around 51,700 years ago, Neanderthal artifacts appear again. That group of modern humans arrived, lived briefly in a continent otherwise inhabited entirely by Neanderthals, and then disappeared.

"What strikes me most is not mixture but proximity without fusion," Slimak told Live Science in an email. In other words, the two groups left no trace of cultural exchange or shared practice.There were "two human populations occupying the same landscape, probably encountering one another, while remaining culturally and biologically very different," Slimak said.

Genetics also paints a portrait of two very different social architectures. Two sites exemplify the trends: At Sunghir, a burial site in Russia dating to around 34,000 years ago, two H. sapiens adolescents were interred head to head beneath thousands of ivory beads and mammoth-bone spears. Ancient DNA analysis showed they were not immediate family members, yet they were buried together in an elaborate ceremony that implies a social world much wider than their immediate group.

Graves from more than 30,000 years ago in Sunghir in Russia show that two adolescents buried together were not closely related, suggesting Homo sapiens had wider and more flexible social networks than Neanderthals.

In contrast, at Chagyrskaya, a cave site in Siberia, Neanderthals buried in what appears to be a single community layer included a father and his teenage daughter, and a second pair of individuals who shared roughly a quarter of their DNA.

While these are just two sites, they reflect a broader trend that shows up repeatedly in genetic data: Human groups tended to operate through what Alex described as a nested structure: Tens of thousands of years ago, small groups of perhaps 20 or 30 individuals maintained broader ties through ceremonies, intermarriage between human groups and exchange with other groups.

In contrast, data from Neanderthal sites reveal that they tended to cluster in small, tightly knit groups that remained relatively separate from other Neanderthal populations.

Homozygosity, or DNA regions where a person inherited two copies of the same gene variant, is an inverse measure of genetic diversity. Adapted from Skov et al, 2022.

Unlike modern humans, Neanderthals didn't regularly mate with individuals in other communities, Alex said. The result, written in their genomes, is that individuals within a single Neanderthal group were often closely related. Their genomes show low genetic diversity across the board, — "kind of suggesting they're always a population on the verge," Alex said, "like an endangered species."

Still, there had to be some out-group mating. At sites where researchers have extracted genomes from several Neanderthal individuals, the pattern is consistent: Male Neanderthals were more closely related to each other than female Neanderthals were to each other. Females, by contrast, seemed more likely to have come from elsewhere. This is the signature of a "patrilocal" social structure in which males stay in their birth groups and females move between them.

Neanderthals' insularity sharpens a key question: If Neanderthal groups weren't regularly folding in Neanderthal females from distant communities, they would probably be even less likely to incorporate female H. sapiens. So how did modern-human women end up producing offspring with Neanderthal men at all?

Fernando Villanea, a population geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder, thinks the question may be framed backward. The image of Neanderthal males raising hybrid children with modern-human females within Neanderthal communities, he argues, probably inverts what actually happened.

Something the genomes of late Neanderthals — those living toward the end of their long history in Eurasia — make clear is that they were roughly 10 times more inbred than the modern human ancestors who were then expanding out of Africa in large numbers, he noted. That level of inbreeding isn't usually a choice; it reflects how small and fragmented Neanderthal populations likely were.

We need to imagine scenarios where a majority of modern human groups traveling into Eurasia are encountering a vanishing minority of Neanderthals.

Archaeological and paleoclimatic data fill in the context: The ecosystems Neanderthals were best adapted to were shrinking as the planet entered a warmer, more humid period. Modern humans, who had evolved in hotter, wetter African environments, were simply better suited to Europe's new conditions, experts think.

The resulting numerical imbalance changes how scientists think about mating between Neanderthals and modern humans.

"We need to imagine scenarios where a majority of modern human groups traveling into Eurasia are encountering a vanishing minority of Neanderthals," Villanea told Live Science.

In the crucial period between roughly 50,000 and 44,000 years ago, when much of the interbreeding that left a trace in our DNA took place, Neanderthal DNA made up 5% of the modern human genome. Given how heavily humans outnumbered Neanderthals at the time, "that's a lot of matings occurring between the two." The most likely story, Villanea proposes, is "human groups absorbing surviving Neanderthal individuals and raising their children in a mostly human group."

His 2018 study in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution established that this happened across multiple distinct episodes — and the later ones are particularly telling. Some ancient H. sapiens genomes from Europe around 40,000 years ago, according to the study, carry Neanderthal ancestry from individuals who lived just a few generations after archaeologists can no longer find any physical trace of Neanderthals in the region at all.

Even the very last Neanderthal survivors were still contributing to the H. sapiens gene pool. A 2024 study by Leonardo Iasi and colleagues similarly determined that almost 90% of total Neanderthal ancestry in humans today came from a main pulse roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago, likely in the Middle East, with the rest trickling in from more sporadic encounters scattered across Eurasia.

That paints a picture of meetings becoming rarer and rarer as Neanderthals disappeared, with hybridization continuing whenever they did meet up. "This, to me, says deliberate integration of Neanderthal individuals into human groups," Villanea said.

We know that some hybrid Neanderthal-H. sapiens survived because "we still carry the legacy of their existence," Alex said. However, we know they didn't thrive, because the Neanderthal ancestry of our ancestral populations eroded quickly.

While some hybrids survived, they likely suffered from health problems.

Most genes work in concert with other genes across the genome. When Neanderthal-specific variants entered the modern-human genome, it was like trying to put gears from one machine into a slightly different one; the parts didn't quite fit together. As a result, natural selection removed the Neanderthal variants rapidly. Villanea's calculations, based on the rate at which chromosomes recombine during cell division, suggest the drop from the original approximately 5% Neanderthal DNA roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago to the roughly 2% carried today happened in around 10 human generations.

"That's very fast," he said. "In real-life terms, that means a lot of hybrids did not survive to reproduce, and the ones that did probably had to deal with life-long health problems."

Platt's team looked at genetic evidence from multiple sites across Eurasia and found that the genetic purge ran in the opposite direction, too. Modern-human DNA was also being selected out of Neanderthal genomes.

Neither had inherently superior genes, Platt concluded. The gene variants were simply optimized for the separate evolutionary histories of their respective lineages, hundreds of thousands of years of independent adaptation that made certain combinations disadvantageous, if not fatal.

If Neanderthal males and modern-human females really were producing more surviving offspring than the reverse pairing, where did those children end up?

Villanea was cautious about reading too much into the X chromosome pattern on its own to answer that question. The imbalance Platt found is real, he said — not a statistical quirk. But "there is nothing in the X chromosome data that says it's based on human or Neanderthal mating preference," as Platt proposes.

The same pattern could, in theory, emerge from Neanderthal males leaving their birth groups to find mates, but as archaeological evidence suggests, this was not typical behavior. More likely, he argues, is something biological.

Hybrid children were likely raised in Homo sapiens groups.

In Peromyscus maniculatus and Peromyscus polionotus — two closely related species of North American deer mouse — a phenomenon called genomic imprinting causes hybrid offspring to develop differently in the womb depending on which species was the father and which was the mother. This pattern has nothing to do with behavior or preference. A similar process in early humans could have made Neanderthal father-H. sapiens mother pairings more likely to produce surviving offspring than the reverse, without either group consciously choosing anything.

"We simply don't know enough yet," Villanea said.

Distinguishing between these explanations — social behavior versus biological incompatibility — will require more Neanderthal genomes from the critical period of contact, ideally spanning multiple geographic regions, experts said.

There's another clue in genetic evidence from a 2026 study of 27 late Neanderthals who lived between 50,000 and 40,000 years ago in what is now Belgium and France. None of those individuals showed any sign of recent ancestry from modern humans, even as H. sapiens from the same era demonstrably carried Neanderthal DNA.

If hybrid children had been raised in Neanderthal groups and went on to reproduce there, those groups' genomes should retain traces of those events ‪—‬ but they don't.

As for whether modern-human groups were patrilocal — with males staying, females moving — the answer is considerably more variable than in Neanderthals. Modern-human communities across cultures show a range of patterns, with both sexes leaving their birth groups depending on circumstance, Alex said. That flexibility may have been part of what made human groups better able to absorb outside individuals.

Neither genetics nor archaeology has yet been able to answer the question at the center of this story: whether these encounters were by choice, by circumstance, or by force. Platt's team set it aside deliberately, and Alex is careful about it, too.

"We still wouldn't know if it was consensual or coerced," she said.

It's worth being specific about what different scenarios would look like archaeologically. If Neanderthal and modern-human individuals mingled through peaceful alliances, we might expect to find toolmaking techniques or symbolic objects crossing between groups at contact sites — precisely the kind of evidence that is absent at Grotte Mandrin, where, as Slimak noted, the two groups' technical traditions remained entirely distinct.

Slimak, writing from Grotte Mandrin in the middle of his excavation season, urged even more restraint. The genetic data, he said, are "consistent with an asymmetry" — gene flow moved more successfully through Neanderthal males and H. sapiens females than the reverse — but that is where the certainty ends.

The data says nothing about culture, desire, attraction or intent. "That entire social world has been added afterwards," he said.

The same signal, he pointed out, could emerge from a variety of histories — female mobility, demographic imbalance, alliance, exchange, capture, differential survival among hybrids. And these factors could contribute alone or in combination. Even the categories available for describing female movement may be too blunt. A single instance of migration, in traditional societies, can involve marriage, family strategy, alliance, obligation and violence all at once, in combinations that leave no trace for archaeology to disentangle.

"We may identify that a woman came from elsewhere," Slimak said. "We cannot recover her consent."

However, the convergence of genetics, demography and archaeology does reveal a structural picture, if not a sociological one.

The interbreeding was directional and repeated, patterned in ways that map onto the social organization of both groups — and driven in large part, Villanea's model suggests, by the sheer demographic weight of a growing human population folding in what remained of a disappearing one. Neanderthal males, in dwindling and insular communities, appear to have been the ones whose genes crossed into the larger H. sapiens world. Their children, in all likelihood, were raised as humans.

"Genes do not preserve past loves," Slimak said. "They preserve what was transmitted. And between transmission and lived experience lies almost the whole of human society."

See the new facial reconstruction of a man from Roman-era Scotland who was decapitated after his death and buried near a Roman fort.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers have virtually reconstructed the face of a man who was decapitated after his death almost 2,000 years ago and then buried near a Roman military fort in Scotland.

While it's unclear why the man was beheaded, other burials hundreds of miles away may offer a clue. A chemical analysis of the man's remains suggests that he grew up in southern Britain. Beheading bodies may have been an obscure burial rite for some southern Britons, as other decapitated bodies from about the same time have been found in that region, John H. Reid, an archaeologist at the Trimontium Trust who was not involved in the excavations, told Live Science.

Another mystery is why a southern Briton was on the Roman frontier, but it seems that he was working for the Roman army when he died, researchers at National Museums Scotland said in a statement. However, his skeleton shows the man's right arm had such limited movement that he could not have used a sword, so he was probably not a soldier, they added.

Despite this disability, however, it's possible that the man used weapons in his other hand, or had a job in the Roman army that did not require frontline fighting, such as a clerk.

"He could have been left-handed, or he could have had a 'desk job'," said Reid, who is the author of the book "The Eagle and the Bear: A New History of Roman Scotland" (Birlinn, 2023).

The man was probably about 50 years old when he died between A.D. 142 and 165. His remains were then buried near the Roman fort at Inveresk, on Scotland's east coast just southeast of what's now Edinburgh, according to the statement.

An analysis of the man's skeleton indicated that he had lived an active life. His nose had been broken and healed, and his right elbow showed extensive bone growth, perhaps from arthritis. Reid said the bone growth may have been his body's response to a physical injury.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Researchers at National Museums Scotland and the independent U.K.-based forensic anthropologist Christopher Rynn created the facial construction based on the man's skull.

The facial reconstruction is based on the shape of the man's skull. He is shown here without a beard, which was based on what was common at this time.

The Roman fort at Inveresk was built around A.D. 140 and acted as a command-and-supply center for Roman forts along the Antonine Wall, which ran along the shortest route between Scotland's west coast and east coast — roughly the line between Glasgow and Edinburgh, although neither city existed at the time.

The Romans had hoped to secure all of Scotland under their rule after their invasion of Britain under Emperor Claudius in A.D. 43. They tried to impose control after their victory against a coalition of native Caledonian tribes at the Battle of Mons Graupius (possibly near the Scottish city of Perth) in about 83. But by about 120, the Romans had retreated to the heavily fortified line of Hadrian's Wall, near the modern border of England and Scotland.

The fort at Inveresk was built for a second push that aimed to secure Roman control over southern Scotland by establishing the Antonine Wall. But this failed too, and after A.D. 162, the Romans withdrew again to Hadrian's Wall, until the final collapse of Roman rule in Britain in the early fifth century.

Jess Turner, an osteoarchaeologist at National Museums Scotland, with the skull of the man buried outside the Roman fort at Inveresk.

Reid told Live Science that Scotland's soil seldom preserved human skeletons, making the discovery of a Roman-era burial an uncommon find. Although the man had been decapitated after his death, other aspects of his grave indicated he was buried with dignity. In other words, his burial was unlike those of executed criminals, who were often decapitated in Roman-era Britain, he said.

The remains from six Roman-era burials have been found at Inveresk, and four of the dead had been similarly beheaded, the statement said.

There are several ways non-Romans could have served with the Roman army, Reid told Live Science. They might have been employed as servants or artisans attached to the Roman legions, or they might have been soldiers in Roman auxiliary units or even citizen-based legions, he said. By the time of the Antonine Wall, few members of the Roman army in Scotland would have been from the Italian peninsula, he added.

The chemical analysis looked at the ratios of isotopes, or variations of chemical elements, in the man's remains. This analysis suggested that the man had grown up in southern Britain. Alternatively, he may have been recruited from a nearby region, such as the coast of what's now the Netherlands, that gave the same isotopic profile, Reid said.

Reid and his colleagues have found extensive evidence of the Roman army at the Burnswark site in southern Scotland, including the deadly whistling sling bullets they used against their "barbarian" foes. Archaeological work there is ongoing.

What do you know about the Empire's conquest of the British Isles? Find out with our Roman Britain quiz!

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.
