#6429. Want to lose weight? The type of protein you eat may matter

A new study links eating less animal protein and more plant protein to greater weight loss, but other dietary changes may also explain the results.

When you’re trying to lose weight, protein advice can turn meals into a daily tally of grams. A new study suggests there’s more to consider than the total.

Among adults with overweight who tried two diets, those who reduced animal protein the most and ate more plant protein tended to lose the most weight.

They also ate less fat and more carbohydrates, though, so the researchers couldn’t pin the weight loss on protein alone.

Hana Kahleova, director of clinical research at the Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine, was the study’s senior author. The nonprofit, based in Washington, DC, ran the trial.

“Patients are constantly told to worry about getting enough protein,” Kahleova said.

The trial ran from February to October 2019 and involved 62 overweight adults in Washington. At the start, they weighed about 216 pounds (98 kilograms) on average.

About half began with a low-fat vegan diet and half with a Mediterranean diet. They followed their assigned plan for 16 weeks, took a four-week break, then spent another 16 weeks on the other diet.

On the vegan diet, volunteers ate vegetables, fruit, grains and legumes such as beans.

Meat, fish, dairy and eggs were off the menu, as were added fats and cooking oils.

The Mediterranean plan included plenty of vegetables, fruit, legumes, fish and nuts, with nearly four tablespoons (50 grams) of extra-virgin olive oil each day. The plan favored lean white meat over red meat.

Neither plan set a calorie limit. At four points in the trial, volunteers wrote down everything they ate for three days, and a registered dietitian analyzed the records.

In all, 52 people finished the full 36 weeks. An earlier report on this trial found that volunteers lost about 13 pounds (six kilograms) while eating the vegan diet, but their weight didn’t change reliably on the Mediterranean plan.

The new study revisited those food records, this time focusing on protein.

The question was whether changes in the amount and type of protein went along with changes on the scale.

On the vegan plan, animal protein fell from about 51 grams a day to fewer than three. Plant protein went up, from roughly 29 grams to 43 grams daily.

That extra plant protein didn’t replace all the animal protein people had given up. Total protein intake dropped by about 33 grams a day, from roughly 80 grams to 46.

So this wasn’t a straightforward exchange of one protein source for another. Volunteers ate less protein overall, which makes it difficult to separate the effects of the amount from the effects of its source.

The Mediterranean diet brought little change in either animal or plant protein. Total intake stayed near 73 grams a day.

For this comparison, the team used the first 16 weeks, when about half the volunteers were on each diet. They compared each person’s change in protein intake with that person’s change in weight.

Those who cut animal protein the most generally lost the most weight. The same pattern appeared among people who increased plant protein the most, and among those who made the largest cuts to total protein.

All three links were moderate. Each passed a stricter statistical check the researchers used to guard against chance findings.

“This doesn’t mean protein is the enemy,” Kahleova said. “It means the source matters.”

Protein is made of smaller molecules called amino acids, and foods contain different amounts of each one. Using the food records, the team estimated how much of each amino acid volunteers ate.

Volunteers ate less of every amino acid the researchers tracked on the vegan diet, with methionine dropping by more than half, from about 1.8 grams a day to 0.7 grams.

Lower intake of almost every amino acid went along with more weight loss.

Only four of those links passed the strictest statistical check: isoleucine, lysine, methionine and tyrosine.

Earlier research cited in the paper found less isoleucine, lysine and methionine in plant protein than in animal protein.

Methionine contains sulfur. In a 2024 trial cited by the authors, people on a vegan diet low in sulfur-containing amino acids lost about 20% more weight than a comparison group.

None of this tells us what would happen if people changed their protein source and left everything else alone. The volunteers’ meals changed in several ways at once.

On the vegan diet, fat supplied about 17% of daily calories, down from 38%. Carbohydrates went the other way, rising from 42% to 69% of calories.

Daily cholesterol intake fell by more than 270 milligrams, and each gram of food contained fewer calories. The authors also pointed to fiber and other nutrients as possible parts of the explanation.

Earlier analyses of the same volunteers also linked weight loss to other features of the vegan diet, including a score measuring the proportion of plant-based foods in their diets.

These are all correlations drawn from the same dietary changes, rather than separate proof of what caused the weight loss.

Food records depend on people remembering and accurately reporting what they ate, so errors are possible. About 78% of the volunteers were women, and the average age was 57.

They also all lived in one city. The findings may not hold for men, younger people or more diverse groups.

The Physicians Committee promotes plant-based diets and paid for the study. Three of the five authors work there, although the authors stated that the funder did not influence the results.

People lost weight while eating the vegan diet, but how much of that came from plant protein itself remains unknown.

The authors described the findings as a starting point for ideas to test, not proof.

They called for trials that change only the protein source while keeping calories, fat and fiber the same. That would give researchers a clearer way to tell whether protein deserves the credit.

The study is published in the journal BMJ Nutrition, Prevention & Health.

#6428. Roller coaster safety is a matter of science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Extreme ride guidelines don't all reflect the latest findings

Current industry guidelines for roller coaster design don’t account for all the forces riders face on extreme coasters from previous decades. Hershey Park’s Fahrenheit, pictured here, briefly held the world record for steepness when it opened in 2008.

The first roller coaster in the United States to loop upside down tucked riders by twos into bench seats, secured them with a single seat belt and subjected them to an estimated 7.5 times the force of gravity (some say it was closer to 12 g). The Flip Flap Railway opened in New York City’s Sea Lion Park in 1895, where the roller coaster reportedly strained backs, wrenched necks and dazzled spectators until the park closed in 1902.

Now, roller coaster safety is in the news again. In September, three lawsuits were filed against Six Flags and ride manufacturer S&S Global, alleging that riders sustained “catastrophic” brain injuries on the roller coaster X2 at California’s Magic Mountain theme park. These are just the most recent cases related to the ride, filed after a CNN investigation found dozens of injuries on X2 leading to hospitalization, disability and death. On September 29, Six Flags announced X2 would shut down permanently even though it said the ride “consistently passed a multitude of safety tests.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Weeks later, the company said it would temporarily close another nine coasters across the United States and Canada after a man fell from his seat on the roller coaster Goliath and died at Six Flags Over Georgia. Six Flags announced Oct. 24 that it would add seat belts to Goliath and other coasters, and a spokesperson told Science News that the company is “committed to rigorous ride inspection, maintenance and safety procedures.” But the incidents and closures are prompting new questions about coaster design and safety — particularly when they are operating correctly — and whether guidelines overlook crucial factors.

Roller coasters are not regulated at the federal level in the United States; each state has its own approach to their management. But an international technical group comprising over 1,000 industry professionals, the ASTM Committee F24 on Amusement Rides and Devices, publishes recommendations that are considered industry standards.

The first ASTM standards for roller coaster design were released in 1982. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission had been stripped of authority to regulate fixed-site amusement rides the year before. In the wake of this newfound freedom, it was a “roller coaster arms race,” says Brian Avery, an event and tourism management researcher at the University of Florida in Gainesville who studies risk and amusement ride safety protocols. The period was characterized by attempts to “build it taller, faster, longer.”

When X2, originally called X, opened in 2002, it was the world’s first fourth-dimension coaster. It catapulted people 60 meters high, traveling 122 kilometers per hour while its seats rotated independently on their own tracks. In the 24 years since, only 20 or so other fourth-dimension coasters have been built, and several have closed.

As roller coasters grew more extreme, injuries increased and were more publicized, sparking calls for further research and regulation.

Generally, roller coasters are quite safe. Out of 1.7 billion annual amusement park rides across North America, just 652 roller coaster injuries were reported in 2024 by parks choosing to share data. Studies suggest that riding a roller coaster is very unlikely to cause a brain injury, although most research on roller coaster brain impacts is about a decade or more old.

In 2002, a study used reported g forces from three roller coasters in a mathematical model to determine that their acceleration levels were below those predicted to cause head injuries. A 2017 study found brain effects on three roller coasters that were low on average, but “comparable with mild sports impacts,” like those sustained by heading a soccer ball, at their peak.

“The limiting of g forces alone might be an insufficient design criterion for roller coaster rides,” wrote the authors of the 2017 study.

In 2020, David Eager, a biomechanical engineer at the University of Technology Sydney, coauthored a paper on under-acknowledged forces affecting roller coaster safety, including jerk (the rate at which acceleration changes), snap (the rate at which jerk changes) and vibration.

“Roller coaster passengers need time to sense acceleration changes and adjust their muscle tension or suffer conditions such as whiplash,” Eager wrote.

The ASTM standards are exacting in some ways. Research conducted during the space race led to a 6g recommended limit on roller coaster acceleration exposure. However, ASTM doesn’t make recommendations about other types of motion on a roller coaster that might impact the neck, head and brain. It disregards forces lasting less than 200 milliseconds, no matter how intense.

But each tiny imperfection and variation in the circumference of the track — especially plentiful in coasters built before modern manufacturing techniques — causes a jolt, says Jurnan Schilder, a mechanical engineer and researcher who teaches roller coaster design at the University of Twente in Enschede, the Netherlands. He studies ways to create smoother roller coaster rides.

Schilder’s research suggests that at each track imperfection, “theoretically, you experience infinite jerk.” On a fourth-dimension coaster, he says, two sets of tracks mean double the variations. “Not only is the train sometimes shaking, but also the tilting mechanism is shaking.”

Research beyond rides also suggests intense and repeated rattling, jostling and vibration could meaningfully impact the brain. The U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration recommends limiting the duration and intensity of whole-body vibration. In April, the Virginia Tech Helmet Lab, which studies the science of brain injuries, published an article suggesting some concussions experienced by baseball players may result from just milliseconds of vibration.

North Carolina high school student Kayleigh Bonner’s quest to understand her father’s death exposed similar risks. After her father, a retired U.S. Coast Guard surfman who captained boats through rough waves for 21 years, experienced symptoms of a brain injury and died by suicide, Kayleigh surveyed 77 other elite surfmen for a senior capstone project. She found that 89 percent of those she spoke to had some symptoms of brain injury likely caused by the intense, rapidly changing forces traveling through their bodies as their boats were tossed by waves. Her quest to understand her father’s death was written about in July in the New York Times, and soon after acknowledged by the Coast Guard.

Of course, professional baseball players and Coast Guard surfmen have more significant and prolonged exposure to these forces than occasional roller coasters riders. But as researchers discover more about how different kinds of motion impact the brain, safety standards seem to lag behind. Minimizing jerk and snap is “an important consideration,” Eager says.

The mounting roller coaster-related headlines have renewed scrutiny of both the existing coaster safety standards and the lack of federal regulation. U.S. Rep. André Carson, a Democrat from Indiana, has called to pass a bill he first introduced in 2025 that would create federal oversight of amusement rides. Since 1999, Democratic U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has repeatedly introduced legislation to regulate fixed rides, but the bills have consistently stalled.

The amusement industry has long opposed federal oversight. In 2010, Avery coauthored a paper asserting that “the industry needs to find a collective voice and establish consistent self‐regulating policies in order to curb the incidents rates and avoid federal regulation.”

But Schilder says: “It makes you wonder: Are the current safety standards sufficient?”

For modern rides, Schilder says he believes they are. Modern manufacturing techniques mean roller coasters designed and built today are much smoother than predecessors. ASTM standards that filter out brief but intense forces, like vibration and jerk, are likely fine for rides that don’t vibrate and jerk very much. But at many parks, the ambitious and intense rides born of the roller coaster arms race are still in place.

Riders are “flirting, if you would, with danger when they experience rides and devices. They know that they’re more likely than not going to be safe,” Avery says. The point is to be “right on the cusp.”

#6427. A common substance in everyday foods is linked to better memory

Older adults in the study who ate more lecithin, found in eggs and soybeans, tended to score better on thinking tests.

Eggs for breakfast, beans with lunch, meat at dinner: each can provide lecithin, a mixture of fatty substances found in many foods.

Lecithin has a reputation as a memory aid, although the evidence is thin.

In a Chinese study, older adults with more lecithin in their diets had slightly better memory and thinking scores.

They also had lower odds of mild cognitive impairment: thinking problems that are worse than normal aging, but haven’t reached dementia.

The researchers assessed everyone just once. That gave them a snapshot of diet and memory, but no way to tell whether lecithin caused the difference.

Two hospital researchers in Beijing, Xiaoying Li and Chengyan Qi, are the first authors. Both hospitals are affiliated with Capital Medical University, where coauthor Yuandi Xi, a public health professor, studies nutrition, memory and muscle loss in older adults.

Cells use lecithin in the thin membranes that surround them. When we digest lecithin, we also get choline, which the body uses to make a chemical messenger that carries signals between nerve cells.

So there is a reason to look at lecithin and memory together.

A Finnish study involving 2,497 middle-aged men linked higher dietary phosphatidylcholine intake with a lower risk of dementia.

But lecithin has a less promising record as a treatment for dementia. A review of randomized trials, published in 2003, found that the evidence didn’t support using it that way.

Li and Qi’s team wanted to know about the years before dementia. Was getting more lecithin through ordinary meals linked with better memory and thinking?

The work involved 1,917 people in three Chinese cities: Beijing, Jincheng and Linyi.

The team recruited them between 2020 and 2023 from census or village records; every participant was 60 or older and had lived locally for at least a year.

In face-to-face interviews, they talked about their health and the foods they ate. A questionnaire recorded how often they ate different foods.

Using those answers and China’s food composition database, the researchers estimated each person’s daily lecithin intake.

About 88 milligrams marked the midpoint, so the main comparison was between people who ate more and those who ate less.

The team used a 30-point test called the Montreal Cognitive Assessment to screen for memory and thinking problems. A low score meant different things depending on a person’s education.

A score of 13 or below flagged possible trouble for someone who could not read. For people with seven or more years of schooling, the cutoff was 24 or below.

Neurologists examined everyone flagged by the screening. They used criteria from the U.S. National Institute on Aging and the Alzheimer’s Association to decide who had mild cognitive impairment.

They diagnosed 1,023 of the 1,917 participants, just over half the group.

The two intake groups were separated by about half a point, with the advantage going to those above 88 milligrams a day.

That calculation took account of age, sex, schooling, calories, blood fats, body composition and seven chronic diseases, including diabetes and stroke.

Half a point was a modest difference on this test. The typical score was 23 for people without mild cognitive impairment and 19 for those with it.

The higher-lecithin group had about 20% lower odds of a diagnosis. Dividing participants into thirds by intake gave a similar result: the top third had about 27% lower odds than the bottom third.

The team described the work as epidemiological evidence, meaning it revealed a health pattern across a group of people.

“This study provides important epidemiological evidence that ensuring adequate lecithin intake through a balanced diet could be a feasible approach to support cognitive health in the elderly,” the research team wrote.

The authors pointed to China’s daily reference intake for choline: 450 milligrams for men and 380 for women. These are choline targets, so they should not be confused with the lecithin amounts measured here.

According to the authors, a balanced diet with eggs, legumes and lean meats can readily meet those choline targets.

Earlier studies, they noted, have also linked eating patterns such as the Mediterranean diet with better thinking later in life.

The clearest link appeared among people with the least education. Of those taking part, 1,025 had gone no further than primary school, including 387 who could not read.

Within this group, people eating more lecithin scored nearly a point higher. For the other 892, who had reached junior high school or beyond, there was barely any gap.

The pattern didn’t vary reliably with age, sex or the chronic diseases the team checked. Education was different, and the authors think cognitive reserve could help explain why.

Schooling and mental effort may give the brain more ways to cope with damage.

Someone with less of that reserve might be more sensitive to dietary differences, although the study cannot establish whether changing their meals would help.

Red blood cell membranes offered another way to compare the groups, since they can reflect fats eaten over time.

For this part, the team randomly chose 15 people with mild cognitive impairment and 15 without it, then examined blood samples.

There was less lecithin in the cell membranes of people with impairment. And what was there contained a different mix: less of it carried polyunsaturated fatty acids, while more carried saturated fatty acids.

One member of the polyunsaturated family is DHA, a fat found in high amounts in nerve cells.

A form of lecithin carrying linoleic acid, another polyunsaturated fat, was one of six membrane fats that best distinguished the groups.

This was a small comparison, with only 30 people in all. The analysis also could not single out lecithin carrying DHA.

One thing this study cannot settle is the direction of the link. Diet and thinking were measured together, so it’s possible that memory problems had already changed people’s eating habits.

The team had no information on household income or household size, which can influence both diet and brain health. Participants also had to remember what they ate, leaving room for errors.

All participants came from three cities in China, and doctors made diagnoses without a full set of memory tests.

Studies elsewhere might find a different pattern.

The authors suggested that asking about lecithin intake could eventually become an inexpensive first step in community memory screening.

A model that combined intake with age, sex, schooling, calories and several health measures told the two groups apart reasonably well.

For now, the study cannot tell us whether eating more lecithin slows memory decline. To find out, the authors called for research that follows older adults for years, tracking their meals and their thinking.

The study is published in the journal Chinese Medical Journal.

#6426. I Can ‘Smell’ Thoughts. You Can Too—and It’s Secretly Shaping Your Life.

You may be able to sniff out everything from emotions to political beliefs.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Staring into the crowded refrigerator, I pushed containers of cold leftovers to and fro, willing a more appetizing late-night snack to appear. Over the low electric hum, I heard footsteps approaching from the other side of the open door. Before I saw my father’s somber face, a smell, or something like it, caught my attention. Instantly, I recognized it—not from the actual odor, as I couldn’t put my finger on any one recognizable scent, but more so from a memory.

This was the same way my dad smelled when he sat me and my sister down to tell us his own father had died. The same way he smelled when he picked me up early from high school to break the news about my maternal grandmother. The sadness in my dad’s voice came as no shock to me. Someone was dead. I knew with complete certainty that it was true. What I didn’t understand was how my nose knew it first.

Olfaction—or your sense of smell—is an integral part of human perception. It alerts us to potentially dangerous environmental factors such as smoke or gas, supports other senses such as taste, and a good sense of smell is even linked to lower rates of cognitive decline. Thinking back to that day in the kitchen, I began to wonder whether my sense of smell had tuned me into a silent conversation everyone else was missing. As it turns out, a growing volume of research suggests that scent is quietly shaping how we perceive one another and, more broadly, our reality. For some, it even appears to be a superpower—allowing them to detect, just through their sense of smell, illnesses and undiagnosed diseases in others.

One of these super smellers is a woman named Joy Milne, whose sense of smell is so acute that she’s able to detect when someone has tuberculosis, cancer, diabetes, Alzheimer’s disease, or Parkinson’s disease. Researchers put Milne’s nose to the test in a 2019 study published in ACS Central Science. The team asked two groups—one afflicted with Parkinson’s disease and the other healthy—to wear identical T-shirts overnight. When Milne smelled the shirts the next day, she was able to correctly sort all but one using just the power of her sniffer.

Months later, the participant whose smell Milne had mistakenly slotted into the Parkinson’s category reported that he had been diagnosed with the disease. Milne’s nose had picked up on something long before doctors had diagnosed it.

Pamela Dalton, PhD, MPH, studies the link between human olfaction and our cognitive and emotional processes at the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia, a scientific institute researching taste and smell. She says that, while not everyone has a nose attuned to medical maladies, the human olfactory system is constantly working overtime to decode and process the world in much more subtle ways.

In fact, when I confessed the story about my father announcing that my great-uncle had died, Dalton wasn’t fazed.

Dalton says humans communicate their feelings to each other through chemical molecules released in sweat, tears, or breath. These are called emotional chemical signals or emotional chemosignals. When the signals you give off reach another person, their olfactory system detects and interprets the chemicals. However, these aren’t processed the same way as regular smells.

Most of the time, we connect our smells to other senses stored in our memories—how a food tastes, or how salty ocean air may feel calming. If you’re sitting in front of a slice of pizza, for example, those molecules bond with the sensory receptors in your nose, generating an electric current that ends up in two areas of your brain that are associated with your sense of smell—the olfactory bulb and olfactory cortex. As the current continues traveling through your brain, regions associated with memory and emotional regulation complete higher processing to link that signal with your previously stored understanding of the smell of pizza.

With chemosignaling, on the other hand, a final association is never made. This is likely why the scent on my dad was familiar but not recognizable. In fact, to most people, chemosignals have no recognizable fragrance at all—so you won’t find a Yankee Candle that smells like sadness or an air freshener that reeks of stress.

Instead, chemosignaling acts as an invisible guiding force. It’s something most of us do all the time. We unconsciously filter our perception of people and the world around us through these involuntary olfactory noticings. These signals cause us to constantly make little judgments about others, everything from what someone’s feeling to whether they’d be a good romantic partner.

You May Be Able to Smell Political Beliefs

Opposite-party partnerships are uncommon, according to an ever-growing body of research. Researchers put that partisan divide to the test in a 2014 study published in the American Journal of Political Science where they tried to determine whether our sniffers play a role. The team found that participants were more attracted to the smell of people whose political beliefs aligned closely with their own. Crucially, the study subjects didn’t see the people whose scents they were analyzing, meaning visual attraction played no role in the end results.

Dalton says the process of sending and receiving chemosignals usually bypasses conscious thought, meaning that we do it involuntarily and without noticing it. “It’s not like we’re [observing these chemical signals] and going, ‘Oh… she’s sad, I’m smelling her sad odor,’” Dalton says.

However, that doesn’t mean that these signals go completely unnoticed. When your olfactory system senses someone else’s chemosignals, it can trigger changes in your perception, mood, or physical reaction, Dalton adds. In everyday terms, this may look like feeling inexplicably on edge around a friend who’s secretly stressed about a presentation they have at work the next day.

Nicholas A. Christakis, MD, PhD, MPH, is a social scientist at Yale University and the director of the school’s Human Nature Lab, a project dedicated to understanding human interaction. Christakis affirms Dalton’s ideas about chemosignals, pointing to something much deeper in our species’ history. He explains that humans evolved in a “very logical way,” since we emit volatile chemicals into the air during our most vulnerable, fear-filled moments. These chemicals then change the behavior of those around us in ways that, theoretically, would enhance survival, he says.

Christakis poses a few scenarios in which our ancestors might have felt danger, such as seeing a lion or a fire. “It’s not hard to imagine why, as a social animal, it would be useful to us to communicate to our brethren, ‘I'm afraid,’” he says. In terms of his analogy, if Christakis sees the lion and subconsciously emits these stress chemicals, you may realize he’s in trouble. “By signaling that I’m afraid, I might elicit from you some help,” he adds.

In a more modern example, Christakis points to the intoxicating aroma of a newborn baby. He says that a key part of this smell is an organic compound called hexadecanal. Hexadecanal is completely odorless, meaning that, if you smelled a sample on its own, your brain wouldn’t immediately conjure images of babies.

Despite this, a study published in Science Advances showed that participants unconsciously changed their behavior when asked to smell samples of hexadecanal. Specifically, men showed decreased aggression levels while women displayed the opposite. The theory, Christakis says, is that smelling a baby unconsciously causes people to become more nurturing and protective.

Unlike the participants in the study, I was more conscious of the odor that clung to my dad all those years ago. Still, Dalton explains that what I “smelled” most likely wasn’t the scent of death itself. My olfactory system responded with amplified alertness because it registered the release of chemical signals, perhaps those associated with stress, sadness, or anxiety. Simply put, I didn’t smell the future—I recognized an olfactory pattern I had previously encountered.

Dalton says it’s actually not that uncommon to become attuned to the chemical signals of people you spend a lot of time with. For instance, in a 2010 study published in Social Neuroscience, participants were able to detect heightened emotions in their romantic partners just by smelling their body odors. Additionally, people were more accurate when smelling their partner’s samples compared to those of strangers.

In fact, Dalton herself has even developed a keen nose after years of working with thousands of fear and anxiety sweat samples—a skill that she showed off on an episode of MythBusters. She notes that stress sweat has “a very different quality” than exercise sweat, though she avoids describing the scent to keep herself open to variations, since not everyone’s signals smell the same.

While Dalton acknowledges that there is still much to be learned in this field, she believes that these signals play a major role in shaping human interaction and perception. In short: It seems like sometimes you really should follow your nose.

#6425. Corals have a secret weapon against ocean heat

Scientists discovered that bacteria living inside corals produce hormones that help regulate their immune systems during extreme ocean heat.

Coral reefs are disappearing at an alarming rate as ocean temperatures climb.

Scientists understand how extreme heat causes coral bleaching, but one question has remained difficult to answer: Why do some corals withstand heat that devastates others?

A study has found part of the answer in an unexpected place.

Bacteria living inside the coral tissue produce steroid hormones – including testosterone and progesterone – that help the coral’s immune system survive the heat.

The work was led by scientists from the New York University Abu Dhabi.

First author Amin Mohamed and senior author Shady Amin led a team combining field sampling, genomics, metabolomics, and controlled lab experiments.

Their subject was a group of bacteria called Endozoicomonas, one of the most common coral-associated bacteria on earth.

Everyone studying coral health knew it mattered, but nobody had figured out exactly why.

The Arabian Gulf is one of the hottest seas on earth, regularly exceeding 36°C at the surface.

The team sampled Acropora pharaonis corals along a natural temperature gradient there – healthy colonies at 27°C, 32°C, and 34°C, plus corals showing signs of white syndrome disease.

They extracted metabolites and DNA from the coral tissue for analysis.

Most steroid precursors behaved as expected: their abundance fell as temperatures rose, because thermal stress suppresses steroid hormone production.

But testosterone and progesterone didn’t fall. They stayed elevated at 34°C, and at disease lesion sites too.

The decline in steroid precursors suggested that the coral itself was not responsible for the elevated hormone levels.

Something else within the coral and its microbial community appeared to be producing them.

That something was Endozoicomonas. Its genome encodes 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, an enzyme that synthesises testosterone from androstenedione. This is a reaction normally associated with vertebrates, not bacteria.

The team confirmed it in the lab with three Endozoicomonas isolates collected from hosts as far apart as the Great Barrier Reef, Taiwan, and Abu Dhabi.

All three converted cholesterol into testosterone and progesterone. In some strains, the transformation was temperature-regulated, kicking in at 34°C.

Across a broader pangenome of 29 Endozoicomonas genomes, 66 percent carried the relevant steroid metabolism genes.

This suggests the genes are conserved across the genus, in corals around the world.

“When temperatures become high, corals lose some of their ability to produce steroid hormones that are important for regulating their immune system,” Mohamed said.

“We found that their bacterial partners can compensate by producing these hormones themselves, allowing the coral to activate an immune response that helps its cells survive the heat.”

To test that directly, the team dosed Acropora downingi nubbins with 10 nM testosterone or progesterone, then raised the temperature to 33°C – 1.5°C above the local summer maximum.

They tracked gene expression across 27 immune-related pathways.

Both hormones amplified the coral’s innate immune response. TNF receptor signalling went up, NF-κB subunits increased, and kinase cascades linked to cell survival were activated.

Progesterone had an additional effect. It reduced signals associated with inflammation while increasing activity in pathways that help keep immune responses under control.

The pattern looks less like the immune system being switched on and more like it being tuned. The transcriptional changes were largely gone after 24 hours, so the modulation was transient.

Bacterially derived steroids influencing host immune signalling aren’t entirely without precedent. Gut bacteria in mammals, including Bacteroides acidifaciens and Ruminococcus gnavus, do something similar.

But nobody had seen it in coral until now. The evolutionary conservation of the pathway across Endozoicomonas strains from different oceans and different host species suggests it isn’t accidental.

These bacteria may provide an important advantage by helping corals regulate their immune responses as ocean temperatures rise.

Coral conservation has focused almost entirely on the coral itself – heat-tolerant selective breeding, assisted gene flow, nurseries, restoration.

This study suggests the microbiome deserves more precise attention than it has received.

The right bacteria may be performing chemical work that corals struggle to carry out when ocean temperatures climb.

Scientists still need to determine whether these microbial partnerships can be strengthened or managed to improve coral survival. But the discovery reveals another layer of reef resilience, one that has been hiding inside the coral itself.

The study is published in the journal Nature Microbiology.

The outer solar system will descend into chaos just a few billion years after the sun exhausts its fuel ‪—‬ much sooner than scientists previously thought, a new study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When the sun inevitably dies, not even the outer solar system will be safe from the resulting chaos, new research hints.Scientists have long thought the outer solar system ‪—‬ which comprises the four giant planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — would mostly retain its present-day appearance for hundreds of billions of years to come. But a new study suggests that the outer giants may develop weirdly shaped orbits as the sun runs out of fuel, causing the planets to cross paths and destroy themselves through collisions within three billion years of the sun's transformation into a red giant.

The findings, published Sept. 21 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, could change our understanding of what kinds of exoplanets orbit certain stars.

In about 5 billion years, the sun will balloon outward as a red giant after exhausting all of the hydrogen in its core. During this red giant phase, our star will swell to 100 times its present-day size, gobbling up Mercury, Venus and possibly even Earth in the process, Nathan Kaib, a planetary scientist at the University of Oklahoma who wasn't involved in the new research, told Live Science in an email. Following this violent swelling, the sun will crumple into a collapsed core called a white dwarf.

Until now, scientists thought the four outer planets would escape this phase relatively unscathed. A 1998 simulation-based study suggested that the gas the sun spews from its outer layers will push this planetary quartet outward, doubling the radius of each planet's orbit. Only the gravitational impact of a runaway star could destabilize this new order, and such events are thought to occur only once every billion billion years.

These predictions hinged on the assumption that the sun will eject its outer layers smoothly. However, recent observations of stars suggest a jerkier loss of mass, with gas clouds lofted by plumes of plasma in the sun — as though our star were spitting out mass blobs. "They're kind of like coronal mass ejections, except much larger," Jim Fuller, a professor of theoretical astrophysics at Caltech and co-author of the new study, told Live Science in an email.

Each "blob" pushes the star backward, similar to how a fired bullet causes a gun to recoil. Although every push is small, moving the sun just a few feet per second, many pushes can, over time, impart the equivalent of an enormous kick that alters the sun's speed by several hundred feet per second. In fact, astronomers have already seen white dwarfs suffer such kicks in other star systems.

An illustration of the sun releasing a giant mass of plasma. As such large explosions increase in the sun's dying days, the recoil could disrupt the gravitational balance of the outer solar system.

When Fuller, who studied these kicks, described them to Konstantin Batygin, a professor of planetary science at Caltech and the study's first author, Batygin "realized this would have important consequences for the evolution of our own solar system," Fuller said. That's because the kicks change the sun's gravitational pulls on everything around it.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To determine how the sun's mass loss would influence the giant planets, Batygin created computer-based simulations of the sun and the outer planets. The researchers considered three scenarios: if the sun lost its mass smoothly, if it spit out distinct mass blobs during its entire time evolving as a red giant, and if the sun spewed the blobs only during its last stages. The researchers also varied each ejected blob's mass.

The first scenario produced results similar to those of previous studies, with the outer solar system retaining almost all of its features for billions of years. In contrast, the other two cases had drastically different results. Using 672 simulations, the researchers found that if the sun lost mass in blobs, the giant planets would be thrown into chaos, switching places, developing weirdly oval-shaped orbits, and even getting ejected out of the solar system entirely. Most dramatically, in 96% of the simulations with the heaviest ejected mass packets, the planets get destroyed as they crashed into each other.

These developments also happened much more rapidly — less than a few hundred million years after the sun transformed into a white dwarf, or even during the red giant phase, in the most extreme scenarios.

The study's findings hint that analogues of the present-day outer solar system around white dwarf stars are less likely to exist than previously thought. Kaib noted that the study's results suggest that planets with oval-shaped orbits should dominate instead. It's thought that habitable planets could exist around white dwarfs, but this study's findings show that our understanding of those distant star systems may be incomplete, and that such worlds may, in reality, be unstable.

Batygin, K., Fuller, J., & Adams, F. C. (2026). Terminal instability of the solar system triggered by stochastic solar mass loss. The Astrophysical Journal Letters, 1009(2), L22. https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/aea290

#6423. Ancient Indigenous practice may help clams survive ocean acidification

Scientists found that adding crushed shells to clam beds may help young clams cope with ocean acidification, supporting a traditional Indigenous practice.

For a young clam, growing a shell takes energy. As the ocean absorbs more carbon dioxide and becomes more acidic, that job gets harder.

A new lab experiment suggests that mixing crushed shells into the sand can ease some of that strain. The practice has long been part of how some Indigenous communities care for clam beds.

Young clams in acidified seawater showed substantial changes in gene activity.

When researchers added crushed shells to their sand, those changes largely disappeared, and their gene activity looked much like that of clams in regular seawater.

Hannah Kempf led the study as a doctoral student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at the University of California, Davis. Her team raised the clams in buckets at Bodega Marine Laboratory for 90 days.

The ocean’s surface has become about 30% more acidic since the industrial era began.

As seawater absorbs carbon dioxide released by people, it loses some of the chemical building blocks that animals need to make shells.

That means clams, oysters and mussels must spend more energy building their shells. Acidic water can also dissolve them.

In the early 2000s, coastal acidification contributed to widespread losses at Pacific Northwest oyster hatcheries.

Scientists and hatchery workers tested ways to help, including adding soda ash to tanks holding oyster larvae.

Burrowing clams face the problem beneath the sand.

Pacific littleneck clams live about two to six inches (five to 15 centimeters) below the surface, where water between the sand grains, called pore water, is usually more acidic than the seawater above.

Along North America’s Northwest coast, some Indigenous communities have long cared for beaches as clam gardens.

That care can include mixing crushed shells, known as shell hash, into the sediment.

These gardens reflect traditional ecological knowledge built through generations of tending coastal habitats.

Near Bodega Bay, about 60 miles (97 kilometers) north of San Francisco, archaeological sites show that Coast Miwok communities managed clam beds.

Coast Miwok clam gardening ended in the 1930s under a federal policy based on the belief that harvesting would reduce clam numbers.

The restrictions instead led to smaller clam populations across the region, with clams nearly disappearing from some places.

The experiment began with 19 adult Pacific littleneck clams from Bodega Harbor.

They spawned overnight in the lab, and their offspring grew for 200 days before the test began.

Researchers divided the young clams between regular seawater and water made more acidic by adding carbon dioxide.

Within each water treatment, some clams lived in plain sand and others lived in sand mixed with crushed shells.

The team broke the shells with a mortar and pestle. Shell pieces made up 10% of the sand mixture by weight.

The acidified seawater averaged a pH of 7.3, compared with 7.8 in regular seawater. A lower pH means more acidic water.

Each week, researchers collected pore water from about three inches (eight centimeters) below the sand’s surface. In plain sand beneath regular seawater, this water became more acidic as the experiment continued.

Adding crushed shells helped keep the pore water’s acidity steadier. It also left that water less acidic than pore water in plain sand under the same seawater conditions.

The team also calculated how favorable the water was for forming aragonite, a mineral that clams use to build their shells.

Under acidified seawater, this measure stayed below 0.5 for most of the experiment in plain sand, while crushed shells kept it close to one.

Before the experiment, the clams spent a day in a dye that marked their shell edges and glowed under a special microscope.

At the end, researchers measured how much shell had grown beyond that line in 130 clams.

In acidified seawater, clams in plain sand added new shell equal to 4.7% of their length. Those living with crushed shells added 6.4%.

Under regular seawater, the two groups grew by similar amounts: 7.7% in plain sand and 7.9% with crushed shells.

Clams generally grew less in acidified water. Although those living with crushed shells showed greater growth, the difference was not statistically significant.

The genetic results revealed a clearer pattern than the growth measurements.

The team examined tissue from 24 clams and found 284 genes whose activity was at least four times higher or lower in one group than in another.

Clams raised in acidified water over plain sand had gene activity that stood apart from every other group.

Among the other three groups, no more than 11 of those 284 genes differed between any two of them.

So the clams living in acidified water over crushed shells had gene activity much like that of clams in regular seawater.

Researchers couldn’t match most of the 284 genes to a known job.

One that they could match resembles a gene for a protein that helps some mollusks control shell formation, and earlier research found that oysters need that protein to grow proper shells in acidified seawater.

The experiment used only two buckets for each condition, making differences harder to detect. The clams also began at different sizes, which the analysis did not account for.

The buckets contained clean quartz sand. Real beaches have microbes, mixed sediments and changing tides, and field studies have produced mixed results.

On a mudflat in the northeastern United States, an earlier study found that a shell-mineral reading around 0.4 killed many young hard clams. Adding crushed shells tripled their survival over 30 days.

But on a mudflat in New Brunswick, Canada, crushed shells raised the pH only slightly, and the effect disappeared after two months. The authors suggested that the approach may work best in small, local patches of habitat.

Study co-author Tsim Schneider, an associate professor of anthropology at UC Santa Cruz, described how this research could support communities.

“If there’s a history of adding shell hash to clam beds in California, for example, western science might be able to better support communities interested in reawakening dormant cultural knowledge and coastal stewardship practices,” said Schneider.

The team did not test the thin surface layer of sand where baby clams first settle.

The authors called for field studies of clam bed tending, designed for individual sites in partnership with Indigenous communities.

The study is published in the journal Biogeosciences.

#6422. How brain implants turn thoughts into speech

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Casey Harrell, here at home in the summer of 2026, uses a brain-computer interface to communicate with his family.

Regents of the University of California, Davis

Casey Harrell lost his voice to ALS or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. As a volunteer in a clinical trial, he’s helping scientists test a brain-computer interface. Electrode arrays that are implanted in Casey’s brain send signals to nearby computers, where those signals are translated into words he intended to say.

Casey uses this system every day to talk with his wife, daughter, friends and work colleagues. The moment he realized that it worked was “pure joy,” Casey says. Even though the researchers scripted his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”

This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me follows Casey and the fast-moving neuroscience that enables him to speak.

Patients paralyzed from the neck down can manipulate robotic arms with their thoughts. The woman in this video is controlling a robot with her mind. The so-called BrainGate system relies on a sensor of electrodes implanted in the motor cortex of the brain. Researchers hope by implanting electrodes in the brain it can read the brain signals meant to move the muscles involved in speaking, and translate the person’s intention to speak into comprehensive speech produced by a computer.

Laura Sanders: Controlling things with your mind. It sounds like science fiction, but it’s definitely real. Today, we’re going to explore what it’s like to communicate with a brain implant that decodes your thoughts and turns them into words.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? The voice is absolutely an integral part of your identity. Hello? That added layer of it being you. Do you want to talk? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: From Science News, I’m Laura Sanders, and this is The Deep End, Talk to Me. Okay, so what is BrainGate? It’s an experimental system that connects electrodes that are implanted in a person’s brain to a nearby computer. It’s called a brain-computer interface, or BCI. The goal here is big: to help people with paralysis or brain injuries or missing limbs regain control over their world.

Leigh Hochberg: BrainGate clinical trials have now been going on for nearly 22 years. It’s 21 point something at the moment.

Sanders: Leigh Hochberg is the director of the BrainGate Consortium and Clinical Trials. He also has a job at Massachusetts General Hospital, Brown University and the VA.

Hochberg: People who may have had a brainstem stroke and suddenly lost the ability both to move and to speak, or for somebody with ALS who is progressively losing the ability to move or to speak, there’s long been a hope that particularly implantable brain-computer interfaces could restore communication and could restore mobility.

Sanders: In 2004, a BrainGate device was implanted into a person’s brain for the very first time. That person was a man named Matthew Nagle, and he had been paralyzed in an accident. With BrainGate, he could control a computer cursor with his thoughts. Here’s a 2008 report from IT World.

Technology gave him hope. He was one of four testing BrainGate, a new technology where a chip is implanted in the brain that picks up electrical impulses. A computer then interprets those impulses as actions.

Hochberg: Those early studies have been really encouraging, and I think speaks to the potential for the field.

Sanders: Over the years, there’s been amazing examples of people using BrainGate. People have used it to click around on the internet, play video games, one woman who was paralyzed was even able to drink a cinnamon latte with a robotic arm.

Hochberg: And she was able to think about using her own arm and reach out with a robotic arm and pick up that thermos and bring it to her mouth, and tip it towards her mouth, and then put the straw in her mouth and then to take that sip. And while it wasn’t the first time in nearly 15 years that she had had something to drink, it was the first time that she was really able to do so solely of her own volition. I remember the smile on her face when she did that.

Sanders: Over the decades, BrainGate has had a lot of research success in a lot of ways. But what about talking? Hochberg says that when it comes to decoding speech, the science here is still very, very young.

Hochberg: We are at early days, just to be super clear. This is the very beginning of this field. There are only a small handful of people in the world who have had any type of implantable BCI that has been decoding speech.

Sanders: Where does the science stand when it comes to decoding the intention to talk? In the past few episodes, we’ve heard the stories of people who have lost their ability to speak. One of those people was Casey Harrell, and Casey also happens to have a BrainGate device implanted in his brain.

Casey Harrell: My name is Casey Harrell and I am 47 years old.

Sanders: Casey wakes up in the morning, and plugs in.

Casey: The first thing I will usually do after getting out of bed is to plug into the Matrix, so to speak.

Sanders: By that, he means attaching two wires to two pedestals that come out of the top of his head. These two black wires then snake down to nearby computers. Collectively, these electrodes in Casey’s brain, wires from his head, and computers are called the BrainGate 2 neural interface system. So Casey gets it all fired up and then he’s off.

Casey: Unless I have a medical appointment or something that will move me out of the house, I will sit in this position for most of the day, with specifically small breaks in between.

Sanders: All the while, Casey is generating brain signals as he thinks about saying words. These are small, precise electrical pulses made by Casey’s neurons, specifically the cells in his speech motor cortex. Remember how we learned there are over 100 muscles that are involved in speech? These are the parts of the brain that control those muscles.

Casey: I am using a decoder for about ten to 14 hours a day, seven days a week, for the past almost two years, making me the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.

Sanders: Like Jules, Casey has ALS. The disease has slowly taken away his ability to move and to talk.

Casey: I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020. Then it became a slow motion car crash of multiple years before almost no one would be able to understand me.

By the time of my surgery, only my assistant and my wife, Levana, could really understand me fully. A few other friends who were around often would be able to understand some of what I was saying. I relied upon my assistant and my wife to basically serve as my translators to other people. I did not go anywhere, even a video call without them, either one or both.

Sanders: In July of 2023, Casey volunteered for a clinical trial called BrainGate 2. A UC Davis neurosurgeon put four small electrical arrays onto the left side of Casey’s brain. I wanted to know more about how these arrays worked, so I talked to the neurosurgeon who put Casey’s devices into his brain.

David Brandman: My name is David Brandman, and I am the co-director of the UC Davis neuroprosthetics lab, developing next-generation neurotechnology to help people with paralysis. A brain-computer interface is a device that records brain signals from people that are paralyzed and then translates those brain signals to allow people to control objects in their environment using their minds.

Sanders: Casey’s implant is made of four arrays. Each of them are square and they’re about as wide as a peppercorn. Each array has a bunch of pointy ends that go down into his brain. They look a little like those metal cat brushes. Altogether, the four arrays contain 256 electrodes. These electrodes are all listening to Casey’s brain activity when he thinks about saying a word.

Brandman: The way this device works is by recording the electrical activity of the brain as he tries to speak.

Sanders: The wires from Casey’s head carry those neural signals to nearby computers. That’s where machine learning algorithms attempt to do a very complex sort of matching. The algorithms match Casey’s brain activity patterns to the patterns that predictably occur with certain sounds called phonemes.

Brandman: We translate his brain signals into one of 39 different English phonemes. Now, a phoneme is a building block of language. So if I say the word hello, the word hello can be broken down into ha, uh, uhl, and oh. Hello.Sanders: Next up, those algorithms assembles these phonemes into words by making its best guess about what Casey wants to say.

Brandman: So I translate this brain activity into a phoneme and then, using artificial intelligence, turn phonemes into words, words into sentences, and sentences into paragraphs.Sanders: So that’s the process, and it allows Casey to type messages on Slack, text his friends, and send emails. Brandman: Using this prosthesis, he’s in the ballpark of 50 words per minute. Now, as I’m speaking to you right now, I’m speaking on the order of 120 to 150 words per minute, depending on how excited I am, right? So we’ve got him back to about a third of how quickly he spoke as an able-bodied person.

Sanders: I had emailed Casey some questions a few days before our talk. But he didn’t answer them by email. Sanders: My interview with Casey was unlike any I’ve ever had. I’m used to being flexible for interviews. There’s time zone problems, language barriers, mathematicians who sometimes answer my questions in symbols and formulas. I’d ask Casey a question and then another one before he had a chance to answer. I accidentally interrupted him a few times. Casey: It is hard for people in your position to stay focused because you were not used to the cadence of a conversation this slowly.

Sanders: He’s right. I was not used to it. And timing, in conversations and in life, is everything. Here’s Greg Bryant of UCLA.

Bryant: Turns, conversational turns, happen at the level of hundreds of milliseconds at the longest. Two hundred milliseconds is a long turn. That’s a fifth of a second. I mean, that’s really fast. So if you are slow at all, it’s noticeable. We have to coordinate our talk so our terms make sense. I can’t take too long or be too quick to respond to your questions. I have to know when to stop and start. We get into this flow, kind of a dynamic, and that is hugely consequential for how we feel about the conversation, the other person, ourselves. MA: And in his brain, you know, you can imagine he’s doing all these mental gymnastics, to, right now, he’s listening to us. Jules: It is a challenge to communicate with people who don’t interact with me on a daily basis. I have a major bottleneck from my thoughts to actually speaking.

Casey: It is incredibly undignified and a terrible consequence of the health care system to treat me like this very quickly.

Sanders: At this point in the testing, Casey was asked to say some pre-specified sentences so researchers could test their system out.

Casey: Most of the sentences were what we called closed loops.

Sanders: That means that the researchers already knew what brain activity patterns should go with the words Casey thought about saying. It was a test to see if the system was working.

Casey: The decoder would be able to verify whether I was right or wrong, giving me short preloaded sentences to say. I was asked to say, “What good is that?”

Sanders: “What good is that?” is not the most poignant sentence ever uttered, but it had a big effect both in the room and for researchers joining remotely by video.Casey: “What good is that?” Everyone is crying after I am successful.

Hochberg: On the second session, came back and gave him the full 125,000 plus word English dictionary to be able to select from. And the first thing that he said was something along the lines of, “Is this thing on?” Kind of a funny statement.

The next thing that he said on the second day of using brain-computer interface, or the second thing that we decoded was, “I’m looking for a cheetah.” And it’s the second day. We know there’s all kinds of opportunities for decoding errors. And when I saw that, I said, you know, there’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using an implanted brain-computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah. You know, that’s obviously a decoding error and that’s fine.

Sanders: Hochberg could see Casey on the screen, but he couldn’t see something really important that had just happened in the room.

Hochberg: His four-year-old daughter had just walked into the room dressed as a cheetah.

Sanders: Here’s Casey remembering the same moment.

Casey: Yes, I remember this time very well. It was the second session of talking that I experienced early in August 2024. My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit. This was one of her favorite animals. They were going through a phase where everything they did was super fast, running from thing to thing. Everyone was thinking that it must have been a mistake that I could not use this language. It was so random. This was only from the people like Leigh who were not in the room with us. The researchers who were there could validate that, yes, I said this. I meant it because of the unique context.

Sanders: It’s one of those moments that many parents have. A kid does something cute, a parent plays along. But in this moment for Casey and his child, it was anything but ordinary.

Hochberg: And she was born around the time that he was diagnosed with ALS. And one could imagine that because the voice that was coming out of the computer was a version of his own voice, and then the rest of the interaction was between dad and daughter. And it was between parent and child.

Sanders: The BCI had given Casey something priceless, a minute to play with his sweet little cheetah.

Casey: I was quietly confident that it would work the way it ended up working for me. I had done a lot of research and the thing was that the technology was on the cusp of a breakthrough. And why not me? I asked myself.

Sanders: Early on in the research project, Casey and his wife had been told not to expect it to work. This was an experiment and the outcome was far from certain. Casey, however, was optimistic.

Hochberg: So to me, seeing it work that quickly and that powerfully really, really emphasized that these are technologies that are going to be able to restore not only activities of daily living, not only key kind of instrumental activities of daily living, but they’re going to restore communication between parent and child. They’re going to restore communication between friends and family and care partners and health care providers.

Sanders: Because this is a podcast about the human voice, I’ve been asking people I interview what their voice means to them. Here’s Casey’s answer.

Casey: It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: Getting it back, even in a limited form, is everything.Casey: It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond, respond to my daughter, especially because that was lacking completely from my life up to that point.Sanders: Casey’s restored voice changed his life.

Casey: It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends. Timing is everything, and that is why having nothing, this is completely revolutionary. And to look back on my previous answer, it is something that really can still improve.

Sanders: At the beginning of the experiment, the research team had told Casey and his wife that they’d be able to try using the BCI for casual chats just a few hours a week. Those hours felt like a huge gift at the time, considering that they hadn’t been able to talk meaningfully for a long time. Here’s Brandman.

Brandman: As we kept coming to his house two or three times a week, things kept getting better and better. And it got to a point where Casey wanted to use the system to say all the things that he wanted to say.Sanders: Early on, only the researchers could set Casey up with the system, plugging him into the Matrix, as he puts it.Brandman: And so our research technologist would start coming to his house three, four, five times a week to don and doff the system to enable him to communicate so that he could go about his day. And so at a certain point, we saw, well, he really wants to use the system. Can we streamline this for him? And so we petitioned the FDA to actually allow us to change the clinical trial protocol slightly so that we could train his care partners to don and doff the system without us being there. And so since then, he’s been a near daily user of the system.

Sanders: That’s a far cry from a few hours a week. I’m going to read you some numbers from a research paper Brandman and his colleagues published about Casey’s BCI in Nature Neuroscience in June of 2026.“Over nearly two years, the participant, that’s Casey, used the BCI for more than 3,800 hours at home with no researchers present to maintain rich, interpersonal communication with his family and friends, independently control his personal computer, and sustain full-time employment, despite being paralyzed. He communicated 183,060 sentences, totaling 1,960,163 words, at an average rate of 56 words per minute. He labeled 92 percent of sentences as being decoded at least mostly correctly.”

Those numbers in this very bare-bones science kind of way are dry, if we’re being honest. But when you stop to think about it, each sentence, each of those nearly two million words, is a tether that connects Casey to his life. They’re messages to his daughter, jokes with his partner, texts to his friends. They’re games of Wordle with his wife and kid. Here’s Casey and his family in a video shot by UC Davis Health.

Okay, so no A, but we got an E. M-I. O. M-I. Good job, team. We are almost there.

Sanders: We’ve talked a lot about words here and the fundamental ways that Casey’s BCI has restored his ability to say them. But Casey’s BCI goes a little bit farther than that. It gives him the ability to add some extras. He’s got some bells and whistles up his sleeve.Casey: It is really a communication device, first and foremost, and less of a tool that I use to make funny remarks. But I do have that as well in my repertoire. For example, I have the ability to add sound effects to what I am saying.

Sanders: For instance, Casey has a sad trombone sound.

Casey: So if I find something funny and want to say, LOL, the theme from the TV show, Seinfeld, will play.

[theme song]Sanders: This is what he means. These jokes make me think of Jules, which made me wonder if Casey, like Jules, could also swear with his system.

Casey: To answer your question of whether I can curse with this device, I most certainly [beep] can.

Sanders: So for all your inquiring minds, there you have it. Looking ahead a bit, there’s a lot happening on the horizon. The science here is moving fast and many companies are working on similar systems. We’re going to cover that in a few episodes. But for now, Casey is alone. He is an N of 1, as the scientists say – the only person using a brain-computer interface for communication this heavily.

Casey: I hope to have this changed very soon because I feel like everyone who wants this should have the opportunity to have it, especially those who are with my disease.

Sanders: Hochberg tells me that this drive to help others is common among people who volunteer for these sorts of clinical trials.

Hochberg: Each participant in the trial has been just so generous and so clear that they recognize that it’s early days in the research, but they’ve told us that they want to help other people with paralysis. They want to be able to allow people with brainstem stroke or cervical spinal cord injury or ALS or other paralyzing illnesses or injuries to have improved function, to be able to regain control over that computer or regain the fluent speech and communication that they had previously. So it’s that generosity of spirit that has really defined the participants in our BrainGate studies.

Sanders: Casey’s generosity, his drive to help other people, really shines through as we talk. But I want to get back to him. I ask Casey what it’s been like to have this technology in his home, in his brain. He tells me how precious our voices are, and how easy it is for many of us to forget that.Casey: We take them for granted. The ability to scream when you are running and want to get out some stress. The ability to say sweet nothings into your partner’s ear. These are the things that life is all about. And when you are robbed of those times, you want them back at all costs. And this is why this is good enough for now, and we should have accelerated approval for devices like this.

Sanders: Casey’s BCI is slow compared to the pace of a normal conversation. And it gets things wrong occasionally.Casey: Sorry, I am trying to answer you. And it is changing what I want to say. And I am being stubborn instead of trying to say it another way, which I will do now.[Sanders audio] I’m not in any rush. You take as much stubborn time as you want.

Sanders: And it needs an internet connection and power. And let’s not forget that Casey has an adapter coming out of the top of his head. But these are solvable problems, one that scientists are actively working on. So not perfect, but as Casey puts it, good enough for now.

Scientific efforts to restore voices have been transformative for Jules, Casey, and others. But the ability to separate a voice from a body also raises new possibilities for our societies and for our lives.

MA: His voice will live on in whatever videos or things we’ve captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally, and that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: On the next episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into a strange new digital world where voices might not be what they seem.

Hany Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time. And somehow those are coexisting.

Sanders: What changes are coming in a world where voices can be so easily cloned?Farid: Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

#6421. A Mysterious Statue Emerged on Easter Island. More Could Be Hiding Right Beneath It.

Three years after the discovery, archaeologists still can’t say how old it is—or whether there are more.

In February 2023, a moai was found lying face-up among reeds in a dried lakebed on Rapa Nui, also known as Easter Island. The roughly five-foot statue was small by the island’s standards, but its location surprised archaeologists. It was the first moai reported in the lakebed inside Rano Raraku, the volcanic crater where islanders carved many of their statues.

“The statue was a completed one meant for an ahu platform,” Terry Hunt, an archaeologist and professor of anthropology at the University of Arizona, tells Popular Mechanics. An ahu is a ceremonial platform where moai are displayed. Hunt says this one was carved from the bedrock on the nearby crater walls, then brought to the place where it was discovered.

As reported in our earlier coverage, Hunt described the surprise to Good Morning America. “There have been no moai found in the dry bed or in what was previously a lake, so this is a first.”

The location wasn’t the only surprise. The statue’s small size led Hunt to suggest, in a 2023 University of Arizona account, that it was probably carved early in the period between Polynesian settlement around 1200 and European arrival in 1722—small moai could have been made later, he allowed, but the largest ones likely came after those first years. That possibility is what gives the find its weight: if other early, small statues lie beneath the lakebed, archaeologists could compare them with later moai and trace how the island’s carvers progressed from modest figures to giants. Yet more than three years after the discovery, no one knows how old this moai is or whether it has company. Hunt says there’s been no further investigation.

The small statue could tell a bigger story

In 2023, Hunt was considering ground-penetrating radar to look for buried moai or architecture, particularly in the lakebed. Today, he’s more confident about finding statues buried in quarry rubble than beneath the lakebed. “There are almost certainly statues buried in the rubble and back dirt from quarrying activities in Rano Raraku,” he says. “Perhaps there are others buried in the lakebed sediments.”

A group of statues beneath the lakebed would give researchers more than another addition to the inventory. If they turned out to be early, their appearance and locations could offer clues to how the islanders carved moai and what they were doing around the lake. “Buried statues could be associated with new radiocarbon dates and give us a better idea of the early quarrying activities,” Hunt says. He adds that the statues could reveal stylistic differences that developed over time.

The dates have changed the argument before

Hunt and his colleagues have already shown how much a date can change the story of Rapa Nui. Their research challenged the claim that islanders stopped building monuments after their society collapsed, before Europeans ever arrived.

A 2020 study in the Journal of Archaeological Science examined the chronology of ahu construction at eleven sites. The researchers pieced together radiocarbon dates and evidence from the platforms themselves, alongside accounts from European visitors. They found that islanders kept building and using the monuments for at least 150 years after 1600, when their society was supposedly already in collapse.

The 2020 research changed the account of how long monument-building continued. Early lakebed statues could help fill in the other end of that history, showing what people were carving as the tradition developed.

Finding those statues and studying them are two different problems. “However, excavations in the quarry would be highly unlikely given conservation issues and the islanders’ sentiments about the site,” Hunt says. A geophysical survey could map buried moai without disturbing the ground, but it can’t date them or reveal the carving details that would show how the tradition developed. For that, archaeologists would need to see the stone itself. Conservation pressures cut the other way, too: the Easter Island Statue Project’s discovery report called for stabilizing the newfound moai and protecting its fragile surface, and Hunt notes the soft volcanic tuff continues to erode. The result is a strange bind. A survey could show exactly where Rapa Nui's early history lies, while the most revealing evidence stays underground.
