#6420. Nearly one million hospital stays reveal a surprising pattern in patient survival

Patients treated by female doctors had lower death rates in a study of nearly one million hospital stays, with the greatest difference among female patients.

When you need hospital care, you usually don’t get to choose your doctor. Who looks after you often depends on the hospital’s rotating schedule.

A study of nearly a million hospital stays in Ontario found that patients were less likely to die within 30 days of admission when a woman led their care.

That finding shows a link, but it doesn’t prove that the doctor’s sex caused the difference.

Angela Jerath, a scientist at ICES, an independent health research institute in Ontario, led the study. She is also an associate professor of anesthesiology at the University of Toronto’s Temerty Faculty of Medicine.

“Past research has largely focused on surgical patients and the admitting physician only,” Jerath said.

“Our findings add to the growing body of research examining the relationship between physician sex and patient outcomes, broadening the evidence beyond surgical care to a wider range of medical conditions and other physicians.”

The researchers studied health records for 958,150 adults admitted to Ontario hospitals between 2008 and 2022. Each patient had one of seven common conditions.

These included heart attacks, heart failure, strokes, and pneumonia.

The team also included patients with bleeding in the digestive tract, a long-term lung disease that makes breathing difficult, or an irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation.

When patients or referring doctors choose a physician, that doctor’s patients may differ in ways medical records don’t capture.

Researchers call this referral bias, and Jerath said assigning hospital doctors through rotating schedules helps limit it.

Those schedules also mean that several doctors may care for one patient. A typical hospital stay for a medical illness lasts about five days, so a patient might see a male doctor one day and a female doctor the next.

The researchers accounted for these changes by measuring care in two ways. First, they identified each patient’s main doctor, meaning the physician responsible for the most days of their stay.

They also calculated how much of the hospital stay female doctors managed. This let them look beyond the doctor who first admitted the patient.

Of the 15,165 doctors in the study, about 36% were women. A woman served as the main doctor for 259,759 patients, a little more than a quarter of the total.

Before comparing deaths, the team adjusted for patients’ age, income, frailty, and other illnesses. They also accounted for doctors’ age, experience, and workload.

After those adjustments, an estimated 12.3% of patients whose main doctor was female died within 30 days. Among patients whose main doctor was male, the figure was 13.7%.

Each additional 10% of a hospital stay managed by female doctors was associated with about 7% lower odds of dying within 30 days.

Both measures pointed to the same result, which the authors listed as a strength of the study.

The lower death rate appeared in six of the seven illnesses, in teaching and community hospitals, and among patients of both family doctors and specialists. Patients of female doctors were also slightly less likely to return to the hospital within 30 days.

Earlier US research involving older Medicare patients found a similar pattern. That included a 2017 study of patients treated by hospital internists, doctors who specialize in medical care for adults.

The difference was larger among female patients. Their 30-day death rate was about 1.3 percentage points lower when a woman was their main doctor, compared with about 0.75 percentage points among male patients.

Female patients treated by female doctors had the lowest 30-day death rate of any patient-doctor pairing in the study.

A 2024 US study of Medicare patients also found a larger benefit for women treated by female doctors. The Ontario researchers said their finding raises a question for future research, rather than explaining why this happens.

Patients with female main doctors continued to have lower odds of dying over longer periods, but the gap narrowed. Their odds of death were about 12% lower at 30 days, 8% lower at 90 days, and 4% lower at one year.

The pattern for hospital readmissions changed too. By 90 days, patients of male and female main doctors had returned to the hospital at similar rates.

By one year, patients of female doctors were slightly more likely to have been readmitted. Their initial hospital stays also lasted about 5% longer.

Atrial fibrillation was the exception to the early survival finding. For patients with that condition, neither measure showed a link between the doctor’s sex and deaths within 30 days.

The study couldn’t tell the researchers why patients of female doctors had better survival rates. Medical records don’t reveal how much time a doctor spent at the bedside or what the doctor and patient discussed.

Earlier research cited by the authors offers some possible explanations. Female doctors may spend more time with patients, involve them more in decisions, and show more empathy.

They may also order appropriate tests and prescribe treatments that follow clinical guidelines more often.

Some studies suggest that female doctors take a more cautious approach to treatment and seek advice from colleagues more frequently.

“The goal is not to favor one group of physicians over another but to identify practices and behaviors that may help improve care across the health system,” Jerath said.

The researchers used the sex doctors reported when registering to practice, which doesn’t capture gender.

They had no information about ethnicity or disability, or about how trainees and other team members contributed to care.

The female doctors were generally younger, had less experience, and treated fewer patients each year than the male doctors. Their patients were slightly older and frailer.

The team adjusted for those differences, but medical records can only tell part of the story. Factors the researchers couldn’t measure might still explain some of the gap.

They also couldn’t account for handoffs between doctors, differences in how doctors practiced, or expectations about workload and pay.

The study covered people admitted to hospitals, so its findings don’t apply to patients treated in clinics.

The researchers called for closer examination of how doctors deliver care, including their decisions about tests, treatments, and communication with patients.

They also recommended studying hospitals in other countries to see whether the same pattern holds.

Understanding what drives these differences could help improve hospital care for everyone.

The study is published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

People who had no recollection of a lucid dream over the past three years developed the skill after one month of performing a novel training regimen twice a week, neuroscientists report.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming — in which the dreamer is aware that they are dreaming and can sometimes influence the dream's trajectory — is a skill that can be honed, a new study finds. And the researchers found that doing this is surprisingly easy, after training participants to do exactly that using virtual reality (VR) twice a week for just one month.

The study's results could have practical benefits, said Daniel Morris, a cognitive neuroscientist at Northwestern University who studies dreams and was not involved with the work. "Lucid dreaming can benefit people with nightmares by allowing them to transform their nightmares into positive dreams and feel greater agency in their dreams," Morris told Live Science in an email.

Before this study, published Sept. 28 in the journal Frontiers in Psychology, neuroscientists tried to induce lucid dreaming with various methods. These included meditation exercises and so-called reality checks, in which participants ask themselves while awake whether unusual phenomena they encounter — such as people wearing odd Halloween costumes — are real or if they're dreaming. The idea is that they will ask themselves the same question in their sleep during bizarre dreams.

However, "for most people, our day-to-day lives may not feel 'dream-like,'" Morris said, explaining why reality checks have had mixed results and don't reliably trigger lucid dreaming.

Since dream-like scenarios are rare in waking life, the neuroscientists behind the new study used VR simulations of bizarre situations to complement reality-check exercises.

The team, based at the University of Trento in Italy, recruited university students and asked them to meditate and then perform the VR training. The meditation was intended to increase students' awareness of what they were thinking about in a given moment. Each time they encountered bizarre happenings in the VR environment, such as objects or people violating laws of physics or rapid switches from one scene to another, they performed reality checks.

After the training, participants went home and were asked to keep a dream diary that they wrote in every morning. They also filled out daily questionnaires, citing the number of dreams they recalled and how many they remembered being lucid.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The participants experienced lucid dreams four times more often than participants did in a second group that did reality checks without performing any meditation or VR training. The study also included another comparison group, in which participants carried out reality checks during realistic rather than dream-like VR simulations; these participants were over eight times less likely to report lucid dreams. This latter comparison ensured that the results were not caused solely by the use of VR, the researchers said.

When participants encountered something strange, like branches covering a door, they actively asked themselves whether it was real.

It was particularly surprising to find that such little training with the dream-like VR simulations was needed to develop lucid dreaming as a skill, said study co-author Nicola De Pisapia, a neuroscientist at the University of Trento. His team ran the experiment for only a month because any longer would have been too demanding for the participants, De Pisapia noted.

Study co-author Andrea Signorelli, a doctoral student in De Pisapia's lab, thinks the VR intervention is at the heart of why the approach worked. People often don't realize that they're dreaming because the dreams "fool" your senses and feel realistic in the moment, he explained.

"Virtual reality is the technology to fool you on stereoscopic vision and auditory information," he said. The term "stereoscopic" refers to techniques that create 3D illusions from 2D images by mimicking how human eyes see.

"It's basically the most immersive technology that we have at the moment," making it a good intervention for reality check exercises, Signorelli said.

The team also compared the number of lucid dreams participants reported against their total number of recalled dreams, which revealed an interesting pattern. On average, participants in each group recalled more dreams after starting the experiment than they did beforehand. However, the dream-simulating VR group recalled the fewest dreams overall after entering the experiment, even though they had the highest number of lucid dreams.

Signorelli speculated that perhaps it takes a lot of energy to have lucid dreams, which could divert resources away from recalling other dreams. Morris argued that, alternatively, participants in the lucid-dream VR group "may have been less motivated to report non-lucid dreams than the control groups." So there may have been some bias in the reporting.

The study had some limitations, such as its small sample size of 38 participants. Plus, neither of the two control groups were asked to meditate, so it is impossible to say whether the meditations or the dreamlike VR sessions had more influence over lucid dreaming in the test group.

The team is now doing a follow-up study in which the meditation part has been removed, Signorelli said, to reveal whether the VR dream scenarios are the critical factor, as suspected.

Signorelli said that he would like to see lucid-dream training tailored for each individual. For example, the VR simulations could be personalized to simulate a recurrent nightmare that a given person experiences, training them to recognize triggers specific to that dream, he said.

"Other future research could explore the potential therapeutic benefits of this intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety, or PTSD [post-traumatic stress disorder]," Morris suggested.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6418. Satellites reveal hidden flooding along the North Carolina coast

Scientists combined satellite data to create detailed daily flood maps of North Carolina wetlands, revealing hidden flooding that could influence methane emissions.

Flooding along the North Carolina coast doesn’t always look dramatic. There may be no raging rivers or streets swallowed by water.

Sometimes, the difference between dry land and a flooded landscape is just a few inches.

The Albemarle-Pamlico Peninsula just sits there, nearly flat, less than a meter above sea level across almost half its surface, buffered from the Atlantic by a thin chain of barrier islands.

The soils are organic muck. The forests are part hardwood swamp, part moss.

More than 70 percent of the land spends some portion of the year underwater – and has done so long before anyone started worrying about sea-level rise.

It is also, for exactly these reasons, one of the harder places on earth to watch from space. A team at North Carolina State University spent five years trying.

They used a method that fuses radar and optical satellite data into daily flood probability maps at six-meter resolution. That’s fine-grained enough to catch the small, short-lived inundation events that standard products miss entirely.

Wetlands are the planet’s largest natural methane source.

How much methane a wetland releases depends partly on how long and how deeply it floods.

Waterlogged soils contain less oxygen, creating conditions that allow methane-producing microbes to thrive. Brief and small floods matter too.

And yet current global estimates of inundated area carry enough uncertainty to account for roughly a third of what we don’t understand about atmospheric methane.

Most of that uncertainty comes from wetlands smaller than 1,000 square meters. These wetlands are flooding and draining faster than satellites with 30-meter pixels and 16-day revisit cycles can follow.

The study compared three sensors before combining them. Sentinel-2, the European Space Agency’s optical satellite, achieved 93.9 percent accuracy classifying dry land, inundated vegetation, and open water.

PlanetScope, the commercial CubeSat constellation operated by Planet Labs, reached 88.4 percent and resolved fine-scale open-water features particularly well.

Sentinel-1, which uses radar to observe Earth’s surface, achieved 84.6 percent accuracy. Unlike optical satellites, it can collect observations through clouds.

These limitations make it difficult to monitor flooding consistently throughout the year. Persistent cloud cover can block optical satellite observations for weeks at a time.

PlanetScope lacks the shortwave infrared band that most reliably separates water from waterlogged vegetation. Stack those limitations and a single-sensor flood record has systematic gaps.

The team chose to classify each sensor independently and then combine the results, rather than training a joint model from scratch.

The logic was practical: with limited training data, a combined model risks learning the quirks of the training set rather than the actual landscape.

Keeping the sensors separate preserves what each does best – Sentinel-2’s infrared sensitivity, Sentinel-1’s backscatter ratios, and PlanetScope’s spatial density. Using them together handles the disagreements.

To combine the observations, the researchers used a statistical technique called fixed-rank kriging. The method analyzes how flooding changes across both space and time.

Instead of simply averaging the satellite measurements, it accounts for differences in their reliability. This allows scientists to estimate where flooding is likely to occur, even when direct observations are missing.

The result is a five-year record of daily flood probability maps at six-meter resolution, complete with estimates of uncertainty.

The maps were validated against water-table measurements from two AmeriFlux flux towers, a USGS stream gauge, and lake-elevation records. They caught short flood pulses that no individual sensor detected.

The peninsula includes the Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge and one of the East Coast’s largest pocosin complexes.

It’s threaded with drainage ditches and canals dug over centuries for agriculture and forestry, now interacting in unpredictable ways with rising groundwater and Atlantic storm surge.

The microtopography alone makes inundation complex. Tree bases sit on hummocks above the waterline while the surrounding ground stays permanently saturated. No single satellite pass, on any given day, can fully capture that.

That complexity is increasingly normal for low-lying coastal wetlands globally. The framework here is modular and sensor-agnostic.

New data streams can be added as they become available. They might include the forthcoming L-band radar satellites.

These should be able to detect flooding beneath the tree canopy that current instruments can’t reliably penetrate.

The immediate use is methane and carbon modeling.

Inundation probability can be fed directly into biogeochemical models rather than handing them a single deterministic map and pretending the uncertainty doesn’t exist.

The longer ambition is a continuous, high-resolution record of the brief floods that rarely make headlines but matter enormously. They drive greenhouse-gas exchange, support migratory wildlife, and recharge aquifers.

They also signal early-stage hydrological change – the kind that sea-level rise is forcing across the coastal zone faster than most monitoring systems can follow.

The study is published in the Journal of Remote Sensing.
